2a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: for three days before gentile festivals, business, loans, and debt dealings with gentiles are prohibited.
Rabbi Yehuda permits collecting debts from gentiles, because the repayment distresses them.
The Rabbis object: after repaying, the gentile is happy, so he may thank his idol on the festival.
Rav and Shmuel disagree about whether the Mishnah's word is spelled with an alef or an ayin.
Both spellings are considered correct, and each teacher is supported by a scriptural source.
Deuteronomy 32:35 uses the alef spelling, referring to the day of their calamity.
The teacher of the ayin spelling is likewise not mistaken.
Isaiah 43:9 uses the ayin spelling, for witnesses who will justify the nations.
Why did the alef teacher not also use the ayin spelling?
A term referring to calamity is preferable.
Why did the ayin teacher not also use the alef spelling?
The idols' testimony against themselves is what brings the calamity, so testimony terminology is preferable.
Isaiah 43:9 seems to refer to Jews, not to the nations, so how can it be read about gentiles?
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: Jewish mitzvot testify for them, and the nations later admit their righteousness.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua gives another basis for the ayin reading.
Isaiah 44:9 shows that idols and their adornments will serve as witnesses against their worshippers.
Rabbi Chanina bar Papa, or Rabbi Simlai, teaches that God will bring a Torah scroll and reward its students in the future.
In the future, gentiles will gather together and come in a disorderly mass.
Isaiah 43:9 says all the nations are gathered together, supporting the gathering.
God tells the nations not to enter intermingled, but each nation should enter in its own turn.

2b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The nations gather as kingdoms, since the term for a nation means kingdom.
Genesis 25:23 uses the same term le'om for one kingdom versus another, supporting that meaning.
Is there really intermingling before God, so that each nation must be addressed separately?
The nations are separated so that they will not mix together and each can hear what is said to it.
The Roman Empire enters first before God.
Why does Rome enter first, and from where do we know it is the most important?
Daniel 7:23 describes the fourth empire devouring and treading down the earth.
Rabbi Yochanan identifies that devouring empire as Rome, whose fame spread across the world.
From where do we know that the more important one enters first?
Rav Chisda teaches that a king enters first for judgment, when king and community are judged together.
I Kings 8:59 speaks of judging the king's servant and the people of Israel, supporting that order.
What is the reason it is proper for the king to enter first?
Either it is improper for a king to wait outside, or he is judged first before God's anger grows.
God asks the Roman Empire what they occupied themselves with.
Rome replies that they built markets, bathhouses, and wealth, all for the sake of Israel's Torah study.
God rebukes Rome: all of it was for their own needs, and the silver and gold belong to God.
Haggai 2:8 says the silver and the gold are God's, supporting God's claim of ownership.
God challenges them: is there anyone among you who can declare this?
Isaiah 43:9 repeats the phrase who among you can declare this, supporting the challenge.
This refers to nothing other than the Torah.
Deuteronomy 4:44 says this is the Torah that Moses set before Israel.
The Roman Empire leaves disappointed, and the Persian Empire then comes forward.
Persia enters after Rome.
Why does Persia enter next, and from where do we know this?
Daniel 7:5 describes a second beast like a bear, which represents Persia.
Rav Yosef explains the bear imagery as referring to Persians who eat, shed hair, and never rest.
God asks the Persian Empire what they occupied themselves with.
Persia replies that they built bridges, conquered cities, and fought wars, all for Israel's Torah study.
God rebukes Persia: the bridges, cities, and wars were for their own gain, and God fought the wars.
Exodus 15:3 says the Lord is a man of war, supporting God's claim to the wars.
God again challenges them: is there anyone among you who can declare this?
Isaiah 43:9 repeats who among you can declare this, supporting the challenge.
This refers to nothing other than the Torah.
Deuteronomy 4:44 names the Torah that Moses set before Israel.
The Persian Empire leaves disappointed.
Once Persia sees Rome's claims are ineffective, why do they still come forward?
They think their claims will work better, since Cyrus encouraged the building of the Second Temple.
Why do the other nations come forward when Rome and Persia's claims failed?
They think Rome and Persia subjugated Israel, but they themselves never subjugated Israel.
What is the difference between the empires named in Scripture and those not singled out?
Rome and Persia's kingship lasts until the Messiah comes, so they were singled out.
The nations say to God: did You give us the Torah, and we did not accept it?
How can they claim the Torah was never offered to them?
Deuteronomy 33:2 and Habakkuk 3:3 describe God coming from Sinai, Seir, Paran, and Teman.
What did God require in Seir and in Paran, where the Torah was not given?
God offered the Torah to every nation and language, and only Israel accepted it.
The nations reformulate their claim: did we accept the Torah and then not keep it?
The Gemara notes that this refutes them: why did they not accept it in the first place?
The nations say that God overturned the mountain over them as a basin, as He did for Israel.
Exodus 19:17 says they stood at the nether part of the mountain.
Rav Dimi bar Chama teaches that God overturned Sinai over Israel like a basin.
God told Israel that if they accept the Torah it is good, and if not, their burial will be there.
God says to the nations that the first mitzvot will let them declare the truth.
Isaiah 43:9 says let the first things be declared to us, supporting this demand.
God asks where the seven Noahide mitzvot were kept, and how we know they were not kept.
Habakkuk 3:6 says God saw and made the nations tremble, supporting the explanation given by Rav Yosef.
God saw the seven mitzvot the descendants of Noah accepted, and saw that they did not keep them.
Since they did not keep them, God released them from the obligation.
If so, does a sinner profit from his transgression?
Mar son of Ravina begins a reply that continues on the next daf.

3a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Even when gentiles keep the Noahide laws, they do not receive a reward for doing so.
A baraita of Rabbi Meir says a gentile who studies Torah is like a High Priest, which suggests reward.
Leviticus 18:5 says the person who does them shall live, and the verse names no separate groups.
From the verse's general term, we learn that even a gentile who studies Torah is like a High Priest.
The verse teaches that gentiles do not receive reward like one who is commanded, but like one who is not commanded.
Rabbi Chanina teaches that one who is commanded and performs a mitzva is greater than one who is not commanded.
The nations ask God: Israel accepted the Torah, so where is the evidence they kept it?
God answers that He testifies that Israel kept the entire Torah.
The nations object that a father cannot testify about his son, as Israel is called God's firstborn son.
God replies that heaven and earth will testify that Israel kept the entire Torah.
The nations object that heaven and earth are interested parties, so their testimony is tainted.
Jeremiah 33:25 shows that heaven and earth are bound to God's covenant, supporting the nations' objection.
Resh Lakish offers an explanation of this matter.
Genesis 1:31 says there was evening and morning on the sixth day, which Resh Lakish reads as a condition.
God made a condition with Creation: if Israel accepts the Torah all is well, otherwise the world returns to chaos.
Hizkiyya's teaching is similar, on a different matter.
Psalm 76:9 says the earth feared and was silent after sentence was heard from heaven.
If the earth feared, why was it silent, and if it was silent, why did it fear?
The earth first feared, and afterward was silent, so heaven and earth are interested parties.
God tells the nations to bring witnesses from among themselves who will testify that Israel kept the Torah.
Nimrod, Laban, and Potiphar's wife are proposed as witnesses to the righteousness of Abraham, Jacob, and Joseph.
Nebuchadnezzar and Darius are proposed as witnesses for Hananiah, Mishael, Azariah, and Daniel.
Job's friends and Elihu are proposed as witnesses who will testify that Israel kept the entire Torah.
Isaiah 43:9 says the nations will bring their witnesses that they may be justified.
The nations ask God to give them the Torah now so they can fulfill it.
God rebukes them as fools: one must prepare on Shabbat eve to eat on Shabbat, and it is too late now.
God still offers an easy mitzva, the sukka, which they can perform now.
How can you say one can still perform a mitzva after this world, given Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's teaching?
Deuteronomy 7:11 says today is the time to do the mitzvot, not tomorrow, and today is not the time for reward.
God does not deal tyrannically with His creatures, but judges them fairly.
Why does God call the sukka mitzva an easy mitzva?
Because performing it involves no monetary loss.
Each gentile builds a sukka, and God heats the sun so they kick it and leave.
Psalm 2:3 has the nations say they will break their bands and cast off their cords.
Why does God heat the sun over them, if He does not deal tyrannically with His creatures?
This is not tyranny, because the Jews also sometimes face such trials.

3b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: In certain years the Tammuz heat lasts until Sukkot, making sitting in the sukka painful for gentiles.
If one who is pained in the sukka is exempt, why are gentiles criticized for leaving it?
Granted they may leave the sukka, but kicking it is still improper.
God sits and laughs at those gentiles immediately after they kick the sukka.
Psalm 2:4 says He who sits in heaven laughs, supporting God's laughter at them.
Rabbi Yitzchak says there is no laughter before God except on that day alone.
Some teach Rabbi Yitzchak's statement in connection with a baraita.
Rabbi Yosei teaches that in the future gentiles will come and convert.
But do we accept converts from them at that time?
A baraita says converts were not accepted in the days of the Messiah, David, or Solomon, so this cannot be right.
Rabbi Yosei means converts who attach themselves to Israel and take on mitzva objects like tefillin and mezuza.
When these converts see Gog and Magog's war, they ask the enemies why they came.
Psalm 2:1-2 says the nations plot in vain against God and His anointed.
Each convert then drops his mitzva bindings and leaves the war.
Psalm 2:3 has them say let us tear their bands asunder and cast off their cords.
God sits and laughs at the gentiles, as the verse describes.
Psalm 2:4 supports the claim that God sits and laughs.
Rabbi Yitzchak repeats that God laughs only on that one day.
Is that so? Is there no laughter before God at all?
Rav says God spends the first hours studying and judging the world, and sustaining it in the third set.
In the fourth set of hours, God sports with the leviathan.
Psalm 104:26 says the leviathan was formed to sport with, showing God sports daily.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that God sports with the leviathan but laughs at creatures only that day.
Rav Acha says that since the Temple was destroyed there is no laughter before God.
From where do we derive that there is no laughter?
Isaiah 22:12 describes a day of weeping, which may suggest that day alone was sad.
That proof is inconclusive, since perhaps only that day was called for weeping.
Psalm 137:5-6 has Jerusalem remembered and not forgotten, supporting the derivation from Scripture.
That proof is also inconclusive, since God might not forget Jerusalem yet still laugh.
Isaiah 42:14 says God held His peace and refrained, and now cries like a travailing woman.
If God no longer sports, what does He do during the fourth three-hour period?
He sits and teaches Torah to schoolchildren.
Isaiah 28:9 says whom shall one teach knowledge, them weaned from milk, supporting the teaching of children.
Who taught the schoolchildren before the Temple was destroyed?
Either the angel Metatron taught them, or God did both, sporting and teaching.
What does God do during the twelve hours of the night?
The night is like the day, or God rides a light cherub through eighteen thousand worlds.
Psalm 68:18 describes God's chariots as twenty thousand, read as eighteen thousand.
Or God sits and listens to songs sung by the angelic creatures.
Psalm 42:9 says by day God commands kindness and at night His song is with me.
Rabbi Levi says anyone who interrupts Torah for idle talk is fed coals of the broom tree.
Job 30:4 describes eating the roots of the broom, supporting that punishment.
Reish Lakish says one who studies Torah at night has a thread of kindness drawn over him by day.
Psalm 42:9 supports the derivation that God draws kindness by day for night Torah study.
What is the reason that kindness comes by day?
Because at night the song is with me, referring to occupation with Torah at night.
Some say Reish Lakish means Torah in this world, like night, earns kindness in the World-to-Come, like day.
Psalm 42:9 is cited for the day and night comparison.
Rav Yehuda says Shmuel explains a verse about people being like fish of the sea.
Habakkuk 1:14 says people are made like fish of the sea, with no ruler over them.
Why are people compared to the fish of the sea?
Just as fish die once they reach dry land, people die once they leave Torah and mitzvot.
Alternatively, just as fish die when the sun heats them, so people die when the sun heats them.
This may apply in this world or in the World-to-Come.
Rabbi Chanina says everything is in Heaven's hands except colds and obstacles that one must guard against.
Proverbs 22:5 says colds and snares lie on the path of the crooked, so one should keep far from them.
Reish Lakish says there is no Gehenna in the World-to-Come, since God brings out the sun to punish the wicked and heal the righteous.

4a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Malachi 3:19 says the day burns the wicked, leaving them neither root nor branch in either world.
Malachi 3:20 says the righteous are healed by the sun of righteousness rising with healing in its wings.
The righteous are not only healed by the sun, but also enjoy it.
Malachi 3:20 says they go forth and leap like calves of the stall, showing their enjoyment.
Alternatively, as among fish, a larger one swallows a smaller one, so people would do so without fear of government.
Mishnah Avot 3:2 says to pray for the government, since without its fear people would swallow one another alive.
Rav Hinnana bar Pappa notes an apparent contradiction between verses about God's power.
Job 37:23, Psalms 147:5, and Exodus 15:6 describe God's power in seemingly conflicting ways.
No contradiction: one refers to a time of judgment and the other to a time of war.
Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina notes an apparent contradiction about God's fury.
Isaiah 27:4 says fury is not in Me, while Nahum 1:2 says the Lord is a furious God.
No contradiction: one refers to Israel and the other to the nations of the world.
Rav Hinnana bar Pappa explains Isaiah 27:4 as God wishing He had not sworn to spare Israel.
Rabbi Alexandri offers a similar interpretation of a verse about God's judgment.
Zechariah 12:9 says God will seek to destroy all the nations on that day.
From whom does God seek, if He needs no permission?
God searches their records: if they have merit He spares them, and if not He destroys them.
Rava offers a similar reading of a verse in Job.
Job 30:24 says no one stretches out a hand to a ruinous heap, nor is help found in calamity.
God tells Israel that He does not judge them as He judges the nations of the world.
Ezekiel 21:32 describes the nations being destroyed for all their transgressions together.
God punishes Israel little by little, like the pecking of a hen's beak.
Alternatively, even when Israel performs only a few mitzvot, God counts them to a large reckoning.
God combines their small mitzvot into a large reckoning, as hens peck in a dunghill.
Job 30:24 speaks of those who peck being saved, supporting the hen image.
Alternatively, God saves Israel as a reward for their crying out and praying before Him.
Rabbi Abba offers another reading of a verse in Hosea.
Hosea 7:13 says God would redeem them, but they spoke lies against Him.
Rav Pappi, citing Rava, reads Hosea 7:15 about God training and strengthening their arms.
God says He afflicts Israel in this world so their arms will be strengthened in the World-to-Come.
Rabbi Abbahu praised Rav Safra as a great man, so the heretics remitted his taxes for years.
The heretics challenge Rav Safra with Amos 3:2, asking why God punishes those He loves, and torment him when he is silent.
They wrap a scarf around his neck and torment him.
Rabbi Abbahu comes, finds them tormenting Rav Safra, and asks why.
The heretics answer that Abbahu called him a great man, yet he could not explain the verse.
Abbahu replies that his praise applied only to Oral Law, not to knowledge of Scripture.
The heretics ask what makes the Babylonian Sages so knowledgeable about Scripture.
Abbahu says they debate heretics and so must analyze verses carefully, while the Babylonians need not.
The heretics ask Abbahu to tell them the meaning of the verse.
Abbahu offers a parable of a lender collecting little by little from a beloved debtor and all at once from an enemy.
Rabbi Abba bar Kahana turns to Abraham's prayer about Sodom.
Genesis 18:25 has Abraham say far be it from You to slay the righteous with the wicked.
Abraham says it would be a profanity for God to slay the righteous with the wicked.
Does God not act this way, given Ezekiel 21:8 about cutting off the righteous with the wicked?
That refers to a person who is righteous but not completely so.
Does Ezekiel 9:6 about beginning at My Sanctuary show that completely righteous people perish too?
Rav Yosef reads the word as those sanctified to God, who kept the whole Torah from alef to tav.
Those who could have protested but did not are considered righteous but not completely so.
Rav Pappa raises a contradiction between verses about God's indignation.
Psalms 7:12 says God is indignant every day, while Nahum 1:6 says who can stand before His indignation.
No contradiction: one refers to an individual and the other to the community.
The Sages teach how long God's indignation lasts, and that only Balaam the wicked knew the moment.

4b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Numbers 24:16 says Balaam knew the knowledge of the Most High, which is cited to be explained.
Was it possible that Balaam knew God's mind but did not know his own donkey's mind?
When the princes of Moab saw Balaam riding his donkey, the story of the donkey begins.
The princes ask why Balaam does not ride a horse, which is more fitting for him.
Balaam says he left his horse in a meadow to graze.
Numbers 22:30 has the donkey ask whether it is not Balaam's donkey.
Balaam replies that the donkey is only for carrying burdens, not for riding.
The donkey says Balaam rode it at irregular times, and promises daytime riding and nighttime intercourse.
The donkey's word hiskanti is compared to sokhenet in Kings about Abishag, alluding to intercourse.
What then is the meaning of knowing the knowledge of the Most High?
Balaam knew the precise hour when God was angry, and at that moment his curse would be fulfilled.
Micah 6:5 has God remind the people of what Balak and Balaam did, to know God's righteous acts.
Rabbi Elazar says God told Israel He did not become angry during Balaam's attempts, so no remnant would be left.
Numbers 23:8 has Balaam say he cannot curse whom God has not cursed.
How long is God's indignation, and how long is a moment?
Ameimar, or Ravina, says a moment lasts as long as it takes to say the word rega.
From where do we derive that God's anger lasts only a moment?
Psalm 30:6 says His anger is but for a moment, and Isaiah 26:20 says hide until the anger passes.
When is God angry?
Abaye says during the first three hours, when the rooster's crest whitens with no red streaks.
A heretic constantly challenged Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who tried to curse him at the moment of anger but fell asleep.
Rabbi Yehoshua concludes it is improper to curse people, even wicked ones, since God's mercy extends to all His works.
Proverbs 17:26 says punishment even for the righteous is not good, so one should not punish another.
Rabbi Meir says God grows angry when kings bow to the sun; Rav Yosef says one should not pray alone then, lest he be rejected.
If so, the community's prayer should also not be recited at that time?
The community's prayer is not rejected because its merits are many.
If so, the individual's morning prayer should also not be recited at that time?
Since a community is praying the morning prayer at that same time, his prayer is not rejected.
Didn't you say God sits and studies Torah in the first three hours, not judgment?
Torah is called truth, so God does not go beyond the letter of the law, but judgment involves mercy and compromise.
A mnemonic is given for the statements of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asks the meaning of Deuteronomy 7:11 about doing mitzvot today.
Deuteronomy 7:11 shows that today is the time to do mitzvot and not to receive reward.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says mitzvot performed by Jews will bear witness for them in the World-to-Come.
Isaiah 43:9 says let them bring witnesses and hear, which refers to Jews and nations respectively.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says Jewish mitzvot will strike the faces of the nations in the World-to-Come.
Deuteronomy 4:6 says the mitzvot are wisdom in the eyes of the nations, read literally as striking them.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says Israel made the Golden Calf only to give penitents an opening.
Deuteronomy 5:26 says who would give that they had such a heart, supporting the claim about the Golden Calf.
Rabbi Yochanan says in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai that David and Israel were not fit for those incidents.
Psalm 109:22 says my heart is wounded within me, showing David had overcome his inclination.
Israel too was not fit for the Golden Calf incident.
Deuteronomy 5:25 says who would give that they had such a heart to fear Me always.
Why then did they commit these sins?

5a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Teaching that an individual who sinned is pointed to David as a model of repentance, and a community to its own sinful precedent.
Explains why both the individual case and the community case must be taught, since each alone could suggest repentance is impossible.
Bar Nachmani transmits Rabbi Yonatan's teaching as parallel support for the idea that repentance is always possible.
A verse about David's final words is read as showing that David raised up the path of repentance through his own example.
Rabbi Yonatan teaches that one mitzva performed in this world goes before a person into the World to Come.
Isaiah's verse that righteousness walks before a person is cited to support the claim that a mitzva leads one onward.
Rabbi Yonatan teaches that one transgression wraps a person and leads him to judgment on the Day of Judgment.
Job's verse about the paths of the wicked being entangled is cited to show how sin ensnares the sinner.
Rabbi Elazar teaches that a transgression clings to a person like a dog that will not leave him.
Joseph's refusal to lie with Potiphar's wife is read as refusing this-worldly sin so as to avoid its consequence in the World to Come.
Reish Lakish urges gratitude to the ancestors who sinned with the Golden Calf, since otherwise the nation would never have come into being.
Psalm 82 is cited to show that Israel became like angels at Sinai and would have been immortal had they not sinned.
Asks whether this means that had they not sinned, they would not have had children, given the command to be fruitful and multiply.
Objects with Genesis 9:7 and the Sinai instruction to return to the tents, suggesting procreation continued after Sinai.
Explains that the Sinai instruction refers only to the enjoyment of conjugal rights, not to procreation.
Objects with Deuteronomy 5:26 about good for them and their children forever, which implies children would continue to be born.
Explains that this verse refers only to the children who stood with them at Sinai, not to future generations.
Raises a difficulty by citing Reish Lakish's own reading of the verse about Adam's book, to test the view just stated.
Asks whether Adam the first man really had a book, questioning the literal meaning of the verse.
Explains that God showed Adam each generation and its leaders, and that Adam rejoiced at Rabbi Akiva's Torah while mourning his death.
Adam's quotation of a psalm about God's thoughts is cited as evidence that future generations were known from the start.
Rabbi Yosei teaches that the Messiah son of David will not come until all the souls destined for bodies have entered them.
Isaiah 57:16 is cited to show that souls are still being created and entering bodies.
Responds that we would still have been born, but it would be as though we had never come into the world.
Asks whether had they not sinned they would not have died, given the earlier reasoning about the ancestors.
Objects that the chapters on levirate marriage and inheritance were written in the Torah, which suggests death still occurs.
Asks whether verses can really be written as conditional at all.
Affirms that verses can be conditional, citing the teaching of Reish Lakish.
Asks the meaning of the verse about the evening and the morning of the sixth day, which Reish Lakish uses as a source.
God made a condition with the works of creation: if Israel accepts the Torah all is well, otherwise the world returns to chaos.
Objects with a baraita on Deuteronomy 5:26 that the Angel of Death could not be nullified for Israel.
The baraita adds that the decree was already issued and that Israel accepted the Torah only so no nation would rule over them, undermining Reish Lakish.
Deuteronomy 5:26 is quoted as proof that the purpose of accepting the Torah was that it be good for them forever.
Explains that Reish Lakish follows the view of this particular tanna.
Rabbi Yosei's baraita teaches that Israel accepted the Torah only so that the Angel of Death would not rule over them.
Psalm 82 is quoted as Rabbi Yosei's proof that Israel had become immortal like angels before the sin.
Rabbi Yosei is challenged with Deuteronomy 5:26, which seems to imply that death still exists.
Rabbi Yosei responds that since there is no death, there is no greater good than this promised immortality.
Objects that the first tanna's view also conflicts with the verse saying you shall die like a man.
Explains that death in the verse means poverty, as a known teaching states.
Teaching that four are considered as dead: a pauper, a blind person, a leper, and one who has no children.
Exodus 4:19 is cited for the pauper, since the men who sought Moses' life are described as dead.
Asks who the men mentioned in that verse were.
Identifies them as Dathan and Abiram.
Objects that Dathan and Abiram were not really dead, since they survived to join Korah's rebellion.
Explains that the verse means they lost their property and became impoverished, so a pauper is like the dead.
Lamentations 3:6 is cited for the blind person, who is said to dwell in darkness like those long dead.
Numbers 12:12 is cited for the leper, with Aaron's plea that Miriam not be as one dead.
Genesis 30:1 is cited for the childless person, with Rachel's plea that without children she is as one dead.
A baraita teaches that the word if in Leviticus 26:3 is a term of supplication, expressing God's hope that Israel will observe the Torah.
Psalm 81:14-15 is cited to show a similar supplicating hope in God's wish that Israel listen to Him.
Isaiah 48:18 is cited as another expression of God's hope that Israel would listen and be blessed.
A baraita teaches that Deuteronomy 5:27 expresses a wish that the people's hearts be inclined to fear God.
Moses calls Israel ungrateful, a charge that the people merited for their response to God's wish.
When God expressed this wish about their hearts, Israel should have responded by asking that God grant them such a heart.
Israel should have answered that God Himself should be the one to act, rather than showing ingratitude.
Numbers 21:5 is cited as an example of the people's ingratitude, in speaking of their soul being disgusted.

5b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Moses called Israel children of ingrates, recalling that Adam blamed Eve for giving him the forbidden fruit.
Adam's complaint in Genesis 3:12 is cited as an example of ingratitude, blaming his wife rather than accepting her as a helpmate.
Even Moses did not hint at this teaching to Israel until forty years had passed since the revelation at Sinai.
Deuteronomy 29:3-4 is cited to show that Moses spoke forty years after Sinai, when God had not yet given Israel understanding.
Rabba concludes that a person does not grasp his teacher's opinion until forty years have passed.
Rabbi Yochanan attributes the following teaching to Rabbi Bana'a as a continuation of the discussion.
Isaiah 32:20 about those who sow beside all waters and send forth the feet of ox and donkey is quoted as the basis for interpretation.
Israel, when occupied with Torah and acts of kindness, has its evil inclination placed under its own control rather than the reverse.
The verse about sowing beside waters is read as sowing charity, with Hosea 10:12 cited to support that reading.
Reaping according to mercy and the waters are taken to mean charity and Torah respectively.
Isaiah 55:1 is cited to show that waters refer to Torah, since the thirsty are called to come to the water.
One of the school of Eliyahu teaches that a person should always subject himself to Torah like an ox under a yoke or a donkey under a burden.
The mishna's rule: for three days before gentile festivals one may not conduct business or lend items with them.
Asks whether it is really necessary to require all this, since a gentile would not buy an animal so far in advance.
A mishna from Hullin is cited requiring a seller to inform a buyer about the mother or daughter of an animal sold for slaughter.

The mishna lists the four occasions: the eve of the last day of Sukkot, the eve of Passover, the eve of Shavuot and the eve of Rosh HaShana, with Rabbi Yosei HaGelili adding Yom Kippur eve in the Galilee.
Explains that the Hullin case concerns eating, which needs only one day of preparation, while sacrifices need three days.
Objects with a baraita that Passover questions begin thirty days ahead, or two weeks per Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, so more than three days are needed.
Explains that Jews need thirty days because blemishes are common, while gentiles need only three days since they disqualify only a missing limb.
Asks from where we know that an animal missing a limb is forbidden to Noahides as a sacrifice.
Genesis 6:19 is cited, requiring bringing every living thing, which is read as requiring animals with intact limbs.
The Torah says to bring an animal whose extremities are alive, meaning its limbs must be intact.
Asks whether the verse is needed instead to exclude a tereifa, an animal with a fatal wound, rather than a missing limb.
Answers that a tereifa is excluded by the phrase keep seed alive, since a tereifa cannot propagate.
Asks whether this derivation works only according to the view that a tereifa cannot give birth.

6a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks how the view that a tereifa can give birth can still account for excluding tereifot through the phrase keep seed alive.
The verse with you is read as referring to animals similar to you, meaning animals that are not tereifot.
Asks whether Noah himself might have been a tereifa, arguing that the words complete and righteous do not establish that his body was whole.
Replies that Noah could not have been a tereifa, since God would not have told him to bring tereifot into the ark while excluding whole animals.
Asks why keep seed alive is needed at all if the disqualification is already derived from the term with you.
Explains that with you alone would suggest mere companionship, so keep seed alive teaches that only animals able to breed were admitted.
Raises a dilemma about whether the three days before gentile festivals include the festival day itself or count only the days without it.
Cites Rabbi Yishmael's mishna counting three days before and after gentile festivals, and reasons about whether the festival day would be counted twice.
Rejects the proof by suggesting the festival day may be counted among the first three days, with the later phrasing merely parallel.
Cites Shmuel's teaching on Rabbi Yishmael that trade with them is always prohibited, arguing that otherwise two days of the week would remain permitted.
Clarifies that the dilemma does not arise according to Rabbi Yishmael, and that the open question concerns only the view of the Rabbis.
Ravina cites the mishna's list of gentile festivals and Rav Hanin's explanation of their timing around the solstice, with a mnemonic.
Ravina's inference would require ten prohibited days, which is rebutted by saying the tanna counts the whole festival of Kalenda as a single day.
Rav Ashi's proof: the mishna's phrasing before their festivals implies that all three prohibited days precede the festival.
Objects that before the festival might only exclude the days after it, and that the mishna would have said at the time of the festival if it meant the festival itself.
Upholds the proof by concluding that the wording shows the three days are counted without the festival itself.
Raises a dilemma about whether the prohibition stems from giving the gentile profit or from the verse forbidding a stumbling block before the blind.
Asks what practical difference the two reasons make, such as whether someone who owns the animal would transgress the verse.
Objects with a baraita attributed to Rabbi Natan, introducing a challenge to the conclusions drawn so far.

6b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks from where we derive that one may not hand a nazirite wine or a limb from a living animal to a Noahide.
The verse forbidding a stumbling block before the blind is cited as the source for these prohibitions.
Objects that in these cases the recipient could take the item himself, so the giver should not transgress by helping him.
Explains the case is two people on opposite sides of a river, and that the baraita's word extend shows this is meant.
Raises a dilemma about whether profits from business done before gentile festivals may be used.
Rabbi Yochanan holds such profits are forbidden, while Reish Lakish holds they are permitted.
Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish with a baraita prohibiting profits from gentile festival business, read as including the days before the festival.
Shimon ben Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan by inferring from the baraita that business before the festival is permitted.
Rabbi Yochanan responds that the tanna calls both the days before and the festival itself by the same name, their festivals.
A baraita in line with Reish Lakish: the prohibition applies only to enduring items, and even then profits from such dealings are permitted.
Rav Zevid teaches a baraita: one may sell non-enduring items to them, but may not buy from them.
A story: a heretic sent a Caesarean dinar to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia on his festival, and Reish Lakish was present.
Rabbi Yehuda Nesia asks what to do, since taking the dinar would thank the idol but refusing would breed enmity.
Reish Lakish advises him to take the dinar and throw it into a pit in front of the heretic.
Rabbi Yehuda Nesia objects that this would still cause enmity, and all the more so.
Reish Lakish clarifies that he meant the dinar should be tossed in an unusual manner, looking like an accidental fall.
The mishna teaches that lending to and borrowing from gentiles is prohibited during the three days before their festivals.
Asks why borrowing is forbidden, since lending benefits them while borrowing reduces their property.
Abaye says borrowing is forbidden as a decree, lest one come to lend to them.
Rava says both lending and borrowing are prohibited for the same reason, since the gentile would thank his idol.
Asks the same question about money: why is borrowing it forbidden, when lending money gives them a profit?
Abaye again explains that borrowing money is forbidden as a decree, lest one come to lend money to them.
Rava again explains that all of it is due to the concern that the gentile would give thanks to his idol.
The mishna's next clause: repaying them and being repaid by them is likewise addressed.
Asks why being repaid by them is forbidden, since repaying them benefits them while collecting reduces their property.
Abaye explains that collecting repayment is forbidden as a decree, lest one come to repay them.
Rava explains that it is all because the gentile would give thanks to his idol, as before.
Explains that both clauses are needed, since business alone would be prohibited for profit while borrowing might be considered harmless.
Continues the hypothetical about why each clause would be needed, considering the trouble of borrowing and that the money is never returned.
Continues the argument, considering a debtor forced to repay, and why the separate clause on collecting debts is needed.
Rabbi Yehuda says one may collect debts from them.
Asks whether Rabbi Yehuda holds that they are happy later even though they are distressed now.
Objects with a baraita attributed to Rabbi Yehuda about women on festival days, which seems to contradict his stated view.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says to leave aside festival laws, since in all such cases the gentile is distressed now and pleased later.
Ravina says that for repayment the gentile is always distressed, so the mishna does not follow Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha.
A baraita of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: one may not collect from them on a written debt, but may on an oral debt, since collecting is like rescuing from them.
A narrative setup of several sages seated in a specific order while they discuss the ruling.
The halakhic ruling: the law follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, then Rabbi Yehuda, and then Rabbi Yehoshua again.
What we said follows Rabbi Yehuda, as taught in a baraita about a person who gave wool to a dyer to dye red and it came out black, and vice versa.

7a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Meir holds that the dyer must pay the owner the value of the wool, treating him like a robber who changed the stolen item.
Rabbi Yehuda holds the dyer does not acquire the wool, and the owner reimburses the dyer's costs or the enhancement, whichever is lower.
Rav Yosef turns his face away in displeasure at Rav Huna's ruling.
Explains Rav Yosef's displeasure: Rav Huna's ruling for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha was needed to show a single sage is followed over the majority.
Asks why the ruling for Rabbi Yehuda needs stating at all, since it seems obvious.
Principle: where a dispute is followed by an unattributed mishna, the halakha follows the unattributed opinion, applied here across Bava Kamma and Bava Metzia.
Cites the Bava Metzia mishna on changing agreed terms and reneging, as an unattributed ruling that matches Rabbi Yehuda's view.
Explains Rav Huna's reasoning: the mishna is not necessarily sequential, so an unattributed view may have been taught before the dispute.
Challenges that if the mishna is not sequential, this would apply to every such case and undermine the principle.
Explains that a mishna is sequential within one tractate but not across tractates, and that Rav Yosef treats the Nezikin order as a single tractate.
Alternatively, Rav Yosef holds that the unattributed ruling appears among decided halakhot and is evidently accepted, so Rav Huna's statement was unnecessary.
A baraita: one may not ask a neighbor on Shabbat whether he will join him that evening, since it hints at hiring him for work after Shabbat.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha permits asking this on Shabbat, as long as the request is not stated explicitly.
Rabba bar bar Hana reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha.
A baraita: one who got a ruling of impurity or prohibition from a sage may not seek a different sage to rule the opposite.
When two sages disagree, follow the one greater in wisdom and number, and otherwise follow the stringent ruling.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: follow the stringent ruling for a Torah law and the lenient ruling for a rabbinic law.
Rav Yosef rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha.
A baraita: those whose sins made them untrustworthy are never accepted again, even after repentance, according to Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda: if they retracted in private they are not accepted, but if they repented publicly they are accepted.
Another version of the discussion: if their sins were done in private, society accepts them when they repent.

7b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha hold that penitents are accepted both when their sins were public and when they were private.
Jeremiah 3:14, return backsliding children, is cited to support accepting penitents whether their sins were public or private.
Rabbi Yitzchak of Akko reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that the halakha follows that pair, so penitents are always accepted.
Mishnah: Rabbi Yishmael prohibits business with gentiles on the three days before and after their festivals.
The Sages hold that business is prohibited before the festival and permitted after it.
Rav Tahlifa bar Avdimi reports Shmuel: by Rabbi Yishmael's view, trade with a gentile whose festival recurs weekly is always prohibited.
Restates the Sages' position that business is prohibited before their festival but permitted after it.
Asks why the Sages' position is not identical to the first tanna's view, which also prohibits business before the festival.
Explains that the dispute is whether the three days count the gentile days without the festival, as the first tanna holds, or include the festival.
Offers an alternative: the dispute concerns whether profits from business done before the festival may be used, with the first tanna permitting them.
Offers an alternative: the dispute concerns Shmuel's view that outside the land of Israel trade is prohibited only on the festival day itself.
Offers an alternative: the dispute concerns Nachum the Mede, who forbids trade only on the day before the festival, a view the later Sages accept.
Nachum the Mede holds business is prohibited only on the day before the festival, but the Sages reply that the matter should be lost, as it is not halakha.
Asks whether later Sages follow Nachum's view, since it seems some of them do.
Explains that the only one who agrees with him is Nachum the Mede himself, while the other Sages disagree.
A baraita: Nachum permits selling a male, elderly horse to gentiles in wartime, which the Sages reject as not halakha.
Asks whether ben Beteira agrees with Nachum, since ben Beteira permits selling a horse to gentiles.
Explains that ben Beteira does not distinguish male from female horses while Nachum does, so Nachum follows the Rabbis except in this specific case.
A baraita: Nachum the Mede holds dill is subject to tithes whether used as seed, vegetable or pod, and the Sages reject this as not halakha.
Asks whether Rabbi Eliezer agrees with Nachum, since a mishna has him say dill is tithed as seed, vegetable or pod.
Answers that the mishna refers to a specific kind of dill, so it is not a full match with Nachum's view.
Narrative: Rav Acha son of Minyumi tells Abaye that a great man came from the districts, and everything he said was dismissed as not halakha.
Abaye says one practice follows Nachum the Mede: a baraita permits one to ask for one's needs while hearing prayer.
Bar Minah replies that this case is different and depends on a specific circumstance, not on a general rule.
Rabbi Eliezer holds that one should first ask for one's needs and only then pray.
Psalm 102:1 is cited: the poor man who wraps himself pours out his complaint before God, showing that prayer comes first.
The word siha, complaint, is taken to mean prayer.
Genesis 24:63, Isaac going out to meditate in the field, is cited to show that siha means prayer.
Rabbi Yehoshua holds that one should pray first and then ask for one's needs.
Psalm 142:3 is cited: I pour out my complaint before Him and tell my trouble before Him, supporting Rabbi Yehoshua's view.
Objects that the same verse also supports Rabbi Eliezer, since it speaks of pouring out a complaint before God first.
Explains that the verse means one pours out a complaint at the time one tells one's trouble before God.
Objects that the verse about the prayer of the poor man who wraps himself also seems to support Rabbi Yehoshua's view.
Explains that the verse means prayer for the poor applies when he pours out his complaint before God.
Asks what the actual point of disagreement is, since the verses can be read in different ways.
Explains the dispute by reference to Rabbi Shmelai's exposition of the verses.
Rabbi Shmelai's rule: a person should always first arrange the praise of God and then pray.
Asks how we know this rule.
Answers from Moses, whose prayer in Deuteronomy 3:24-25 begins with praise before he asks to cross into the good land.

8a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehoshua derives from Moses that one should praise God in prayer before making personal requests.
Rabbi Eliezer rejects that inference, since Moses was unique in his ability to pray this way.
The Sages reject both positions and rule that a person requests personal needs in the blessing of hearing prayer.
Shmuel rules that the halakha is to make personal requests within the blessing of hearing prayer.
Rav Yehuda attributes the same ruling to Rav, relayed through a transmitter.
Although the Sages said requests belong in the hearing-prayer blessing, one may add them at the end of every blessing.
Rav Ḥiyya bar Ashi attributes a similar teaching to Rav.
Rav gives specific blessings for requests about a sick household member or for sustenance and the years.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi permits lengthy personal supplications after completing the Amida prayer.
The mishna lists gentile festivals, birthdays and death days, and attributes the list to Rabbi Meir.
The Sages hold that a death accompanied by public burning involves idolatrous festivity, and otherwise it does not.
The mishna notes that the shaving, sea-rescue and prison-release days are restricted to one day and one man.
Rav Ḥanan bar Rava says Kalenda falls eight days after the solstice and Saturnalia eight days before it.
A mnemonic verse from Psalms, where behind precedes before, matches the order in which the mishna lists the festivals.
A baraita reports that Adam feared his punishment when he saw the days growing shorter.
Adam mourned the shortening days, fasting and praying for eight days.
Seeing the days lengthen, Adam set eight festive days for Heaven, which later generations turned into idolatrous festivals.
The Gemara asks how Adam could have considered shortening days a punishment, given the Nisan creation view.
Adam had seen short days, but not days as short as those before the winter solstice.
A baraita tells of Adam's fear when the sun set on the day he was created.
Adam fasted and wept all night while Eve wept opposite him, until dawn broke.
At dawn Adam concluded that sunset and night are the normal order of the world.
Adam sacrificed a bull whose horns preceded its hooves in creation.
A verse from Psalms about a bullock with horns before hooves is cited to support this description.
Rav Yehuda, in Shmuel's name, says that bull had a single horn on its forehead.
The same Psalms verse is cited as support for the one-horned bull.
The plural makrin seems to indicate two horns, which creates a difficulty.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak says the word is spelled defectively, indicating a single horn.
Rav Mattana asks whether business with towns subject to Rome's Kalenda festival is forbidden or permitted.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds that Kalenda is forbidden for business with everyone.
Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that business is forbidden only with those who worship the festival.
A baraita is cited in agreement with Rabbi Yoḥanan, limiting the prohibition to the festival's worshippers.
The baraita continues with Saturnalia, Kratesis and royal days, plus the feast-for-son case, limited to that day and man.
Rav Ashi says the mishna also supports Rabbi Yoḥanan's view.
Rav Ashi cites the mishna's cases of shaving, sea-rescue and prison-release as proof.
Rav Ashi asks what the phrase that man excludes, if the prohibition is already limited to that day.
The phrase must exclude those ruled by the gentile, so the prohibition applies only to worshippers.
A baraita: Rabbi Yishmael says Jews outside Eretz Yisrael unwittingly engage in idolatry in certain cases. He asks how this occurs.
Illustrates with a gentile's son's wedding feast to which all local Jews are invited, which the verse counts as eating sacrifices.
Exodus 34:15 is cited: sacrificing to their gods and eating from their sacrifice applies to these Jews.
The Gemara asks why the verse should not criticize them only once they actually eat.
Rava says the words and they call you show the prohibition begins at the moment of the invitation.

8b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The ruling: for thirty days after a wedding, attending a gentile feast is forbidden whether or not the host mentioned the wedding.
From then on, attendance is forbidden if the host mentioned the wedding and permitted if he did not.
The Gemara asks until when the feast stays connected to idolatry when the host mentioned the wedding.
Rav Pappa answers: until twelve months of the year have passed since the wedding.
The Gemara asks from when the prohibition applies before the wedding.
Rav Pappa, citing Rava, says it begins when barley is cast into mortars for beer, and ends after twelve months.
A counterexample: Rav Yitzḥak bar Mesharshiyya left a gentile's feast after twelve months, upon hearing thanks offered to an idol.
Rav Yitzḥak is distinctive because he is an important person, so his presence was a special honor for the host.
The mishna's list continues with Kratesis and the day of the festival of their kings.
The Gemara asks what the festival of Kratesis is.
Rav Yehuda, in Shmuel's name, says Kratesis commemorates the day Rome seized control of an empire.
A baraita lists Kratesis and the day of Rome's seizure as two separate festivals, creating a difficulty.
Rav Yosef: Rome seized power twice, once in the days of Cleopatra and once in the days of the Greeks.
Rav Dimi reports that Rome fought the Greeks, then allied with the Jews under a stipulated power-sharing arrangement.
Rome proposes settling the conflict by judgment rather than by battle.
Rome poses a riddle: between a pearl and a precious stone, which should serve as the base for the other.
The Greeks answer that the pearl should serve as the base for the precious stone.
Rome asks which should serve as the base between a precious stone and an onyx.
The Greeks answer that the precious stone should serve as the base for the onyx.
Rome asks which should serve as the base between an onyx and a Torah scroll.
The Greeks answer that the onyx should serve as the base for the Torah scroll.
Rome replies that it holds the Torah scroll and the Jewish people are with it, so Rome should prevail.
Rome subdued the Greeks with Jewish support, and the Jews stood with Rome for twenty-six years.
After that alliance, the Jews became subjugated to Rome, which had initially treated them faithfully.
The Gemara asks which verse was interpreted at first, when Rome acted faithfully, and which verse later.
Genesis 33:12 is cited: Esau proposes traveling together and equates himself with Jacob, reflecting the early treatment.
Genesis 33:14 is cited: Jacob asks Esau to pass before him, reflecting the later subjugation.
The Gemara asks from where we know that Rome acted faithfully for those twenty-six years.
Rav Kahana relates how the Sages asked the ailing Rabbi Yishmael to repeat sayings he had heard from his father.
Rabbi Yishmael recounts dates: Roman rule 180 years before the Temple's fall, impurity decrees 80 years before, and the Sanhedrin's exile 40 years before.
The Gemara asks what halakha depends on knowing where the Sanhedrin convened.
Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Avdimi says it shows that the Sanhedrin no longer adjudicated cases of fines.
The Gemara objects: Rav Yehuda cites Rav praising Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava for preserving the laws of fines.
The Gemara asks whether the fines laws would really have been forgotten, since scholars could simply study them.
Rather, the laws would have ceased to be applied, because Rome barred the ordination of judges.
Rome decreed death for ordaining or being ordained, and destruction for any city or boundary where ordination occurred.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava did in response.
He sat between mountains and cities to ordain five Elders, and Rav Avya adds that Rabbi Neḥemya was also ordained.
When enemies found them, the elderly Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava stayed behind and was killed, showing judges existed after the Temple's fall.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak says the statement should be emended to say they stopped capital cases, not fines.
The Gemara asks what the reason is.
The Sanhedrin relocated because murderers were too numerous to execute, so courts could not carry out death sentences.
Deuteronomy 17:10 is cited to show that the Sanhedrin's place of residence is what makes judgment valid.
The Gemara asks whether Rome ruled exactly 180 years before the Temple's destruction and no more.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yosei ben Halafta himself taught a contrary statement.

9a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Persian rule lasted thirty-four years in the presence of the Temple.
Greek rule lasted 180 years in the presence of the Temple.
The Hasmonean and Herodian dynasties each ruled for 103 years in the presence of the Temple.
Going forward, one can date an event by counting the years since the Temple was destroyed.
The Gemara objects that the total of 206 years contradicts the earlier figure of 180.
Resolution: Rome stood faithfully with the Jews for twenty-six years, so those years are not counted as Roman subjugation.
Rav Pappa: a tanna who forgot the exact count should ask a scribe's dating system and add twenty years.
Genesis 31:41, these twenty years, serves as the mnemonic for the twenty-year adjustment.
The reverse case: a forgetful scribe asks the tanna and subtracts twenty, with a mnemonic contrasting scribes deducting and tannaim adding.
A baraita of the school of Eliyahu: the world lasts six thousand years, two thousand each of chaos, Torah and Messiah.
The Gemara asks from when the two thousand years of Torah are counted, since counting from Sinai leaves too little time.
Rather, counting begins from the verse about the souls made in Haran, when Torah spread through Abraham and Sarah.
Abraham was fifty-two years old at that time.
The Gemara asks how many years are missing from the Messiah's two thousand years under this count.
The tanna's answer: 448 years are missing.
Calculating from the souls in Haran until Sinai gives 448 years, confirming the figure.
Rav Pappa: a forgetful tanna should ask a scribe's count and add forty-eight to correct for the century.

9b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Numbers 35:7 is cited: the Levitical cities total forty-eight, the figure to be deducted.
Restates the rule: a forgetful scribe asks the tanna, deducts forty-eight, with the tosefa mnemonic.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua: one unsure of his place in the Sabbatical cycle adds a year and counts centuries as Jubilees.
Take two years from every hundred and calculate the remaining details by Sabbatical cycles.
Genesis 45:6, these two years of famine, is the mnemonic for subtracting two years per century.
Rabbi Ḥanina: after year 400 since the Temple's destruction, do not buy a field worth a thousand dinars for one dinar, since redemption is near.
A baraita gives the same advice for year 4,231 from creation, a slightly different dating.
The Gemara asks what the difference is between the two dating systems.
The baraita's dating is three years later, which accounts for the difference.
The Gemara introduces a promissory note that bore a written date, to be examined next.

10a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Sages before Rabba think the note is postdated, so it should be held until its stated date arrives.
Rav Naḥman answers that the scribe was exacting and the six extra years count only the Greek rule in Elam, so the date is correct.
A baraita of Rabbi Yosei: the Greeks ruled six years in Elam alone before their rule spread worldwide, supporting Rav Naḥman.
Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov objects: perhaps the years are counted from the Exodus, so the note is postdated after all.
Rav Naḥman replies that in exile years are counted only by the Greek kings.
Rav Aḥa finds this reply deflects his objection, then investigates and discovers that Rav Naḥman was right.
A baraita confirms that in exile years are counted only by the Greek kings.
Ravina: the mishna is precise in stating that years are counted by the Greek kings.
The Gemara asks with regard to what halakha the Nisan New Year for kings applies.
Rav Ḥisda: it applies to the dating of documents.
The same mishna says Tishrei is the New Year for counting years and for Sabbatical cycles.
The Gemara asks with regard to what halakha the Tishrei New Year for counting years applies.
Rav Ḥisda: this too applies to the dating of documents.
The two statements about document dating contradict each other.
Resolution: Nisan applies to the kings of Israel and Tishrei to the kings of the gentile nations.
Ravina notes that we currently count from Tishrei when dating, which supports this resolution.
Ravina's proof: if counting were from the Exodus we would use Nisan, so we must count by the Greek kings.
The mishna cites the geinuseya of their kings as one of the gentile festivals.
The Gemara asks what the geinuseya of their kings means.
Rav Yehuda: it is the day on which gentiles appoint and crown their king.
Objection: a baraita lists geinuseya and the day of appointing a king as two separate festivals.
Resolution: the first is the king's own geinuseya, and the second is the coronation of his son.
The Gemara asks whether the Romans really make a king's son king, challenging that resolution.
Rav Yosef's baraita reads Obadiah 1:2 as showing that Rome does not crown a king's son and has no script of its own.
The Gemara rejects the coronation reading and proposes that geinuseya is the king's birthday.
Objection: a baraita lists geinuseya and birthday as two separate festivals.
Resolution: the first is the king's own geinuseya, and the second is his son's birthday.
Objection: a baraita lists the king's and his son's geinuseya and birthdays, which conflicts with the birthday reading.
The Gemara asks again what geinuseya means.
Resolution: geinuseya is the day of appointing the king, and the other date refers to his son.
Romans do sometimes install a king's son at the king's request, as with Asveirus son of Antoninus.
Antoninus asks Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that his son Asveirus rule and that Tiberias be exempted from taxes.
Antoninus notes that the Senate grants one request but not two.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi answers with a parable of a dove released from a man's hands while he sits on another man's shoulders.
Antoninus interprets the parable: ask for Asveirus to rule and do not raise the matter of Tiberias.
Antoninus resolves to instruct Asveirus to exempt Tiberias from taxes.
Antoninus asks how to deal with important Romans who are troubling him.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi takes him into a garden and uproots a radish each day in front of him as a demonstration.
Antoninus interprets: remove them one by one and do not incite all of them at once.

10b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi did not state his advice openly.
He feared being overheard, and cites Ecclesiastes 10:20 that a bird of the air may carry a whispered word.
Antoninus and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi exchange plant names as coded messages about Antoninus's daughter Gira.
Antoninus sends gold hidden in wheat sacks; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi declines, and Antoninus says it is meant for his descendants.
Antoninus used a tunnel and had a servant killed at each end to keep his visits secret, demanding that no man be present.
Antoninus finds Rabbi Ḥanina bar Ḥama present and sends him to summon the servant at the door, who is found killed.
Rabbi Ḥanina prays and revives the servant; Antoninus remarks that even the least among the Jews can revive the dead.
Antoninus serves Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, offering himself as a footstool, and wishes to be a mattress for him in the World-to-Come.
Antoninus asks whether he will enter the World-to-Come, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi answers yes.
Antoninus objects that Obadiah 1:18 says no survivor of the house of Esau remains.
A baraita explains that the verse refers only to those who act like Esau, based on the words of the house of Esau.
Antoninus objects with Ezekiel 32:29 about the kings and leaders of Edom.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi answers that the verse says her kings and leaders, not all of them, so some may merit the World-to-Come.
A baraita with the same reading excludes Antoninus son of Asveirus and the Roman officer Ketia son of Shalom from the general condemnation.
The Gemara asks what happened with Ketia son of Shalom: an emperor's question about cutting off a diseased foot.
Ketia replies that one cannot destroy all of the Jews, and this is the first reason.
Zechariah 2:10 is cited: I have scattered you as the four winds of heaven.
The Gemara asks what the verse means by the phrase as the four winds.
Interprets the image: just as the world needs winds, it needs Israel, so Israel can never be destroyed.
Ketia's second argument: destroying the Jews would make Rome a severed kingdom.
The emperor praises Ketia's reasoning but notes the custom of executing anyone who defeats the king in argument.
Ketia is thrown into a house of ashes; a matron taunts him, and he removes his foreskin as payment of the tax before going to his death.
As he is thrown into the ashes, Ketia bequeaths all his property to Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues.
Rabbi Akiva derives from Exodus 29:28 that an inheritance is split equally, and applies it to his colleagues.
A divine voice declares that Ketia is destined for the World-to-Come, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi weeps.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi reflects that some acquire their share in the World-to-Come in an instant and others only after many years.
Antoninus waited on Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and similarly the Persian king Adrakan waited on Rav.
When Antoninus died, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said the bundle is separated; when Adrakan died, Rav said the same.

11a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Restates the closing image of the prior account: the bundle is separated.
Onkelos son of Kelonimos converts; the emperor's first troop is won over by his verses, so a second troop is ordered not to speak with him.
Onkelos argues by hierarchy that God, like a superior official, carries a torch before the Jewish people.
Exodus 13:21 is cited: the Lord went before them as a pillar of fire by night.
All of the soldiers convert to Judaism.
A second troop takes Onkelos silently, and he notices a mezuza on a doorway.
Onkelos asks the soldiers what the mezuza is and urges them to explain it.
Unlike an earthly king guarded from outside, God dwells with His people within and guards them from outside, citing Psalms 121:8.
After that, the emperor sends no further troops after Onkelos.
Genesis 25:23 is cited: two nations are in Rebecca's womb.
Rav reads goyim as geyim, meaning proud, applying it to Antoninus and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, whose tables always had vegetables.
Rav explains the benefits: radish cuts food, lettuce stirs it, and cucumbers expand the intestines.
Objection: a baraita of Rabbi Yishmael says cucumbers are called kishuin because they harm the body like swords.
Resolution: the harmful statement refers to large cucumbers, and the beneficial one to small ones.
From the mishna, one infers that Rabbi Meir sees burning as irrelevant, while the Rabbis treat burning as a customary idolatrous practice.
Objection: a baraita permits burning at a king's death as a non-Amorite custom, which conflicts with Leviticus 18:3.
Resolution: all agree burning is a sign of honor rather than a custom, and the disagreement concerns the mishna's cases.
Explains the disagreement: Rabbi Meir holds that any death can lead to idolatry, while the Rabbis hold only a death with public burning matters to them.
Jeremiah 34:5 is cited as the basis for burning at kings' deaths, showing it is not an Amorite practice.
Just as burning is done for kings, it is done for the heads of the Sanhedrin.
Describes what is burned: the kings' beds and utensils, and Onkelos burned seven thousand dinars' worth of goods at Rabban Gamliel's death.
Objection: if only utensils are burned, why did Onkelos burn money? Resolution: the goods burned were valued at seven thousand dinars.
Objection: a baraita says livestock hooves are removed at a king's death, which conflicts with burning only utensils.
Rav Pappa: that baraita concerns the horse the king rode, which became his personal item and so could not be used by others.
Objection: a baraita prohibits removing hooves from kosher animals if it would render them a tereifa, so which method avoids that?

11b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Pappa's interpretation: the case of cut hooves concerns the calf that pulls the king's coach, a kosher animal the king used.
Quotes the mishna's first case: the day of shaving the gentile's beard and locks.
The Gemara asks how the mishna is worded: does it mean leaving the locks, or removing them later?
Come and hear: baraitot teach both versions, which supports either reading of the mishna.
Shmuel: Rome holds a festival every seventy years in which a healthy man rides a lame man, dressed as Adam, with Rabbi Yishmael's scalp on his head.
The Romans hang gold on his neck, cover the markets with onyx, and proclaim Jacob's calculation fraudulent and Esau a forger.
Rhetorically: what does deceit achieve for the deceiver, and forgery for the forger?
They conclude with a warning to Esau that Jacob will rise, bringing about Esau's downfall.
Rav Ashi: the wicked ones' own words brought about their downfall.
Had they said a forger is our master's brother, it would be read as intended; instead it implies the master himself is the forger.
The Gemara asks why the mishna omits this festival, which occurs only once every seventy years.
These listed festivals are the Roman and Persian ones.
The Gemara asks what the Persian festivals are.
Persian festivals: Mutredei, Turyaskei, Moharnekei and Moharin.
The Gemara asks what the Babylonian festivals are, since they differ from the Persian and Roman lists.
Babylonian festivals: Moharnekei, Akenitei, Beḥanunei and the tenth of Adar.
Rav lists five idolatrous temples; Rav Dimi adds marketplaces in Ein Bekhi and Akko, and Rav Dimi of Neharde'a reverses the attribution.
Rav Ḥanan asks Rav Ḥisda what it means that these sites are established.
Rav Ḥisda: they are permanent sites, because worship takes place there year-round, unlike festivals.
Shmuel: in the Diaspora, business with gentiles is forbidden only on their festival day itself.
The Gemara asks whether it is forbidden even on the festival day itself.
Objection: Rav Yehuda permitted Rav Beruna to sell wine and Rav Giddel to sell wheat on a gentile festival day.
Resolution: the Arab merchants' festival has no fixed date, so the Sages did not include it in the prohibition.
Mishna: trade is permitted with gentiles outside a city that has idolatry, and a road leading only to the festival site is prohibited.
The Gemara asks what is meant by outside it.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, citing Rabbi Ḥanina: a bazaar at Gaza outside the city walls counts as outside it.
Alternative version: Rabbi Shimon asked Rabbi Ḥanina whether business at Gaza's bazaar is permitted on its festival.
Rabbi Ḥanina rebukes him: have you not seen Jews and gentiles trading together in Tyre, so the answer is evident?

12a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites the precedent of two pots on one stove, where the Sages were not concerned about the neighboring prohibited food.
Asks what is meant by the Sages not being concerned in that precedent.
Abaye explains: the concern about carrion meat falling into the pot does not apply, just as with idolatrous coins in the bazaar.
Rava introduces a different explanation for the precedent.
Rava asks what exactly the Sages were not concerned about in the case of the pots.
The Sages were lenient only about gentile cooking, which is a rabbinic concern, not a Torah-level prohibition.
Rava concludes that the bazaar case concerns the Jews trading on the gentiles' festival day, a rabbinic matter.
Rabba bar Ulla explains that the splattering case is lenient because it is unlikely and nullified by the majority.
Rabba bar Ulla concludes that the bazaar before the festival is analogous to the splattering case.
Asks the halakha about traveling to a place where a pagan festival is being celebrated.
Baraita: a city with active idolatry may not be entered or left, unless the road also leads elsewhere, per Rabbi Meir and the Sages.
Baraita: a thorn in the foot before an idol may not be removed by bending, since it looks like bowing; if unseen, it is permitted.
Baraita: scattered coins before an idol may not be picked up by bending, but are permitted if one is not seen.
Baraita: a spring before an idol may not be drunk from by bending, but is permitted if one is not seen.
Baraita: one may not put his mouth to idol-shaped fountain figures, since it looks like kissing an idol.
Baraita: one may not drink from a pipe before an idol, because of the danger involved.
Asks what 'not seen' means, and whether it refers to not being seen by others.
Objection: Rav's principle says appearance-based prohibitions apply even in inner rooms, so being unseen by others cannot be the test.
Reinterprets 'not seen' as not appearing to bow, such as turning one's side or back to the idol, which upholds the baraita.
Explains that the thorn case must be taught separately, since one might otherwise think one can walk around to avoid it.
Explains that the coins case must be taught separately, since one might think the stringency stems only from financial loss.
Explains that the spring case must be taught separately, since one might think the other two are prohibited only for lack of danger.

12b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why the baraita needs to teach the figures case separately.
The figures case is included to introduce the continuation about not drinking from a pipe due to danger.
Asks what the danger referred to in the pipe case is.
The danger is swallowing a leech in the water.
Baraita: one may not drink water from rivers or ponds directly or by hand alone, and blood is on his head if he does, due to danger.
Asks what exactly the danger in that baraita is.
The danger is that of swallowing a leech.
Brings a supporting view, namely that Rabbi Ḥanina's position is confirmed by the baraita's concern about leeches.
Rabbi Ḥanina rules that one who swallowed a water leech may have water heated for him on Shabbat.
Continues Rabbi Ḥanina's ruling that heating water on Shabbat for such a person is permitted.
Relates an incident where Rabbi Neḥemya permitted heating water on Shabbat for one who swallowed a leech.
Asks what the swallower should do in the meantime, until the water is ready.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua says he should swallow vinegar to address the leech.
Rav Idi bar Avin says one who swallowed a hornet will die, but vinegar may extend his life briefly to set his affairs in order.
Baraita: one should not drink water at night, and blood is on his head if he does, due to danger.
Asks what the danger of drinking at night is.
The danger is that of the shavrirei, an evil spirit that rules over water.
Asks what the remedy is for one who is thirsty at night.
If another person is present, he should wake him and ask for water to drink.
If no one is present, he should knock the jug lid and recite a protective incantation against the evil spirit.
Completes the incantation, which is directed against the evil spirit.
Mishna: adorned shops in an idolatrous city are forbidden to buy from, while unadorned shops are permitted; the case occurred in Beit She'an.
Resh Lakish limits the prohibition to shops adorned with roses and myrtle, which benefit from their scent, but not fruit.
Asks what the reason is for permitting purchases from shops adorned with fruit.
Brings Deuteronomy 13:18 to show that one may not derive benefit from items dedicated to idol worship.

13a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Resh Lakish's view: deriving indirect benefit from idolatrous stores is permitted.
Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that even stores adorned only with fruit are forbidden to buy from.
A fortiori argument: if deriving benefit from idolatry is forbidden, causing it benefit is all the more forbidden.
Objection from a baraita by Rabbi Natan: a tax reduction for wreath-wearers implies that causing benefit to idolatry is permitted.
Extends the objection: a Jew present must either benefit from idolatry or cause it benefit, so the baraita allows the latter.
The Sages infer that one trading in an idolatrous market must destroy or discard purchased goods.
The baraita is cited to show the same conclusion about leaving or taking goods, depending on benefit.
Rav Mesharshiyya explains that the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Natan, while Rabbi Yoḥanan holds they do not.
Challenges Rabbi Yoḥanan with a baraita permitting purchases at a gentile fair, which seems to show a real disagreement.
The baraita continues: a priest may become impure outside the Land of Israel for litigation, as he may in a cemetery.
Objects that cemetery impurity is Torah law, so the Sages could not permit it in the usual case.
The baraita refers to an uncertain grave area, where impurity is only rabbinic.
The baraita continues: a priest may become impure to study Torah or to marry.
Rabbi Yehuda limits the allowance to when a priest cannot find study in the Land of Israel.
Rabbi Yosei permits impurity even when study is available locally, since one cannot learn from everyone.
Rabbi Yosei supports his view with the case of Yosef the priest, whose teacher was in Sidon, and Rabbi Yoḥanan rules accordingly.
Infers from this that the Tannaim do disagree, which seems to contradict Rabbi Yoḥanan's position.
Rabbi Yoḥanan replies that there is no real disagreement, so no difficulty arises.
Reconciles the baraitot: Rabbi Natan refers to buying from a merchant who pays a tax, the other to buying from a private owner.
Quotes the Master's earlier ruling that an animal bought in the idolatrous market must be destroyed.
Asks whether this destruction conflicts with the prohibition against causing animals suffering.
Abaye explains that causing suffering is permitted when necessary.
Supports Abaye by citing Joshua 11:6, where God commands that the horses be hamstrung.
Restates the definition of destroying an animal: cutting its hooves from the knee and below.
A contradictory baraita says consecrated animals or property must be destroyed, which conflicts with the other rules.

13b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita continues: unwanted money and metal are cast into the sea, and the animal is disposed of by locking it in to starve.
Abaye explains that consecrated animals are handled differently, since slaughtering might lead to misusing sacred meat.
Asks why the animal is not simply mutilated to make it unfit, rather than starved.
Abaye answers by citing a scriptural source.
Deuteronomy 12:3-4 forbids doing to the Lord what idolaters do, so one may not actively destroy sacred items.
Rava says cutting hooves would seem to blemish a sacrificial animal, which applies only while the Temple stands.
Objects that this should count as blemishing an already blemished animal, which is forbidden even when unfit for sacrifice.
Distinguishes: a blemished animal has monetary value to be redeemed, while here the animal has neither value nor sacrificial use.
Rabbi Yona meets Rabbi Elai at Tyre and reports the baraita's rule that a purchased animal must be destroyed.
Asks how a Jewish slave versus a gentile slave bought at the fair should be treated.
Rabbi Elai asks why this is a dilemma at all.
A baraita about gentile shepherds of small animals implies that one may not actively cause their death.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether the baraita's permission to buy slaves refers to a Jewish slave or also a gentile slave.
Rabbi Zeira answers that the baraita must mean a Jewish slave, since a gentile slave would not require permission.
Ravin relays that Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish permits buying a gentile slave, since the Jew brings him under the Divine Presence.
Rav Ashi objects: how can buying an animal bring it under the Divine Presence?
Rav Ashi offers an alternative reason: the purchase diminishes the gentile's property, which is permitted.
Relates that Rabbi Ya'akov bought sandals and Rabbi Yirmeya bought bread at a pagan fair.
The two sages rebuke one another, asking whether the other's teacher would act this way.
They both bought from a homeowner, each assuming the other had bought from a merchant.
Rabbi Abba, son of Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba, teaches that only buying from a merchant who takes a tax is prohibited.
Rabbi Abba adds that had Rabbi Yoḥanan lived where tax is taken from all sales, he would have prohibited even buying from a homeowner.
Asks how the sages Rabbi Ya'akov and Rabbi Yirmeya could have bought at the fair under that standard.
