They bought from a homeowner who sells only temporarily, so no fixed tax was taken from the sale.
Mishna: certain items, such as frankincense and a white rooster, are prohibited to sell to a gentile because used for idolatry.
Rabbi Yehuda permits selling a white rooster among other roosters, or cutting its toe when sold alone, since defective animals are not offered.
Mishna: other items are permitted when sold without specification, but prohibited when specified for idolatry.
Rabbi Meir prohibits selling even a good palm tree, a ḥatzav, or a naklav to gentiles.

14a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what the term itzterubalin refers to in the mishna.
Itzterubalin is identified as the plant torenita.
Objects with a baraita that lists itzterubalin among Sabbatical-year prohibitions, which would be impossible if it meant torenita.
Cites a principle taught in a baraita: only plants with roots are subject to Sabbatical-year laws.
Rav Safra and Rabbi Elazar identify itzterubalin as the fruit of the cedar tree.
Rabbi Yoḥanan explains that benot shuaḥ are white figs, as the mishna lists them among prohibited items.
Rabbi Yoḥanan explains that petotarot refers only to fruit sold with its stems attached.
Rabbi Yitzḥak, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, clarifies that the mishna's frankincense means pure incense.
A Sage teaches that one may sell a large bundle of such goods, which weighs at least three hundred dinars, since it is clearly for sale.
Raises the difficulty that the buyer might resell the items to another gentile who will offer them.
Abaye responds that one is only forbidden to directly place a stumbling block, not to facilitate another's act.
The mishna teaches that selling a white rooster to a gentile is prohibited.
Rabbi Yona, citing Rabbi Zeira and Rav Zevid, rules that a rooster sale is permitted only when the buyer does not specify white.
Objects that Rabbi Yehuda's mishna permits selling a white rooster among others, which contradicts this ruling under either reading.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak resolves the contradiction: the case is one where the buyer names two roosters and one happens to be white.
A baraita supports this resolution and adds that a buyer preparing a feast or tending a sick person may buy a white rooster.
Objects with a baraita that restricts a gentile's feast-day prohibition to that day and person, which conflicts with the earlier ruling.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Rav Mesharshiyya explains that the baraita concerns a social picnic, not a sacrificial feast.
Quotes the mishna's rule that unspecified sales of remaining items are permitted and specified sales prohibited.
Asks what the mishna means by unspecified versus specified sales, and why the rule needs to be stated.

14b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the wheat case: unspecified requests are permitted and specified requests for white wheat for idolatry are forbidden.
Infers from the wheat case that the rooster ruling must also forbid unspecified sales, contradicting Rabbi Zeira.
Replies that the unspecified case means wanting wheat, and the specified case means wanting it for idolatry.
Explains why the mishna needs the specified-idolatry case: the buyer might merely be claiming a purpose to obtain the item.
Rav Ashi asks whether a request for a damaged white rooster allows selling an undamaged one, or is only a ploy.
Poses a further dilemma about buyers who receive substitute roosters, which is left unresolved.
The mishna records Rabbi Meir's view that even a good palm tree and ḥatzav may not be sold to gentiles.
Rav Ḥisda tells Avimei that Abraham's tractate had four hundred chapters, and that the Sages' meaning is obscure.
Rav Ḥisda asks how the mishna can forbid a good palm tree yet permit a bad one.
Objects that another mishna forbids selling anything attached to the ground, which conflicts with the permission for a bad palm.
Avimei explains that the mishna refers to detached fruit of a good palm tree, a view attributed to Rav Huna.
Explains the terms: ḥatzav is kashba dates, and naklas is koreyatei, reported through Rav Dimi.
Abaye objects that the mishna's naklas and koreyatei remain unclear, so the explanation offers no help.
Rav Dimi replies that the term koreyatei is recognized locally, so it helps in locating the item.
Mishna: small animals may be sold where that is customary, but large livestock may not be sold to gentiles, with exceptions by Rabbi Yehuda and ben Beteira.
The Gemara explains that the mishna's rule depends on local custom, which decides whether the sale is permitted or prohibited.
Raises a contradiction from a mishna forbidding stabling animals in gentile inns because of bestiality suspicion.
Rav states that the permission to sell follows the permission to leave animals with gentiles, and likewise for prohibitions.

15a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Elazar holds that even where seclusion with a gentile is forbidden, selling an animal to a gentile is permitted.
Explains that a gentile spares his own animal from bestiality, and cites Rav's reported view that the gentile protects his animal from sterility.
The mishna rules that large livestock may not be sold to gentiles in any place, whole or damaged.
Asks the reason, since bestiality is not the concern here, so the worry must be the gentile working the animal on Shabbat.
Objects that once the gentile buys the animal he owns it, so he may work it on Shabbat without concern.
Explains that selling is forbidden by rabbinic decree against lending and leasing the animal, which would involve Shabbat labor.
Objects that borrowing and leasing transfer temporary ownership, so the same objection applies.
Rami bar Yeiva says the decree concerns testing: the seller might have the animal walk on Shabbat eve to show it works.
Rav Sheisha bar Idi challenges that leasing transfers ownership, citing the mishna forbidding renting a house to gentiles.
Idolatry is treated more stringently, so the house still counts as the Jew's, as Deuteronomy 7:26 requires.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Rav Mesharshiyya raises the same challenge, citing a Terumot mishna on a cow rented from a priest.
Concludes that leasing does not transfer ownership, so the three rabbinic decrees of lending, leasing and testing stand.
Rav Adda permits selling a donkey through a Jewish middleman, since the decrees' concerns do not apply in that case.
Relates that Rav Huna sold a cow to a gentile.
Rav Ḥisda asks Rav Huna for the reason for this sale.
Rav Huna replies that the gentile bought the cow for slaughter, not for labor.

15b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks from where the principle is derived that one assumes an animal will be slaughtered rather than misused.
Cites the mishna in Shevi'it: Beit Shammai forbid selling a plowing cow in the Sabbatical Year, while Beit Hillel permit it since it can be slaughtered.
Rabba distinguishes the cases: a person is not commanded to rest his animal in the Sabbatical Year but is commanded to rest it on Shabbat.
Abaye objects that a field is also one a person must rest in the Sabbatical Year, yet selling it is permitted per Beit Hillel.
Rav Ashi objects that vessels need not be rested, yet the mishna forbids selling plowing implements in the Sabbatical Year.
Quotes the mishna listing the implements a person may not sell in the Sabbatical Year.
Rav Ashi resolves: assume an innocent motive where one is possible, and not where it is not, regardless of the commandment to rest.
Rabba sold a donkey to a Jew who was suspected of selling livestock to gentiles.
Abaye asks Rabba why he sold the donkey under those circumstances.
Rabba replies that he sold it to a Jew, and that the buyer is the one who must be responsible.
Abaye counters that the Jew will resell the donkey to a gentile, so the sale is effectively to a gentile.
Abaye objects with a baraita permitting sale of small livestock to Samaritans, asking why they would be suspected of bestiality.
Baraita: animals may not be left with male or female gentile companions due to bestiality suspicion.
Continues the baraita: Samaritan inns may host animals of either sex together, unlike gentile ones.
Continues the baraita: animals may be entrusted to Samaritan shepherds, and children may be taught by them.
Infers that Samaritans are not suspected of bestiality, which raises a problem for the reason given for prohibiting such sales.
Baraita: weapons, their auxiliary equipment, and prisoner shackles may not be sold to gentiles or Samaritans.
Abaye asks why these items may not be sold to Samaritans, if they are not suspected of bloodshed.
Abaye answers that the prohibition arises because the Samaritan may resell the items to a gentile.
Objects that a Samaritan will not repent, while a Jew will, so the distinction between them makes sense.
Rav Naḥman cites Rabba bar Avuh: a Jew suspected of selling to gentiles is treated as a gentile for sale purposes.
Rabba, having realized Abaye is correct, runs after the buyer to revoke the sale but does not catch him.
Rav Dimi bar Abba teaches that selling to a Jewish armed robber is prohibited, just as selling to a gentile is.
Asks what the circumstances are: if the robber kills, the prohibition is obvious.
Explains that such a robber is the same as a gentile for this purpose.
Asks why it is prohibited to sell to a robber who does not kill.
Rav Dimi's case is a robber who steals and might use weapons in self-defense if caught.
Baraita: shields may not be sold to gentiles, though some permit it.
Asks the reason for prohibiting shield sales, noting that wheat and barley would then also be forbidden.
Rav begins his reply, which continues on the next amud.

16a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Opening principle: if avoiding the gentiles' anger were possible, all sales to them would be forbidden; since that is impractical, only shields are barred.
Some hold shields are barred because gentiles use them to kill once their weapons fail; Rav Naḥman rules this view is halakha.
Rav Adda bar Ahava forbids selling iron blocks to gentiles, since they forge weapons from them.
Asks the reason for the prohibition on iron blocks.
Answer: the iron is used to forge weapons for gentiles.
Objects that hoes and axes, also iron, would then be forbidden too, since they can be forged into weapons.
Rav Zevid replies the ruling concerns Indian iron, used only for weapons, and notes current practice of selling weapons.
Rav Ashi explains that weapons are sold to Persians, who protect the Jewish community.
The mishna's ruling: calves and foals may not be sold to gentiles.
A baraita: Rabbi Yehuda permits selling a damaged animal that cannot recover and live.
Sages object: one can mate her and she will bear young, so the gentile may keep her and the sale looks permitted.
Rabbi Yehuda responds he will worry about that when she actually bears offspring.
Inference: evidently a damaged animal does not accept a male.
Mishna: ben Beteira permits selling a horse to gentiles.
Baraita: ben Beteira permits horses because riding involves no liability for a sin-offering on Shabbat.
Rabbi prohibits horses for two reasons: they are weapons, and they are large livestock.
Why would the large-livestock rationale matter, since riding does not violate Shabbat? What is that rationale?
Rabbi Yoḥanan: an old horse is ground at a mill, so it does perform Shabbat labor.
Rabbi Yoḥanan rules the halakha follows ben Beteira, permitting the sale.
A dilemma: may a fattened ox be sold to gentiles, under Rabbi Yehuda's or the Sages' view?
First horn: Rabbi Yehuda permits only a damaged animal; a fattened ox, which becomes labor-fit, stays forbidden.
Second horn: even the Sages forbid only damaged animals, so fattened oxen may be sold.
Proof from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household, who paid bribes to avoid bringing a fattened ox to the authorities.
Asks whether the bribe reflected concern they would keep the ox until it became fit for labor.
Challenges this reasoning: by the same logic, why do they delay only by one day?
Asks the reason for the gradual approach.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi wanted to abolish the custom gradually, so the proof does not establish the halakha.
Objects that a kept, slimmed ox does not regain health and cannot perform labor.
Rav Ashi reports Zevida's testimony: a slimmed ox is kept and works, equal to two oxen.
Mishna: bears, lions, and other public-harm items may not be sold to gentiles; certain structures may not be built with them.
Rav: a large beast is like small livestock for spasm, but not for sale, so it may never be sold.
Rav Ḥanan adds that even for sale a large beast is like small livestock, sold where customary.
Objects to Rav from the mishna: the reason is public harm, so a non-harmful animal would be permitted.
Rabba bar Ulla replies the mishna refers to a damaged lion unfit for labor, so it fits Rav.

16b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Ashi explains the mishna's lion case: an ordinary lion counts as damaged regarding labor, so no Shabbat concern arises.
Objection from a baraita: large beasts are forbidden to gentiles even where small livestock may be sold, refuting Rav Hanan bar Rava.
Concludes the refutation of Rav Hanan bar Rava's view as decisive.
Ravina raises a contradiction between the mishna and a baraita, and proceeds to resolve it.
Ravina cites the mishna and infers that a beast causing no public harm may be sold to gentiles.
Ravina sets against this a baraita forbidding the sale of any large beast, even where harmless.
Ravina resolves the contradiction: the mishna refers to a damaged lion.
Alternative explanation, per Rabbi Yehuda: Rav Ashi says an ordinary lion is considered damaged regarding labor.
Rav Naḥman objects: why assume a lion is a large beast rather than a small one?
Rav Ashi examines the mishna closely and draws an inference that refutes Rav Hanan bar Rava.
Rav Ashi adds that only a labor-performing beast like a lion is excluded, which presents a difficulty for Rav Hanan bar Rava.
Concludes that the refutation of Rav Hanan bar Rava's view is conclusive.
Asks what labor a large beast could actually perform, if it is not trained for any work.
Abaye reports that wild asses, large beasts, are used to turn mill grinders.
Rabbi Zeira reports Rav Yehuda's teaching: a large beast is like small livestock regarding a spasm at slaughter.
Rabbi Zeira finds Rav Hiyya bar Ashi attributing the same ruling to Shmuel.
Rabbi Zeira finds Rabba bar Yirmeya attributing the same ruling to Rav.
Rabbi Zeira reports Rav Asi attributing it to Rav, through Rav Hama bar Gurya.
Rabbi Zeira objects: why not attribute the ruling to Rabba bar Yirmeya, who disseminated the halakha?
Rav Asi answers that the two attributions combine, so the halakha can be concluded from both.
The chain of transmission is stated in full, from Rabbi Zeira through Rav to Rav Hama bar Gurya.
Cites the mishna that one may not build a basilica in conjunction with gentiles.
Rabba bar bar Hana reports Rabbi Yoḥanan: there are three kinds of basilicas, of kings, of bathhouses, and of storehouses.
Rava holds two kinds are permitted and one forbidden, with a verse as a mnemonic for the royal basilica.
Some report Rava as holding that all kinds of basilica are permitted.
Objection: the mishna forbids building a basilica, so all kinds must be forbidden.
Resolution: the mishna forbids only a basilica used for judgment, tribunal, stadium or platform.
A baraita recounts that Rabbi Eliezer was arrested on charges of heresy and brought before a tribunal.
A judicial officer asks why an elder like Rabbi Eliezer engages in such frivolous matters of heresy.
Rabbi Eliezer replies that he trusts the judge, though the officer misread it as about himself; he meant the Father in Heaven.
The officer rules that, since Rabbi Eliezer trusted him, he is acquitted and exempt.
Rabbi Eliezer's students come to console him, and he refuses their consolation.
Rabbi Akiva asks Rabbi Eliezer for permission to raise one matter from his teachings.
Rabbi Eliezer grants permission: speak.
Rabbi Akiva suggests that perhaps a heretical statement came before Rabbi Eliezer.

17a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Akiva notes Eliezer was arrested for having derived pleasure from the heretical teaching.
Eliezer recalls meeting Ya'akov of Kefar Sekhanya, a student of Jesus, in the upper market of Tzippori.
Ya'akov asks whether a bathroom for the High Priest may be built from a prostitute's wages.
Ya'akov reports Jesus's teaching, drawn from Micah, that such coins may be used since they came from filth.
Eliezer confesses he enjoyed the teaching and so transgressed Proverbs' warning to keep far from heresy.
Alternative reading: distance from heresy and authority, and from a prostitute keep four cubits, per Rav Hisda.
Asks what the Sages derive from the phrase payment of a prostitute in the verse.
Following Rav Hisda: a prostitute who hires out eventually hires others, as Ezekiel 16:34 indicates.
Rabbi Pedat holds the Torah forbids only intimacy amounting to forbidden intercourse, disputing Rav Hisda.
Ulla, returning from the study hall, would kiss his sisters' hands, per one version.
Notes that a version has Ulla kissing their chests, which contradicts his own ruling.
Ulla rules that mere intimacy with a forbidden woman is prohibited, like a nazirite near a vineyard.
Proof from Proverbs 30:15: the horseleech's two daughters cry give, give.
Asks what the phrase give, give means.
Mar Ukva: it is the voice of two daughters crying from Gehenna, heresy and the ruling authority.
Variant: Rav Hisda relays Mar Ukva that Gehenna itself cries out demanding those two daughters.
Proverbs 2:19: none who go to her return or attain the paths of life.
Asks: if those who went astray never return, how could they attain the paths of life?
The verse means those who go to her do not return, and even if they do, regret shortens their lives.
Asks whether whoever leaves heresy must die, citing a woman Rav Hisda told to prepare shrouds, yet she lived.
She did not repent properly, so she did not die; her confession shows she was involved in heresy.
Variant version: repentance from heresy causes death, but repentance from forbidden intercourse does not.
Objects that the same woman died, which contradicts the claim that intercourse-repenters do not die.
Asks whether repenting of forbidden intercourse cannot save one, citing a baraita on Elazar ben Durdayya's promiscuity.
Elazar ben Durdayya, shocked, sits between mountains and asks them to plead for his repentance.
The mountains reply they must first plead for themselves, citing Isaiah 54:10.
He asks heaven and earth to plead for him.
They reply they must first plead for themselves, citing Isaiah 51:6.
He asks the sun and moon to plead for him.
They reply they must first plead for themselves, citing Isaiah 24:23.
He asks the stars and constellations to plead for him.
They reply they must first plead for themselves, citing Isaiah 34:4.
Elazar concludes the matter depends on nothing but himself.
He places his head between his knees and weeps until his soul departs.
A Divine Voice declares Elazar ben Durdayya destined for life in the World-to-Come.
Asks how Elazar died after repenting, given that he was guilty of a sexual sin.
His strong attachment to the sin made it like idolatry, so it resembles heresy and he could die.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi weeps; some earn the World-to-Come over years, others in a single moment.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi adds penitents are accepted and even called Rabbi, as the Voice did for Elazar.
Rabbi Hanina and Rabbi Yonatan reach a fork: one path leads to idolatry, the other to a brothel.

17b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: One proposes entering the brothel to overpower the inclination and earn a reward; the prostitutes yield before the Sages.
Asks the other how he knew the prostitutes would retreat from them.
Cites Proverbs 2:11: discernment will guard you from lewdness, meaning the Torah protects against it.
The Sages ask Rava what the word mezimma means.
Proposed reading: mezimma means counsel of sinners, and etza in Isaiah 28:29 is also linked to Torah.
Objects: if so, the verse should have said zimma rather than mezimma.
Resolution: the verse means from lewd matters the Torah will guard you, so discernment refers to Torah.
A baraita: Rabbi Elazar ben Perata and Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon are arrested; Elazar laments his five charges.
Rabbi Hanina replies that Elazar will be saved, since he combined Torah with charity, while he studied Torah alone.
Rav Huna's principle: one who studies Torah alone is like one without God, citing II Chronicles 15:3.
Asks what is meant by without the true God.
Teaches that one who studies Torah alone is like one who has no God, and who does no acts of kindness.
Asks whether Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon really gave no charity, given a baraita praising him as the trusted charity supervisor.
Resolution: he was trusted to distribute charity honestly, but did not give charity himself.
Asks again, citing a baraita where he gave away his Purim coins mistaken for charity coins.
Resolution: he did give charity, but not as much as his wealth required.
Narration: the Romans bring Rabbi Elazar ben Perata to trial.
The Romans ask why he taught Torah and why he stole.
Elazar: an armed robber is not a scholar and a scholar is not a robber, so neither charge can be true.
Asks why he is called rabbi if he does not teach Torah; he answers he is master of weavers.
To test him, two coils of wool are brought; a miracle occurs as hornets sit on them.
Elazar identifies the warp and the woof, reading the hornets as signs of which coil is which.
The Romans ask why he did not come to the house of Abidan, a gathering place for debate.
Elazar says he was old and feared being trampled by the crowds.
The Romans reply: how many elders have been trampled there until now, so why fear it?
Narration: a miracle occurs and one old man is trampled that day.
The Romans ask why he emancipated his slave.
Elazar denies the matter ever happened.
A witness stands to testify, and Elijah appears disguised as a Roman noble.
Elijah tells the witness that miracles always occur for Elazar, so he only shows his own wickedness; the witness ignores him.
A letter sent to the Emperor's court is hurled four hundred parasangs by Elijah, and the witness never returns, so charges are dropped.
The Romans bring Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon to judgment and ask why he occupied himself with Torah.
Rabbi Hanina replies with Deuteronomy 4:5: as the Lord my God commanded me.
The Romans sentence Rabbi Hanina to burning, his wife to execution, and his daughter to a brothel.

18a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon pronounced God's ineffable name exactly as it is spelled.
Asks how he could do this, given the mishna on who forfeits the World-to-Come.
Cites the mishna: Abba Shaul says one who pronounces the Name as written has no share in the World-to-Come.
A baraita: the prohibition on sorcery permits learning in order to understand and teach.
Asks what the reason for his punishment was.
He pronounced the Name publicly rather than privately, and his wife was executed for not protesting.
Principle: anyone able to protest another's sin but does not protest is punished for that sin.
Asks why his daughter was condemned to sit in a brothel.
Rabbi Yohanan tells of her graceful walk; Resh Lakish says trampled sins return on Judgment Day.
Hanina accepts God's judgment, quoting Deuteronomy 32:4.
His wife continues Deuteronomy 32:4: a God of faithfulness and without iniquity.
His daughter quotes Jeremiah 32:19 on God's great counsel and His eyes upon the ways of men.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi praises these righteous people for reciting verses that accept the judgment.
Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma, ill, rebukes Hanina for teaching Torah publicly despite Roman decrees.
Hanina replies that Heaven will have mercy.
Yosei says Hanina's reply is unreasonable and fears the Romans will burn him and his Torah scroll.
Hanina asks what will become of him, and whether he is destined for the World-to-Come.
Yosei asks whether any incident occurred that might indicate his fate.
Hanina recounts confusing Purim coins with charity coins; Yosei says may my lot be of yours.
Yosei dies within days, Rome's notables eulogize him, and Hanina is found still teaching with a scroll in his lap.
Hanina is wrapped in the scroll and burned slowly, with wet wool on his heart to prolong his death.
His daughter asks whether she must see him die this way.
Hanina says burning alone would be hard, but since the scroll burns with him, He will avenge its insult too.
His students ask what he sees.
He sees the parchment burning while its letters fly up, and refuses to hasten his death by opening his mouth to the fire.
The executioner asks whether Hanina will bring him to the World-to-Come if he raises the flame and removes the wool.
Hanina agrees and swears an oath to the executioner.
The executioner raises the flame, Hanina dies, and the executioner leaps into the fire and dies too.
A Divine Voice declares Hanina and the executioner destined for the World-to-Come.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi weeps: one earns the World-to-Come in a moment, another after years of toil.
Introduces Berurya, the wife of Rabbi Meir and daughter of Hanina ben Teradyon.
Berurya asks Rabbi Meir to save her sister, who sits in a brothel, since this is disrespectful to her.
Rabbi Meir takes a vessel of dinars and plans a test: a miracle means she sinned not, none means she did.
Rabbi Meir disguises himself as a Roman knight and asks her to accede to his wishes.
She replies that she is menstruating.
He says he will wait.
She says many women in the brothel and here are more beautiful than she.
Meir infers she did not sin, since she would say the same to everyone who comes.
Rabbi Meir approaches her guard.
Meir asks the guard to give her to him.
The guard fears punishment from the government.
Meir offers a vessel of dinars: half as a bribe to the government, half for the guard.
The guard asks what he will do once the money runs out.
Meir says the guard should call out: God of Meir answer me, and he will be saved.

18b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The guard doubts that he will be saved by merely saying this phrase.
Rabbi Meir replies: you will see what happens.
Narrative: Rabbi Meir throws a clod at attacking dogs and says God of Meir answer me; the guard is then rescued and the king is informed.
Asks what this incident is about.
Explains that the guard relates the entire story of what happened.
Romans engrave Rabbi Meir's image and chase him; he hides in a brothel and escapes by feigning to eat gentile food.
Rabbi Meir flees to Babylonia, either because of this incident or out of embarrassment over Berurya.
A baraita: attending stadiums or besiegers' camps, where scorners and diviners perform, is the seat of the scornful and leads to neglecting Torah.
Raises a contradictory baraita permitting stadium attendance to save a life, which conflicts with the first baraita.
Partial resolution: the besiegers' camp conflict resolves, but the stadium contradiction remains difficult.
Resolves it as a dispute between tanna'im: Rabbi Natan permits stadiums to save a life or give testimony.
A baraita: Rabbi Meir forbids theaters and circuses for their idol worship, while the Rabbis forbid them as the seat of the scornful.
Asks what practical difference lies between Rabbi Meir's view and the Rabbis' view.
Rabbi Hanina of Sura: the difference concerns profits from business there, which are forbidden in Rabbi Meir's view.
Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi reads Psalms 1:1 as showing how one who walks with the wicked ends up scorning.
Explains the verse: whoever walks with the wicked will eventually stand, sit, and scorn with them, citing Proverbs 9:12.
Rabbi Eliezer says scoffers suffer, citing Isaiah 28:22; Rava urges the Sages not to scoff.
Rav Ketina: a scoffer's sustenance is lessened, citing Hosea 7:5.
Resh Lakish: a scoffer falls into Gehenna, citing Proverbs 21:24 and Zephaniah 1:15.
Rabbi Oshaya repeats the same point: anyone haughty falls into Gehenna.
Rabbi Hanilai bar Hanilai: a scoffer brings about the world's extermination, citing Isaiah 28:22.
Rabbi Eliezer: scoffing is severe, since suffering first comes and ends in extermination.
Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi reads Psalms 1:1 as referring to theaters, bestial contests, and scoffers' company.
Warns that avoiding transgression is not enough; one must actively study Torah, citing Psalms 1:2.
Rav Shmuel bar Naḥmani, citing Rabbi Yonatan, gives an alternative reading of Psalms 1:1.

19a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Psalms 1:1 refers to Abraham, who avoided the counsel of the generation of the dispersion and the sinners of Sodom.
Abraham also avoided the seat of the Philistines, who were scorners, as shown by their mocking of Samson.
Cites Psalms 112:1, happy is the man who fears the Lord, as the basis for the teaching.
Asks why the verse says man, implying the woman is not happy.
Rav Amram: the verse includes women and teaches happiness in repenting while still a man; Yehoshua ben Levi adds triumphing over the inclination.
Rabbi Elazar says one delights in the mitzvot themselves, not their reward, citing Antigonus of Sokho in Avot 1:3.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: one learns Torah only from the part of it that his heart desires.
Narrates Levi and Rabbi Shimon studying before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and finishing their book.
Levi asks for the book of Proverbs, and Rabbi Shimon asks for Psalms.
Levi is compelled to accept Psalms, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi repeats his view; Levi asks to leave.
Rabbi Avdimi bar Hama: God fulfills the desires of one who studies Torah; Rava repeats the desire-based study rule.
Rava: Torah is first called by God's name and ultimately by the name of the one who studies it.
Rava: one studies broadly first and only afterward analyzes, citing Psalms 1:2 and its continuation.
Rava: one should always study and review, even if he forgets or does not understand, citing Psalms 119:20.
Rava reconciles Proverbs 9:3 and 9:14: a student first has no seat, but later is given a seat of honor.
Reconciles Proverbs 8:2 and the path: one first studies privately, and later spreads knowledge publicly.
Ulla reconciles Proverbs 5:15: first drink from one's own cistern, and later produce running waters from one's own well.
Rav Huna, via Rav Seḥora: whoever studies in large bundles loses Torah, whereas gradual study and review increases it.
Rava: the Sages know this but transgress it; Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak says his gradual study and review has endured.
Rav Sheizvi, citing Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya: Proverbs 12:27 teaches that a deceitful hunter who skips review will not live long.
Rav Sheshet reads the verse in reverse; Rav Dimi compares review to breaking birds' wings so they cannot escape.
Psalms 1:3 likens the scholar to a replanted tree; one who learns from a single teacher never sees a sign of blessing.
Rav Hisda tells the Sages he fears they will leave him if he says that one who learns from one teacher sees no blessing.
The students leave Rav Hisda and go to learn from Rava.
Rav Hisda clarifies: many teachers matter for reasoning, but for the oral tradition learning from one teacher is preferable.

19b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Tanhum bar Hanilai: divide one's years into thirds for Bible, Mishna and Talmud, so one is not confused by varying versions.
Asks how a person can divide his life when he does not know its length.
The division refers to each day, not to one's whole life.
Cites Psalms 1:3, that he brings forth fruit in its season, as the basis for the teaching.
Rava: if one acts on what he learns his leaf will not wither; otherwise teacher and student are like chaff.
Rav Huna via Rav: a student who issues rulings before maturity is like a miscarriage, while one who withholds rulings misleads the masses.
Asks until what age a scholar is considered too immature to rule, answering forty years.
Objects that Rava issued rulings before that age.
Resolution: one of equal stature to the city's foremost scholar may rule before forty, as with Rava.
Rav Aha bar Adda, citing Rav and Rav Hamnuna: even the ordinary talk of Torah scholars requires careful analysis.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: Torah study brings success in business, as stated in the Torah in Deuteronomy 29:8.
The same teaching is repeated in the Prophets (Joshua 1:8) and a third time in the Writings (Psalms 1:2-3).
Rabbi Alexandri proclaims like a merchant selling life, and the crowd asks him to give them life.
Alexandri answers with Psalms 34:13-14, who desires life and keeps the tongue from evil.
Explains that one must actively do good, lest he think avoiding evil suffices, and that good means Torah.
Cites Proverbs 4:2: I have given you a good portion, My Torah, do not forsake it.
Mishna: one may not continue building a bathhouse arched chamber where gentiles set up idol worship.
Rabbi Elazar, citing Rabbi Yohanan: if a Jew built such a chamber, his wages are permitted.
Asks whether this is obvious, since accessories of idol worship are not forbidden until worshipped.
Rabbi Yirmeya: Rabbi Elazar's ruling is needed only for a Jew who built an idol itself.
Asks how this works if an idol built by a gentile is forbidden immediately, leaving the ruling unexplained.
Rabba bar Ulla: the ruling applies to the final stroke; wages are earned at each stage, so the idol is not complete until then.
Concludes that Rabbi Elazar holds wages accrue continuously from hiring to the end of the work.
Mishna: one may not make idolatrous jewelry, and may not sell gentiles produce attached to the ground, with Rabbi Yehuda's view.
Asks from where the rule that attached items may not be sold to gentiles is derived; Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina begins to answer.

20a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The verse not to show them mercy is cited and read as forbidding giving gentiles a foothold to settle in the Land.
Why does the verse need to say this, since its plain meaning already forbids giving gentiles favor?
If so the verse should have been spelled without the vav; its spelling teaches two separate prohibitions.
Why not also a third reading, that one may not give an undeserved gift, and why is the spelling without yud?
A baraita gives the same three derivations from the verse, each as a separate prohibition.
The Gemara notes that the question of giving an undeserved gift to a gentile is itself a tannaitic dispute.
A baraita cites the verse on carrion: one may give it to a resident alien or sell it to a gentile, so the baraita derives these permissions.
The baraita asks where the sale to a resident alien is derived from.
The word or in the verse teaches that giving to a gentile is also permitted, through the verse wording.
The baraita asks where giving to a gentile is derived from, given the verse.
The verse wording to eat or to sell to a non-Jew answers that question.
Rabbi Meir concludes that both resident alien and gentile may receive the carrion by giving or by selling.
Rabbi Yehuda holds the verse means as written: resident alien by giving, gentile only by selling.
The Gemara remarks that Rabbi Meir's reading is reasonable.
Rabbi Yehuda objects: if Rabbi Meir were right, the verse would simply say give, eat and sell, so why the word or?
The word or teaches that the matters are to be understood as they are written, which is Rabbi Yehuda's point.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Meir would explain the word or.
Rabbi Meir explains that the word or teaches giving to a resident alien takes precedence over selling to a gentile.
Rabbi Yehuda reasons that one is commanded to sustain a resident alien but not a Canaanite, so no verse is needed for precedence.
Another baraita: the verse not to show them favor teaches that one may not praise gentiles.
The Gemara says this baraita supports Rav, who prohibits saying how beautiful a gentile woman is.
An objection from a baraita: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel praised a beautiful gentile woman, and Rabbi Akiva reacted to a gentile woman, so Rav's view seems contradicted.
Rav's reply: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was praising God for creating beautiful creatures, not praising the woman herself.
The Gemara asks whether one is permitted to gaze at a woman at all.
An objection from a verse, Deuteronomy 23:10, is raised against permitting the gaze.
The baraita teaches that a person must not gaze at a beautiful woman, even unmarried, nor at a married woman, even an ugly one.

20b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita forbids gazing at a woman's colored garments and at animals mating, even if one could see like the Angel of Death.
Lore about the Angel of Death, who kills the sick with a drop of poison from his sword, which makes the corpse putrefy.
Rabban Gamliel did not look on purpose; he saw the woman unexpectedly when they each turned a corner.
Shmuel holds the prohibition on a woman's colored garments applies even when they are spread out on a wall, not only when worn.
Rav Pappa limits the prohibition to garments whose owner one knows.
Rava says the baraita's precise wording, not saying colored garments generally, shows the prohibition applies only to known owners.
Rav Hisda limits the prohibition to old, worn garments; new garments raise no concern.
Rav Hisda argues that otherwise one could not hand a new woman's garment to a launderer who must look at it.
The reasoning is refuted: by the same logic, Rav Yehuda's permission to mate animals would be a problem, so the launderer must be occupied with work.
The Gemara asks whether the Angel of Death's poison view disagrees with Shmuel's father.
Shmuel's father reports the Angel of Death said he would uncover the slaughter place if not for human dignity, implying slaughter.
Perhaps the drop of poison cuts the two slaughter organs, so the Angel kills in a manner like slaughter.
The baraita's clause about putrefaction supports Rabbi Hanina bar Kahana.
Rabbi Hanina bar Kahana teaches that one who wants a dead relative not to putrefy should turn the body face down immediately.
A baraita cites the verse on keeping from evil, linking impure thoughts by day to nocturnal impurity.
Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's chain: Torah leads to diligence, cleanliness, purity, piety, humility, fear of sin, holiness, the Divine Spirit and resurrection.
Piety is greater than all the others, as Psalms 89:20 speaks of the pious ones.
This contradicts Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's view.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds humility is greater than all the others.
Isaiah 61:1 says anointed to bring tidings to the humble, not the pious, which proves humility is greatest.
The Gemara cites the mishna: one may not sell a gentile items attached to the ground, and so on.
A baraita: one may sell a gentile a tree on the condition he cuts it down, as Rabbi Yehuda holds.
Rabbi Meir says one may sell a gentile only a tree that has already been cut down.
Rabbi Yehuda permits selling fodder on the condition that the gentile cuts it down.
Rabbi Meir permits selling fodder only once it has been cut down.
Rabbi Yehuda permits selling standing grain on the condition that the gentile harvests it.
Rabbi Meir permits selling grain only once it has been harvested.
The Gemara explains why all three cases are needed: a tree or grain would be treated differently from fodder, since improvement is visible or not.
The Gemara explains that if only the two cases were taught, one could think Rabbi Yehuda permits sale when improvement is not recognizable, so fodder needs its own ruling.
Likewise, teaching only fodder would leave the tree and grain unresolved, so the dispute must be stated in all three cases.
A dilemma: may large livestock be sold to a gentile on the condition that he slaughters it?
The Gemara explains the two possible reasons for the dilemma, one about the gentile's control over the animal and one about the permissibility regardless.
A baraita resolves it: one may sell large livestock on the condition the gentile slaughters it, per Rabbi Yehuda, while Rabbi Meir allows only a slaughtered animal.
The mishna teaches that one may not rent a house to a gentile in Eretz Yisrael, and certainly not fields, and the same applies in Syria.

21a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: in the diaspora one may sell houses and rent fields to gentiles, according to Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yosei's ruling: in Eretz Yisrael houses may be rented but not fields; in Syria and abroad the sale and rental rules are set out.
Even where renting a house is allowed, it may not be rented as a residence, because the gentile would bring idolatry into it.
The verse about not bringing an abomination into one's house supports that prohibition.
Likewise a bathhouse may never be rented to a gentile, since it bears the owner's name and would look like Jewish operation on Shabbat.
Why is the rule about fields stated as obvious, more than the rule about houses?
Proposed answer: fields carry two problems, aiding gentile settlement and releasing the land from tithes.
If so, houses also have two problems, settlement and releasing them from the mezuza obligation, so the answer fails.
Rav Mesharshiyya replies that mezuza is the resident's obligation, so an empty rented house is not subject to it.
The mishnah: in Syria one may rent houses but not fields to gentiles.
What is the difference that prohibits selling houses in Syria?
The concern is that selling in Syria would lead to selling houses in Eretz Yisrael.
If so, renting houses should also be banned in Syria; and renting fields in Syria is itself a decree on a decree, yet it is issued.
Rabbi Meir holds that a conquest by an individual counts as conquest, so Syria is treated as part of the Land.
Fields carry two problems, so the Sages decreed against renting them in Syria, but houses lack them and were not restricted.
Explanation of Rabbi Meir's ruling: fields outside the Land were restricted for sale because of their two problems, houses were not.
The mishnah: Rabbi Yosei says in Eretz Yisrael one may rent houses but not fields to gentiles.
Fields have two problems so they were restricted, while houses lack them and were not, which explains Rabbi Yosei's rule.
The mishnah: Rabbi Yosei says in Syria one may sell houses and rent fields, but not sell fields.
Rabbi Yosei holds an individual's conquest is not a conquest, so only fields in Syria were decreed against; houses were not.
The mishnah: outside the Land one may sell both houses and fields to gentiles.
What is the reason for permitting this outside the Land?
Because the land is distant, the Sages did not decree, unlike Syria which is near Eretz Yisrael.
Rav Yehuda says Shmuel rules the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei: houses may be sold to gentiles outside the Land.
Rav Yosef adds the condition that one must not make the purchase into a gentile settlement.
A tanna teaches that a settlement must contain at least three people.
Challenge: one Jew may sell to one gentile, and neighbors to two more, creating a gentile settlement anyway.
Abaye replies that we are not commanded to place a stumbling block before one who places it before the blind.
The mishnah adds that even where a house may be rented to a gentile, it may not be rented as a residence.
By inference, the mishnah implies there is a place where no house may be rented to a gentile at all.

21b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The unattributed mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, since Rabbi Yosei would permit renting houses to gentiles everywhere.
The mishnah: in every place one may not rent a bathhouse to a gentile.
A baraita: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel forbids renting a bathhouse to a gentile, since it bears the owner's name and is used for work on Shabbat and Festivals.
What is the halakha for renting a bathhouse to a Samaritan, and may he work during the intermediate days of Festival?
We too heat bathhouses during the intermediate days of Festival, so the concern applies to Samaritans as well.
The Gemara infers: renting a field to a gentile is apparently permitted; what is the halakha on this point?
The reason is that the gentile sharecropper works for his own tenancy, and people know this.
If so, why not say the same for a bathhouse, that the sharecropper works for his tenancy?
People do not usually arrange a sharecropper over a bathhouse, so the gentile is assumed to be a hired worker for the Jew.
A baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar forbids renting one's field to a Samaritan, since it bears the owner's name and he would work on the Festival.
The Gemara infers that renting to a gentile is permitted, so why not say the same sharecropper reasoning applies to a Samaritan?

22a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar does not accept that a gentile sharecropper works for his own tenancy rather than for the Jewish owner.
If so, why is renting to a gentile permitted, and why can one not say the same about a Samaritan?
A Samaritan will not comply, since he claims to be more learned and knows the work is permitted on those days.
Why does R. Shimon ben Elazar give the reason of the owner's name rather than the stumbling-block verse?
R. Shimon ben Elazar gives two reasons: the stumbling-block prohibition, and additionally the field bears the owner's name.
Saffron growers jointly owned a field, with the gentile working Shabbat and the Jew Sunday; Rava permitted dividing profits equally.
Ravina objects from a baraita: a Jew may not split profits by Shabbat work unless the partnership stipulated it from the outset.
Rava was embarrassed, but it emerged the growers had stipulated the arrangement from the start, so Rava ruled correctly.
Rav Geviha says the case concerned orla saplings, one partner tending them in orla years and the other profiting later; Rava permitted it.
Did Ravina not object to Rava's ruling?
No, Ravina meant to support Rava's ruling, not to object to it.
But wasn't Rava embarrassed by Ravina's statement?
That never happened.
If the partners made no specification, and did not calculate profits equally, what is the halakha?
Attempted answer from a baraita: a stipulated arrangement is permitted, implying that unstipulated is prohibited.
Say instead the last clause: calculating profits is prohibited, which implies that unspecified arrangements are permitted.
No inference can be drawn from this baraita, because its two inferences contradict each other.
The colophon closing the chapter, which begins the next chapter's mishnah.
Mishnah: one may not keep an animal in gentile inns, because they are suspected of bestiality.
Mishnah: a woman may not seclude herself with gentiles, because they are suspected of forbidden sexual relations.
Mishnah: a man may not seclude himself with gentiles, because they are suspected of bloodshed; the Gemara follows.

22b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita permits buying animals from gentiles for offerings without concern for bestiality, which seems to contradict the mishnah's suspicion.
Why is there no concern about idolatry or worship, but there is concern about bestiality by the mishnah's own logic?
Rav: a gentile protects his own animal from becoming barren, so he does not engage in bestiality with it.
That works for females, which can become barren, but what can be said about males?
Rav Kahana: gentiles also refrain with males, because bestiality weakens the animal's flesh.
A baraita permits buying animals from a gentile shepherd, which seems to conflict with the concern that he abused the animal.
The shepherd fears forfeiting his wages if caught, so he refrains.
A baraita forbids delivering an animal to a gentile shepherd, which seems to conflict with the wage-forfeit explanation.
Gentiles watch one another and fear being caught, so they do not abuse another gentile's animal, though Jews are not watched; a sinner knows his fellow sinner.
If so, why not forbid buying male animals from a gentile woman, since no harm to the animal would deter her?
She would be seen with the animal following her in public, so she fears discovery.
Rav Yosef: a widow may not raise a dog for fear of bestiality, yet a dog would follow her in public, so it seems she should be allowed one.
The dog would also follow her when she throws meat, so people would attribute it to the meat and not suspect her.
What is the reason that female animals may not be secluded with women?
Mar Ukva bar Hama: gentiles frequent other men's wives, and if he cannot find her, he may bestialize an animal instead.
Alternatively, even when he finds the wife he may still bestialize an animal, since a Jew's animal is more appealing to gentiles, from Rabbi Yohanan on Eve's contamination.
If so, Jews should also be suspected of bestiality, since Eve's contamination affects all people.
The Jewish people at Sinai had their contamination removed, while gentiles who did not stand at Sinai retain it.
A dilemma: with regard to birds, are gentiles suspected of bestiality?
Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel citing Rabbi Hanina: a gentile had sex with a goose he bought, then strangled, roasted and ate it.
Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti saw an Arab carve a thigh of meat to allow penetration, then roast and eat it, showing suspicion regarding fowl.

23a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ravina: the mishnah speaks ab initio, while the baraita permitting such animals speaks after the fact.
From where do we know there is a difference between ab initio and after the fact, given the mishnah on secluding with gentiles?
A mishnah in Ketubot seems to show a woman imprisoned by gentiles is not assumed to have been raped, contradicting the seclusion ruling.
Doesn't this show that ab initio and after the fact are treated differently?
Not necessarily: even after the fact one cannot assume no intercourse; the Ketubot ruling rests on the husband's financial interest.
The latter clause of that Ketubot mishnah, where a capital captive is forbidden, shows the difference is the gentiles' incentive.
Rabbi Pedat: the contradiction is resolved because the mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer and the baraita follows the Rabbis.
Mishnah on the red heifer: Rabbi Eliezer forbids buying it from gentiles, while the Rabbis permit it.
Pedat explains the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer is concerned about bestiality, the Rabbis are not.
But how do we know this? Perhaps everyone agrees there is no concern about bestiality, and Rabbi Eliezer's reason is something else.
Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning follows Rav's ruling, that a load placed on a red heifer renders it unfit, so the concern is about labor.
One Sage is concerned that a gentile used the heifer for labor, and the other is not.
It cannot be that Rabbi Eliezer fears sacks placed on the heifer, since the gentile would not forfeit a sale for so small a gain; likewise bestiality should be counted as small.
With bestiality the gentile's inclination overcomes him, so he would act despite his loss, unlike the labor case.
Alternatively, everyone agrees there is no concern about bestiality, and Rabbi Eliezer's reason is as Sheila taught.
Sheila's baraita: Rabbi Eliezer derives from the verse that the children of Israel take the red heifer, and gentiles do not.
It cannot be so, since the latter clause says Rabbi Eliezer disqualifies all offerings bought from gentiles, and other offerings lack a term of taking.
Perhaps the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Eliezer on the other offerings as well.

23b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Only the red heifer is special because of its high price; for other offerings Rabbi Eliezer's ruling is conceded.
But a baraita permits buying animals from gentiles for offerings, and it reflects neither Rabbi Eliezer's view nor the Rabbis' view.
A baraita explicitly shows Rabbi Eliezer's colleagues answered him with Isaiah 60:7, so the Rabbis permit all offerings.
The disagreement concerns only suspicion; if bestiality is certain the animal is disqualified, so the red heifer is an altar-consecrated animal.
The red heifer differs because the Torah calls its purification offering by the term for a sin-offering.
If so, a red heifer born by caesarean should be disqualified, yet Rabbi Shimon deems it fit, contrary to Rabbi Yohanan's report of his view.
The red heifer differs: a blemish disqualifies it, and corruption, licentiousness and idolatry are also a blemish, as Rabbi Yishmael's school explains.
Corruption refers to licentiousness in the generation of the flood, and to idolatry in Deuteronomy 4:16, so both disqualify the red heifer like a blemish.
Sheila's baraita: Rabbi Eliezer derives from the verse that the children of Israel take the heifer and gentiles do not.
If that is so, the same logic applies to Tabernacle donations and all Temple items, which would then not be bought from gentiles.
This cannot be right: Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel on a story of Rabbi Eliezer and Dama ben Netina, a gentile who honored his father and was approached for ephod stones.

24a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Teaching that the profit from the transaction was six hundred thousand, while Rav Kahana gives eight hundred thousand.
Story of the keys left under the father's head, so the son would not disturb him, showing the ephod stones were bought from gentiles.
The onyx stones mark a break in the list of Tabernacle contributions, so the earlier prohibition does not extend to them.
Objection: a later verse joins the stones back to the list with a connecting conjunction, so the prohibition would apply again.
A baraita about Dama ben Netina's red heifer, where the Sages wished to buy it from a gentile, offered as support for the attack.
Reply: the heifer was actually bought through Jewish merchants, so the purchase was made from a gentile only indirectly.
Objection: the Gemara asks whether Rabbi Eliezer is then not concerned about bestiality, contradicting the view that his reason is only scriptural.
Baraita reporting that the Sages bought the heifer from a gentile named Dama, or Remetz, offered as evidence against Rabbi Eliezer.
Rabbi Eliezer's reply: the case proves nothing, since Jews safeguarded the heifer from birth, which shows his concern about bestiality.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer has two requirements: a Jewish seller, and concern about bestiality with the animal.
Objection: perhaps the mother was subjected to bestiality while pregnant, since Jews guarded only from birth, so the guarding is insufficient.
Rava's principle: the offspring of an animal that gored or was bestially abused is forbidden, as if the mother and offspring were treated together.
Reply: Rabbi Eliezer meant that Jews guarded the animal from the moment of conception, which answers the worry about pregnancy.
Objection: perhaps the mother was subjected to bestiality before conception, which the guarding from conception does not cover.
A mishna in Tractate Temura permits offspring of disqualified animals, and a baraita records that Rabbi Eliezer prohibits them, supporting the concern.
Rava's teaching, which resolves the difficulty: the dispute is only about animals that were consecrated at the time of bestiality.
Rav Huna bar Hinnana's version of Rav Naḥman's teaching, reversing which case is disputed, so the difficulty remains.
Objection: under this version, nothing remains to be said, so Rabbi Eliezer must still worry about bestiality before conception.
Reply: say the Jews guarded the mother from the moment the heifer was conceived.
Objection: perhaps the heifer's grandmother line was subjected to bestiality, which would also undermine the guarding.
Reply: we are not concerned to such an extent, so the earlier guarding suffices without tracing the whole line.
Question: how do we know that the mother would give birth to a red heifer, which is what justified guarding her?
Rav Kahana: they passed a red cup before the mother as the male mounted her, so the offspring would come out red.
Question: if that is so, and a red heifer can be induced so simply, why is its price so expensive?
Reply: two hairs of a different color disqualify the heifer, so this induced method is unreliable and costly.
Question: what is different about Dama's cows, that the Jews preferred to buy from a gentile rather than induce birth?
Rav Kahana: Dama ben Netina owned a herd known to produce red heifers, so they preferred those cows.
Narrative: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa, one of whom states that Rabbi Eliezer disqualified all offerings bought from gentiles.
Question: what did Rabbi Eliezer's colleagues object to him with, in response to his position?
Colleagues cite Isaiah 60:7, saying gentile offerings are accepted on the altar, as support against Rabbi Eliezer.
Rabbi Eliezer's reply: in the future all gentiles will be calculating converts, so they will not be suspected of bestiality.
Rav Yosef asks which verse teaches that the gentiles will convert.
Zephaniah 3:9 is cited: God will turn the peoples to a pure language to serve Him together, indicating future conversion.
Abaye objects that perhaps the nations will only abandon idolatry while still engaging in forbidden sexual relations.
Rav Yosef replies: the verse says to serve Him with one consent, which shows they will accept all of God's commandments.
Rav Pappa and Rav Zevid transmit the same discussion differently, and both say Rabbi Eliezer disqualified all gentile offerings.
Question: what did Rabbi Eliezer's colleagues object to him with?
Colleagues cite Isaiah 60:7 about the flocks of Kedar being accepted on the altar, as an objection to Rabbi Eliezer.
Rabbi Eliezer replies that all gentiles will become calculating converts in the future, so the offerings are not suspect.
Question: what is the verse from which it is derived that the gentiles will convert?
The verse about turning the peoples to a pure language so all call on God's name, cited as proof of future conversion.
Rav Yosef objects that perhaps they will only withdraw from idolatry while continuing their other sexual transgressions.
Abaye replies: the verse says to serve Him with one consent, which is written, so the objection fails.
Objection from Exodus 10:25: Moses asked Pharaoh for offerings, which suggests gentile-sourced animals were acceptable as sacrifices.
Reply: the halakha before the giving of the Torah was different, so the earlier practice does not apply afterward.
Another objection from Exodus 18:12: Yitro, who was not a Jew, brought burnt offerings and sacrifices to God.
Reply: Yitro's incident also occurred before the giving of the Torah, so it does not prove the practice applies later.
Objection: this works only according to the view that Yitro preceded the Torah, but what of the one who holds otherwise?

24b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection: the Yitro incident happened after the Torah was given, so how could his offerings be accepted from a gentile?
Reply: Yitro must have purchased the animals from a Jew, so the offering came from Jewish-owned livestock.
Saul spared the best of the Amalekite flock and herd to sacrifice to the Lord, offered as a proof that gentile-owned animals were sacrificed.
The word best refers to monetary value: the animals were sold, and the proceeds bought other animals for sacrifice.
Question: what is different about the best animals, that they were sold rather than several inferior ones?
Reply: the superior animal was sold so that buyers would eagerly jump at the chance to purchase it.
Verse from II Samuel 24:22 where Araunah offers oxen and cart equipment to David, cited to show acceptance of gentile animals.
Rav Naḥman: Araunah was a resident alien who observed the seven Noahide mitzvot, so he was not suspected of bestiality.
Question: what is the meaning of the term morigim used in the verse?
Ulla explains that it is a turbil bed, a serrated threshing board, and this is what the term means.
Rav Yosef asks which verse is the source for the meaning of morigim.
Isaiah 41:15 describes a new threshing board with sharp teeth, which supports the meaning of morigim as a threshing tool.
Objection from I Samuel 6:14: the Jews sacrificed the Philistines cattle as burnt offerings, apparently accepting gentile-owned animals.
Reply: that sacrifice was a temporary ruling issued for an exceptional situation, so it does not establish general halakha.
The Gemara says this reply is reasonable, since otherwise there is a further difficulty that the offerings were female cows.
Reply: what is the difficulty, since perhaps the cows were offered upon a private altar, which is permitted.
Rav Adda bar Ahava's principle: a female burnt offering is fit to be offered on a private altar.
Question: from where do we derive that a female burnt offering is fit to be sacrificed on a private altar?
Samuel offered a milking lamb as a burnt offering on a private altar, from I Samuel 7:9, showing that females are fit.
Objection: the verb vaya'alehu is in the masculine form, which implies that the lamb sacrificed was male.
Reply: although read as masculine, the word is written in the feminine form, teaching that a female may be offered on a private altar.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: a cow under three years old becomes barren from bestiality, while an older one does not, so the baraita is explained.
The Gemara recaps that every refutation raised was answered by assuming the animals were under three years old.
Come and hear: the verse about cattle offered from animals under three years old is cited as a further objection.
Rav Huna son of Rav Natan objects: if so, the same reasoning must apply to the nursing cows of another verse.
The verse about the cows' calves kept at home is cited, implying the cows had already given birth, which challenges Rabbi Yoḥanan.
Question: can a cow under three years old actually give birth at all?
A baraita states that the first offspring of a cow or donkey bought from a gentile under three is certainly the priest's.
Reply: rather, the matter is clear as first answered, so the actions in that verse were due to a provisional edict.
Verse I Samuel 6:12 describes the cows taking the straight way toward Beit Shemesh, as the basis for the next question.
Question: what is the meaning of the word vayyisharna in the verse?
Rabbi Yoḥanan in the name of Rabbi Meir: they sang a song. Rav: they turned their faces toward the Ark and sang.
Question: what song did they sing?
Rabbi Yoḥanan in the name of Rabbi Meir: they sang the song of Exodus 15:1, as Moses and the children of Israel sang.
Rabbi Yoḥanan's own view: the song is the verse from Isaiah calling to give thanks and proclaim the Lord's name.
Isaiah 12:4 is cited as the text of the song: give thanks to the Lord, call upon His name, and declare His deeds.
Resh Lakish: it was an orphaned psalm, a psalm without a named author, beginning with Psalms 98:1 about the new song.
Rabbi Elazar: the song was the psalm beginning with the Lord reigns and peoples tremble, Psalms 99:1.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani: the song was the psalm beginning with the Lord reigns and is clothed in majesty, Psalms 93:1.
Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa: they sang a non-biblical song about the acacia ark, overlaid with gold, exalted by the palace book.
Rav Ashi teaches Rabbi Yitzḥak's statement in connection with the verse about the Ark setting forward.
Numbers 10:35 describes the Ark setting forward and Moses calling for God to arise and scatter the enemies, which is the verse cited.
Question: what did the Jewish people recite at that moment of the Ark setting forward?
Rabbi Yitzḥak: they recited the acacia song, which he cites as the answer to the question about what was sung.
Rav asks on what basis the Persians call a book devir, by which they refer to a sifra.
Judges 1:11 states that the name Debir was formerly Kiriath Sefer, which explains the Persian term for a book.
Rav Ashi asks on what basis the Persians call a menstruating woman dashtana.
Genesis 31:35, where Rachel says the manner of women is upon her, is cited as the source for dashtana.

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Joshua 10:13 about the sun standing still is cited, asking whether this is not written in the book of Yashar.
Question: what is meant by the book of Yashar?
Rabbi Yoḥanan: it is Genesis, the book of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, called the righteous, citing Numbers 23:10.
Question: where is the sun's standing still for Joshua alluded to in the Torah?
Genesis 48:19 says his seed will become a multitude of nations, offered as the allusion.
Question: when did that multitude of nations come about?
It came about when the sun stood still for Joshua, as Joshua 10:13 says it did not hasten to set for a day.
Question: how long did the sun remain suspended before it set?
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: twenty-four hours, six hours of travel and six of standing, repeated twice, making a full day.
Rabbi Elazar: thirty-six hours, with six hours of travel and twelve of standing, repeated, totaling a full day.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani: forty-eight hours, reading the verse's two phrases as describing an initial and a later suspension.
Some say the Sages disagree about the added time rather than the total, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's view is restated.
Rabbi Elazar's view on the additional time: thirty-six hours added, with the second suspension referred to in the verse.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani's view: forty-eight hours, reasoning from the verse juxtaposing the sun's suspension to its motion.
A baraita teaches that the sun stood still for Moses and for Nakdimon ben Guryon, just as it did for Joshua.
Question: from where do we derive that the sun stood still for Moses?
A verbal analogy between the words I will begin in Deuteronomy 2:25 and Joshua 3:7 teaches the sun stood still for Moses.
Rabbi Yoḥanan derives it from a verbal analogy using the word deliver, comparing Deuteronomy 2:25 with Joshua 10:12.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani: no analogy is needed, since Deuteronomy 2:25 itself shows the nations trembled when the sun stood still for Moses.
Objection: Joshua 10:14 says there was no day like it before or after, so the sun cannot have stood still for Moses too.
Reply: perhaps the hours of suspension for Moses were fewer than those for Joshua.
Alternative reply: there were no hailstones in Moses's case, but hailstones fell in Joshua's case, as Joshua 10:11 describes.
II Samuel 1:18 says to teach the sons of Judah the bow, and that it is written in the book of Yashar.
Question: again, what is the book of Yashar?
Rabbi Yoḥanan: it is the book of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, called the righteous, as written in Numbers 23:10.
Numbers 23:10 is cited: let me die the death of the righteous and let my end be like his.
Question: where is teaching Judah the bow alluded to in the Torah?
Genesis 49:8 says Judah's brothers will praise him and his hand will be on the nape of his enemies.
Question: what form of warfare requires a hand placed opposite the nape?
It must refer to the bow, which is the warfare the verse describes.
Rabbi Elazar: the book of Yashar is the book of Deuteronomy.
Question: why was it called the book of Yashar?
Deuteronomy 6:18 says to do what is right and good in the eyes of the Lord, explaining the name.
Question: where is the bow alluded to in Deuteronomy?
Deuteronomy 33:7 says his hands shall contend for him, offered as the allusion.
Question: what form of warfare requires the use of two hands?
It must refer to the bow, which requires two hands.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani: the book of Yashar is the book of Judges.
Question: why was the book of Judges called the book of Yashar?
Judges 17:6 says every man did what was right in his own eyes, explaining the name.
Question: where is the teaching of war alluded to in Judges?
Judges 3:2 says the generations of Israel were to be taught war, offered as the allusion.
Question: what form of warfare requires teaching?
It must refer to the bow, which needs to be taught.
Question: from where do we derive that the verse in Judges refers to Judah?
Judges 1:1-2 says Judah shall go up first against the Canaanites, which identifies Judah as the referent.
I Samuel 9:24 describes the cook taking up the thigh and what was upon it and setting it before Saul.
Question: what does the phrase and that which was upon it refer to?
Rabbi Yoḥanan: it refers to the thigh and the tail.
Question: why is the tail referred to as that which was upon it?
Because the thigh supports the tail, which rests upon it.
Rabbi Elazar: the verse refers to the thigh and the breast.
Question: why is the breast referred to as that which was upon it?
Because the breast is placed upon the thigh when it is waved as a sacrifice.
Explanation of Rabbi Elazar's reason: the breast is waved, so the thigh is the base on which it is raised.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani: the verse refers to the thigh and the cap, the top part of the leg.
Question: why is the cap referred to as that which was upon it?
Because the cap stands above the thigh.
The mishna teaches that a woman may not seclude herself with gentiles.
Question: what case is the mishna dealing with?
If it deals with a woman secluded with one gentile, is that permitted for a Jewish man with a woman?
Objection: a mishna teaches that one man may not seclude himself even with two women, so one man with one woman is forbidden.

25b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rather, the mishna must refer to a woman secluded with three gentiles, not two, which resolves the earlier difficulty.
Question: is this permitted in the corresponding case of Jews who are steeped in sexual immorality?
The mishna teaches that one woman may be secluded with two men.
Shmuel's teaching, transmitted by Rav Yehuda: the leniency applies only to men of fit morals, and not even ten immoral men may be alone with a woman.
An incident in which ten men carried a woman out on a bier and had relations with her, offered as support for Shmuel.
Reply: the mishna is needed where the gentile's wife is present, since a gentile's wife does not guard him while a Jew's wife does.
Objection: the prohibition should instead be derived from concern for bloodshed, not from sexual immorality.
Rabbi Yirmeya: we are dealing with a distinguished woman whom gentiles fear to kill, though sexual concern remains.
Rav Idi bar Avin: a woman carries her weapons upon her, so her sex itself protects her from being killed.
Question: what is the practical difference between these two explanations?
The difference concerns a woman distinguished among men but unattractive to women, who is therefore not at risk of sexual misconduct.
A baraita in accordance with Rav Idi bar Avin: a woman may not be secluded with gentiles even with her protection, due to suspicion of sexual misconduct.
The mishna's further ruling: a person may not be secluded with gentiles, due to suspicion of sexual misconduct.
A baraita on how a Jew should walk with a gentile on the road: place him to the right if armed with a sword, to the left if with a stick.
A baraita on ascending or descending: the Jew should be above the gentile, and should not bend down before him.
Advice to misstate one's destination and to extend the journey stated to the gentile, as Jacob did with Esau.
Genesis 33:14, where Jacob tells Esau he will journey on to Seir, supports misstating the destination.
Genesis 33:17 says Jacob journeyed to Succoth instead of Seir, showing the misstatement in practice.
An incident with students of Rabbi Akiva who were stopped by bandits, misstated their destination, and were spared by the bandits.
Introduction to another incident involving Rav Menashe, which begins on the next daf.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continuation of the anecdote: thieves meet Rav Menashe on the road, ask where he is going, and he names Pumbedita.
When he reached Bei Torta, he parted from the thieves, who then addressed him as a student of Yehuda the swindler.
The thieves accuse Rav Menashe's teacher of being a swindler, which challenges his honor.
Rav Menashe replies that they cannot know Rav Yehuda well enough to accuse him of swindling others.
Rav Menashe prays that these people be subject to Rav Yehuda's ban of excommunication.
The curse took effect: the thieves failed for twenty-two years, then sought the ban to be lifted.
One weaver who did not come to lift the ban was eaten by a lion.
The adage: a weaver who is impudent rather than shy has a year deducted from his allotted years.
Come and see the difference between the Babylonian thieves, who denounced Rav Yehuda, and the Eretz Yisrael bandits, who praised Rabbi Akiva.
Mishna: a Jewish woman may not deliver a gentile woman's child, since that child will worship idols; the reverse is permitted.
Mishna: a Jewish woman may not nurse a gentile woman's child; a gentile woman may nurse a Jewish child on the Jewish woman's property.
Baraita: the Jewish woman may not deliver for a gentile, and gentiles may not deliver for Jews, since they are suspected of bloodshed, per Rabbi Meir.
The Rabbis: a gentile may deliver for a Jew when other women stand over her, but not when she is alone with the mother.
Rabbi Meir: even when others stand over her, the midwife might press the infant's temple and kill him without it being seen.
A story in which a gentile midwife boasts of killing many Jewish infants, offered as evidence for Rabbi Meir's concern.
The Rabbis reply that she was merely boasting in words to establish herself, and did not really kill anyone.
Restatement of the mishna's second clause: a Jewish woman may not nurse a gentile woman's child.
Baraita: the Jewish woman may not nurse a gentile child because she raises an idolater, and gentiles may not nurse Jewish children, per Rabbi Meir.
The Rabbis: a gentile may nurse a Jewish child when others stand over her, but not when she is alone with the child.
Rabbi Meir: even with others standing over her, she might smear poison on her breast and kill the child while nursing.
The Gemara explains why both midwife and wet nurse cases must be stated, to avoid inferring the wrong conclusion about each.
Conversely, if only the wet nurse case had been taught, the midwife case would be inferred the other way, so both are needed.
Objection from a baraita: a Jewish woman may deliver a gentile woman's child for payment but not for free, which seems to conflict.
Rav Yosef: it is allowed for payment, because refusing paid delivery would create enmity between Jews and gentiles.
Rav Yosef's further proposal: delivering a gentile child on Shabbat for payment is permitted, due to the concern for enmity.
Abaye objects: she can tell the gentile that Jewish women keep Shabbat and we desecrate it for them, while theirs do not, so enmity is avoided.
Rav Yosef's further proposal: nursing a gentile child for payment is permitted, due to the concern for enmity.
Abaye objects: she can give an excuse, such as wishing to marry or not wishing to become repulsive to her husband.
Rav Yosef's analogous proposal: raising a gentile shepherd from a pit for payment is permitted, due to the concern for enmity.
Abaye objects: one may give the gentile an excuse, such as needing to help a son on the roof or attending a court date.
Rabbi Abbahu taught before Rabbi Yoḥanan the baraita about not raising gentiles or small-animal shepherds from a pit.

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: heretics, informers and apostates are lowered into a pit but not raised out of it.
R. Yohanan tells R. Abbahu that his own teaching conflicts with lowering apostates into a pit.
Verse on returning lost property, read to include the apostate within that obligation.
Objection: if apostates are included in lost-property duties, lowering them is wrong; remove the term here.
Proposed reconciliation: the two rulings concern apostates eating from appetite versus from defiance, and defiance makes one a heretic.
Rav Aha and Ravina disagree about how to define an apostate versus a heretic.
One opinion: eating from appetite makes one an apostate, while eating from defiance makes one a heretic.
The other opinion: even eating from defiance makes one an apostate.
Asks who then is the heretic, if defiance alone does not define one.
A heretic is one who worships idols.
Baraita: one who eats a single flea or mosquito is an apostate, seemingly contradicting the defiance view.
Objection: insects are unappetizing, so the eating must be defiance, yet the baraita calls it apostasy.
Reply: there the eater wants to taste forbidden food, so the act comes from appetite.
Quotes the Mishnah that heretics and apostates are lowered but not raised.
If lowering is already taught, why is it necessary to state that they are not raised?
Rav Sheshet: needed for a case with a ledge that lets the trapped person climb, which the rescuer scrapes off under a pretext.
Rabba and Rav Yosef: needed for a stone over the well mouth, which the Jew covers under a pretext.
Ravina: needed for a ladder, which the Jew removes under a pretext.
Baraita: a Jew may circumcise a gentile for conversion, but a gentile may not circumcise a Jew, per R. Meir.
The Rabbis: a gentile may circumcise a Jew only when others stand over him, not when they are alone.
R. Meir: not even with others watching, since the gentile could sever the Jew's penis.
Does R. Meir really forbid gentile circumcision entirely?
Objection from a baraita: in a city without a Jewish doctor, R. Meir prefers an Aramean over a Samaritan to circumcise.
R. Yehuda holds that the Samaritan should circumcise and the gentile should not.
Reply: the opinions are reversed, so R. Meir prefers a Samaritan and R. Yehuda prefers an Aramean.
Does R. Yehuda really permit a gentile to perform circumcision?
Objection: a baraita teaches that R. Yehuda considers gentile circumcision invalid.
Proof from Genesis 17:9 that the covenant, meaning circumcision, belongs only to Abraham's descendants.
Rejects the reversal as the resolution; the two views are not inverted.
What case are the two statements of R. Meir actually about?

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Resolution: the lenient ruling concerns an expert physician, as Rav Dimi reported from Eretz Yisrael.
R. Yohanan: a physician recognized as an expert for the public may be relied on for healing.
Does R. Yehuda really permit a Samaritan to circumcise?
Baraita: a Samaritan may not circumcise a Jew, since he does it for the sake of Mount Gerizim, per R. Yehuda.
R. Yosei objects: circumcision need not be done for its own sake, so a Samaritan may circumcise until death, conflicting with R. Yehuda.
Resolution: reverse the baraita's attributions; the conflict is between R. Yehuda HaNasi and R. Yehuda bar Ilai, not a contradiction.
