Baraita of R. Yehuda HaNasi: Genesis 17:9 shows that a gentile's circumcision is invalid.
Rav Hisda asks the basis for R. Yehuda's view that circumcision must be performed for the sake of the mitzva.
Verses for each view: Exodus 12:48 'to the Lord' for R. Yehuda, Genesis 17:13 'himmol yimmol' for R. Yosei.
Objection: according to R. Yosei, isn't 'to the Lord' written about circumcision?
That phrase refers to the Passover offering, not to circumcision.
Objection: according to R. Yehuda, isn't the doubled verb 'himmol yimmol' written, teaching that anyone may circumcise?
The Torah speaks in ordinary human idiom, so the doubled verb teaches nothing new.
Asked: from where is a gentile's circumcision invalid?
Daru bar Pappa in Rav's name: Genesis 17:9, 'you shall keep My covenant', shows it.
R. Yohanan derives the same from 'himmol yimmol': only one who is already circumcised may circumcise.
What practical difference is there between these two derivations?
Difference: circumcised Arabs and gavnuni may circumcise under the himmol yimmol reading, but not under the covenant reading.
Objection from a mishnah on vows: circumcised gentiles still count as uncircumcised, undermining the proposed difference.
Another difference: a Jew whose brothers died from circumcision may circumcise under the covenant reading, but not under himmol yimmol.
Objection from the same vows mishnah: uncircumcised Jews count as circumcised, rejecting this difference too.
Difference concerning women: the covenant reading excludes women, while himmol yimmol treats women as naturally circumcised.
Is there anyone who says a woman may not perform circumcision?
Objection: Exodus 4:25 says Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son's foreskin.
Read 'vattakkah': she caused a flint to be taken, rather than taking it herself.
Objection: the same verse also says she cut the foreskin.
Read 'vattakhret': she caused another person to cut it.
Alternative: she began the act, and Moses came and completed the circumcision.
Mishnah: one may be treated by gentiles for monetary treatment but not life-threatening care; hair may not be cut by them, per R. Meir.
The Rabbis: a gentile may cut one's hair in the public thoroughfare, but not when the two are alone together.
What are monetary treatment and personal treatment?
Proposed reading: monetary treatment is paid for, and personal treatment is provided for free.
Objection: on that reading the mishnah should simply say treatment is allowed for pay but not for free.
Another reading: monetary treatment is for non-life-threatening matters, personal treatment for life-threatening ones.
Objection: Rav Yehuda forbids treatment even for a bloodletting wound, which is not life-threatening.
Resolution: monetary treatment concerns an animal, personal treatment concerns one's own body.
Rav Yehuda's ruling that even a bloodletting wound may not be treated by gentiles supports this reading.
Mar Ukva: one may follow a gentile's advice that a given potion helps or harms a given ailment.

27b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The gentile reasons that a Jew asks his opinion, so he would not risk his reputation with bad advice.
R. Yohanan: a patient in doubt whether he will live may not be treated by gentiles, but one certain to die may be.
Objection: even when death is certain, temporal life has value, so treatment by gentiles should be avoided.
From where do we know that concern for temporal life is set aside?
Four lepers outside a besieged city chose to risk going to the Arameans rather than starve, per II Kings 7:4.
Isn't there temporal life to lose, so the lepers should have stayed put? Is it not clear that temporal life is disregarded?
Baraita: one may not be treated by heretics even when only temporal life is at stake.
Incident: Rabbi Yishmael's nephew ben Dama was bitten by a snake, and Rabbi Yishmael refused a heretic's treatment.
Ben Dama asked to be treated, promising a verse permitting it, but died before finishing his argument.
R. Yishmael praises ben Dama for not violating his colleagues' ruling that a snake bites whoever breaches a fence.
Heresy differs because it is enticing, and one may be drawn after the heretic's views.
Restates R. Yishmael's point: ben Dama did not transgress his colleagues' words about the snake that bites a fence-breaker.
But ben Dama was also bitten by a snake before that declaration, so how can he be called fortunate?
The snake in the sages' curse has no remedy, whereas ben Dama's snake could be healed.
What verse would ben Dama have cited to justify being healed by a heretic?
Leviticus 18:5: one should live by the commandments and not die by them, which permits violating a prohibition to save a life.
R. Yishmael: this applies only in private; in public one may not transgress even to save a life.
Baraita of R. Yishmael: Leviticus 18:5 and Leviticus 22:32 show that one must not worship idols to save life, even under public duress.
R. Yohanan: one may not be treated by gentiles for any injury whose treatment would desecrate Shabbat.
A variant transmission attributes the same ruling to Rabba bar bar Hana in the name of R. Yohanan.

28a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Yohanan's ruling: one may not be treated by gentiles for an internal injury.
What is the difference between the two versions of R. Yohanan's statement?
Rav: injuries to the back of the hand or foot count as internal injuries, so Shabbat may be desecrated to treat them.
Rav Zutra in Rav's name: any injury requiring medical assessment to determine fatality permits desecrating Shabbat.
R. Yohanan via Rav Shemen bar Abba: a burning fever is like an internal injury, permitting Shabbat desecration.
From what point on the body is a wound considered internal?
R. Ami: from the lips inward.
R. Eliezer's dilemma: are wounds in the gums or teeth like external injuries, or like internal ones since they lie inside the mouth?
Abaye cites a mishnah forbidding sipping vinegar for tooth pain on Shabbat as a source.
Abaye infers that teeth causing great pain may be treated.
Perhaps the tanna means even great pain is mere concern, so the inference fails.
Incident: R. Yohanan obtained a remedy for tzafdina from a gentile matron and publicized it on Shabbat.
Objection: R. Yohanan's oath seems violated; the answer is that he told her beforehand he would reveal the remedy.
Inference: tzafdina is like an internal injury, since R. Yohanan could prepare its remedy on Shabbat.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak: tzafdina differs because it starts in the mouth and spreads to the intestines.
What are the symptoms of tzafdina?
Blood flows from the teeth; it arises from very cold wheat foods, very hot barley foods, and remains of fried fish.
What remedy did the matron give R. Yohanan?
R. Aha bar Rava: leaven water, olive oil and salt; Mar bar Rav Ashi: goose fat applied with a goose feather.
Abaye reports his own failed remedies until an Arab's treatment with burned olive seeds cured him.
How could R. Yohanan be treated by a gentile, given his own ruling against it?
Objection: R. Yohanan ruled that one may not be treated by gentiles for any injury where Shabbat is desecrated, and tzafdina qualifies.
Reply: an important person like R. Yohanan is different, since gentiles would not dare to kill him.
Objection: R. Abbahu was important, yet a heretic gave him a poisoned salve, so important people can still be harmed.
R. Yohanan's healer was an expert who would not risk her reputation by harming him.
Objection: R. Abbahu's healer was also an expert physician.
Abbahu's case differs: heretics willingly risk their own lives to harm Jews, as in 'let me die with the Philistines'.
Shmuel: a sword gash is a mortal danger, so Shabbat may be desecrated to treat it.
What is the remedy for this wound?
Cress soaked in vinegar stops the bleeding; salves of yavla and thornbush scrapings or trash worms encourage flesh to grow.
Rav Safra: these grape-like boils are forerunners of the Angel of Death.
What is the remedy for such boils?
Tigna soaked in honey or parsley soaked in wine; meanwhile rub a grape of matching color on the boil.
Rava: this abscess is a forerunner of fever.
What is the remedy for this abscess?
Snap the boil sixty times, then tear it vertically and horizontally; this applies only before its head has whitened.
R. Yaakov fell ill, opening a new report.

28b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Remedy for R. Abbahu's hemorrhoids: burn ice plant seeds wrapped in cloth, spread the ashes, and place a bramble kernel at the anus.
The bramble kernel treats the upper hemorrhoid; the lower one needs separate remedies.
What should one do for pain in the lower crevice?
Melt the fat of a goat that has not yet given birth, or burn dried pumpkin leaves or snail shells; oiled wax on worn cloth is a last resort.
R. Abbahu had ear pain, and R. Yohanan and other sages instructed him on a remedy.
What did they instruct him to do?
Kidney of a bald goat set on coals, with its tepid fluids applied to the ear; alternatives include beetle fat and a seven-wick flame set in the ear.
Second version: wax tapers oiled with alfalfa oil, one end in the flame and the other in the ear.
Further alternatives: dried uncombed fiber, or a salted century-old reed burned and placed in the ear, with care to avoid drafts.
Mnemonic: moist cures are prescribed for dry ailments and dry cures for moist ailments.
Rabba bar Zutra in R. Hanina's name: one may straighten dislocated ears on Shabbat; variants differ on whether by hand or by medicine.
What is the reason that manual straightening is restricted?
Rav Zutra bar Toviyya in Rav's name: blue eye shadow may be applied to a rebelling eye on Shabbat.
Initial reading: this applies only if the ingredients were ground the day before, not if ground or carried on Shabbat.
R. Yaakov's correction: Rav Yehuda permitted it even when grinding on Shabbat and carrying through a public domain.
Rav Yehuda permitted applying eye shadow on Shabbat.
Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda objects that whoever follows Yehuda desecrates Shabbat.
Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's own eye became ill, and he asks whether he may treat it on Shabbat.
Rav Yehuda: permitted for everyone else, but forbidden for him, since he disdained the lenient ruling.
Rav Yehuda cites Mar Shmuel's ruling, based on a maidservant whose eye popped out, since eye tendons depend on the heart valves.
What eye ailments count as life-threatening?
Discharge, pricking, bleeding, excessive tearing, inflammation, and onset of infection; not final healing stages or vision improvement.
Rav Yehuda: bathing is dangerous for hornet stings, thorn pricks, abscesses, eye pain, or fever; food and water remedies must match hot or cold conditions.

29a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rules on dangerous combinations of bloodletting, fish, cress and fever; a baraita lists foods one who let blood may not eat.
Abaye's remedy after eating forbidden items: drink mixed vinegar and wine, and defecate only east of the city because of the odor.
R. Yehoshua ben Levi: one may lift the unkali, a rib-edge that can bend, on Shabbat.
What is the unkali?
R. Abba: it is the rib-edge near the heart, which sometimes bends inward and must be straightened.
What is the cure for a bent unkali?
A mixture of cumin, caraway, mint, wormwood, satureja and hyssop.
The mixture is taken with wine for heart ailments.
Mnemonic: Psalms 104:15, 'wine that makes glad the heart of man'.
For ailments caused by wind, the mixture is drunk in water.
Mnemonic: Genesis 1:2, 'the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters'.
For childbirth, the mixture is drunk with beer.
Mnemonic: Genesis 24:15, 'with her pitcher upon her shoulder'.
Rav Aha, Rav Ashi and Rav Pappa each tried the herb mixture; Rav Pappa was healed by honey-sweetened water recommended by an Arab.
Baraita: six items permanently heal illness, such as cabbage, beets, chamomile water and animal organs; some add small fish.
Baraita: ten items such as ox meat, roast meat, egg, cress, bathing, cheese and liver return one to illness; some add nuts or cucumbers.
Mishnah: no haircut by gentiles anywhere; baraita: a Jew should watch the gentile barber in a mirror, and a Jew cutting a gentile leaves the forelock.
The Master's rule: a Jew should watch the gentile barber in a mirror.
In what circumstances does the mirror matter, given that in public no harm is expected and in private watching seems irrelevant?
It is a private domain, but the mirror makes the Jew appear important, deterring the barber from harming him.
Incident: Rav Hana bar Bizna had his hair cut by a gentile in a side street of Neharde'a.
The barber jokes that Rav Hana's throat invites the razor; Rav Hana admits he violated R. Meir's ruling.
Didn't Rav Hana also violate the Rabbis' ruling, since side streets are not a public domain?
Rav Hana holds that crowded side streets count as a public domain, so the Rabbis would permit it there.
Baraita: a Jew leaves a gentile's forelock uncut, as it is associated with idolatry.
How much space should be left around the forelock?
Rav Malkiyya in Rav Adda bar Ahava's name: three fingerbreadths in every direction.
Rav Hanina bar Rav Ika: the skewer, maidservant and follicle rulings are by Rav Malkiyyu; the forelock, burnt ashes and cheese rulings are by Rav Malkiyya.
Rav Pappa: rulings tied to a mishnah or baraita are Rav Malkiyya's, while independent rulings are Rav Malkiyyu's; a mnemonic says the Mishna is a queen.
What is the difference between Rav Hanina's and Rav Pappa's views, concerning maidservants?

29b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: gentile wine, vinegar made from wine, Hadrianic earthenware and hides are forbidden for benefit; R. Shimon ben Gamliel limits hides to circular tears.
R. Akiva: meat leaving an idol house is forbidden as offerings to the dead; business with those going to a festival is forbidden, but with those returning is allowed.
Gentile wineskins holding Jewish wine are forbidden for benefit per R. Meir; the Sages disagree.
Gentile grape residues are forbidden for benefit per R. Meir; the Sages forbid only moist residues and permit dry ones.
Gentile fish stew and Beit Unyaki cheese are forbidden for benefit per R. Meir; the Sages disagree.
R. Yehuda reports that R. Yishmael questioned R. Yehoshua while they were traveling.
Why did the Sages prohibit gentile cheeses?
R. Yehoshua: gentiles curdle cheese with the stomach of an unslaughtered carcass, which is not kosher.
R. Yishmael objects: the stomach of a burnt-offering is stricter yet permitted, so why forbid carcass-curdled cheese?
R. Yehoshua: gentiles curdle with the stomach of calves used for idolatry, which are forbidden for benefit.
R. Yishmael: then why forbid only eating the cheese rather than all benefit from it?
R. Yehoshua changes the subject: how should one read Song of Songs 1:2, dodekha or dodayikh?
R. Yishmael reads the feminine form dodayikh, which refers to the Jewish people.
R. Yehoshua cites Song of Songs 1:3, showing the following verse is masculine, so the preceding verse is masculine too.
From where do we know that gentile wine is forbidden?
Rabba bar Avuh: Deuteronomy 32:38 joins the fat of gentile offerings with their libation wine, so wine is forbidden like offerings.
From where do we know that the offering itself is forbidden for benefit?
Psalms 106:28, 'offerings to the dead', equates idol offerings with corpses, which are forbidden for benefit.
From where do we know that a corpse itself is forbidden for benefit?
Verbal analogy of 'there' between Miriam's death and the broken-neck heifer, which is forbidden for benefit.
From where do we know that the heifer is forbidden for benefit?
School of R. Yannai: the term of atonement is written for the heifer as for sacrifices, so it is forbidden for benefit like them.
Mishnah: gentile vinegar that was originally wine is forbidden.
Isn't this obvious, since souring should not lift the prohibition?
Rav Ashi: one seal suffices for gentile vinegar, since gentiles do not libate vinegar and would not bother forging a seal.
R. Ile'a: gentile cooked wine that was originally wine is forbidden.
Isn't this obvious, since cooking should not lift the prohibition?
Rav Ashi again: one seal suffices for cooked wine, since gentiles do not libate cooked wine and would not bother forging a seal.

30a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Ashi's reason: one seal suffices, because gentiles would not bother forging a second seal to swap wine.
Baraita: a gentile's cooked wine and aluntit are forbidden, but aluntit prepared by a Jew before entering gentile hands is permitted.
What is aluntit?
A baraita on Shabbat: one may prepare anomlin but not aluntit, since aluntit is a remedy.
Which beverage is aluntit, since the baraita leaves it open?
Anomlin is wine with honey and pepper; aluntit is aged wine with clear water and balsam, drunk after the bathhouse to cool down.
Rabba and Rav Yosef: diluted wine is not subject to exposure, and cooked wine is not subject to the libation prohibition.
Is cooked wine subject to the exposure rule or not?
R. Yaakov bar Idi testified that cooked wine is not subject to the exposure rule.
Incident at R. Yannai bar Yishmael's sickbed: R. Yishmael ben Zeirud cites R. Hiyya that cooked wine is exempt from exposure, and the Sages rely on it.
Incident: Shmuel tells the gentile scholar Ablet that cooked wine is not subject to the libation prohibition, so he need not withdraw his hand.
Incidents: R. Hiyya and Rav Adda bar Ahava tell their attendants that cooked and diluted wine are exempt from the exposure rule.
Rav Pappa: the exemption applies only to well-diluted wine, since a snake may still drink partially diluted wine.
Objection: on Rabba bar Rav Huna's ship a snake turned away from partially diluted wine, so it does not drink it, undermining Rav Pappa.
Reply defending Rav Pappa: snakes risk exposure for undiluted wine but not for diluted wine, yet still drink unguarded wine.
Objection: a snake poured water into covered wine and drank the overflow, showing snakes risk themselves for diluted wine.
The Sages reply: a snake drinks only wine it diluted itself, so partially diluted wine is not subject to exposure.
Rav Ashi objects: this resolution relies on a case involving danger to life.
Rava's ruling: diluted wine is subject to exposure and to the libation prohibition, while cooked wine is exempt from both.
Incident: an attendant of Rav Hilkiya bar Tovi asks about exposed water beside which he had been sleeping.
Rav Hilkiya: a sleeping person deters snakes from drinking, but only during the day, not at night.
Objection: there is no difference between day and night sleepers; the fear of a sleeping person does not apply either way.
Rav drank water from a widow's house but not from an Aramean's house, since Aramean women do not cover water.
Shmuel rejected a widow's water but drank from an Aramean's, since Aramean women cover water for cleanliness; a variant reverses this.
R. Yehoshua ben Levi: sharp, bitter and sweet wines are not subject to exposure; Rav Hama says these are high-quality wines.
R. Shimon ben Lakish: karina is not subject to the exposure rule.
What is karina?
R. Abbahu: karina is wine that sours quickly; Rava: local wine of that kind is subject to exposure.
Why is this local wine subject to exposure?
Rava: wine that turns sour within three days is subject to both the exposure rule and the libation prohibition.

30b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Declares that from this point the exposure and libation-wine prohibitions no longer apply to the beverage in question.
The Neharde'a sages hold that exposure concern persists even after three days.
Asks for the reason behind the Neharde'a position.
Explains that a snake may at times drink even sour wine, which justifies the concern.
Baraita: wine still fermenting is exempt from exposure concern, and fermentation lasts three days.
Cress-based dishes are exempt from exposure concern, though Diaspora communities treat them as prohibited.
Limits the leniency: if the dishes contain vinegar, which repels snakes, even Diaspora practice permits them.
Babylonian kutah is exempt from exposure concern, yet Diaspora residents treat it as prohibited.
Rav Menashei: if kutah has indentations, they may be fang marks, so it is prohibited.
Shmuel holds that dripping water is exempt from exposure concern while it is being collected.
Rav Ashi limits this to continuous drips, since a snake will not drink from such a stream.
Rav Hiyya bar Ashi, citing Shmuel, says the mouth of a fig is exempt from exposure concern.
Asks in accordance with whose opinion this ruling is stated.
It is stated in accordance with the tanna of the baraita that follows.
Baraita of Rabbi Eliezer permitting eating grapes and figs at night without fear.
The verse about the Lord preserving the simple supports the lack of concern.
Rav Safra: snake venom comes in three kinds, sinking, suspended, or floating, depending on the snake's age.
Asks whether venom weakens as the snake ages, since its strength seems to diminish.
A baraita says three creatures grow stronger with age, contradicting the claim about snake venom.
Reply: the snake's physical strength grows, but the potency of its venom weakens, so young venom sinks.
Asks for the practical halakha that depends on young snake venom sinking.
Baraita: from an uncovered barrel, if nine drank and survived, the tenth may not drink.
An incident in which nine drank from an exposed barrel safely, and the tenth drank and died.
Rabbi Yirmeya explains that this incident illustrates venom that sinks to the bottom.
Parallel baraita on melons: the tenth person may not eat from an exposed melon.
Incident with a melon: nine ate safely, and the tenth ate and died.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi explains that the melon incident shows venom that sinks.
Baraita lists prohibited uses of exposed water: public pouring, household uses, animals, and washing.
Others say washing is forbidden where the body has crevices, and permitted where it has none.
The Gemara observes that the view of Others seems identical to the first tanna's view.
Reply: they differ regarding the back of the hand, the back of the foot, and the cheekbones.
Quotes Mar's earlier ruling that one may not water his animal or another's with exposed water.
A baraita permits giving exposed water to one's own animal, seemingly contradicting Mar's ruling.
That baraita refers to a cat, which is less susceptible to snake venom.
If so, the cat of another should also be permitted; asks why this is not allowed.
The venom would also weaken one's own cat, so the distinction seems unfounded.
Reply: one's own cat will recover from the venom's effect later.
The cat of another would also recover later, so the same objection remains.
The owner may wish to sell the cat and loses profit while it is weakened.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira: there are three kinds of prohibited wine; libation wine is forbidden for benefit and imparts severe impurity.

31a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gentile-owned wine is forbidden for benefit, but wine deposited with a gentile may not be drunk while benefit is permitted.
Objects from a mishnah treating deposited produce as gentile produce, implying that deposited wine should be wholly forbidden.
Asks why, if benefit is allowed in the corner case, drinking should not also be permitted.
Rabbi Yohanan visits Parod and hears a baraita from bar Kappara permitting drinking deposited wine.
Rabbi Yohanan cites Ecclesiastes 11:3 about the tree falling where it falls.
The verse means its fruits will be there, a metaphor for disciples carrying on the master's wisdom.
Rabbi Zeira resolves the contradiction: the permissive baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer, the other follows the Rabbis.
Baraita on a house in a gentile's courtyard stocked with wine: Rabbi Eliezer permits it, the Rabbis forbid it.
A chain of transmission concludes that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer's view.
Rabbi Elazar: all items are secured by one seal except wine, which one seal does not secure.
Rabbi Yohanan: even wine is secured by a single seal.
The two views are reconciled: one follows Rabbi Eliezer, the other follows the Rabbis.
Alternative version: the Sages dispute whether wine is secured by a seal within a seal, both following the Rabbis.
One Sage explains that the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Eliezer only regarding a single seal.
The other Sage holds that the Rabbis prohibit even wine under a seal within a seal.
Asks what constitutes a seal within a seal.
Rava defines a seal within a seal with examples of basins, baskets, and wineskins in sacks.
Baraita: earlier certain Samaritan wines were banned; later only open barrels are forbidden while sealed barrels are permitted.
Asks what the Sages reasoned initially and what they concluded ultimately.
Initially, Samaritans were not particular about gentile contact, regardless of whether barrels were open or sealed.
Ultimately, Samaritans are particular about sealed barrels, so sealed wine is permitted.
Raises a contradiction against the notion that sealed barrels are permitted.

31b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: a sealed wine barrel sent with a Samaritan or gentile is permitted only if the sender recognizes the seal and closing method.
Rabbi Zeira reconciles the baraitot: one concerns barrels in a city, the other barrels carried on the road.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects that city barrels also travel by road, so the distinction seems unfounded.
Rabbi Yirmeya explains the leniency applies between winepresses, where the Samaritan fears losing Jewish customers.
Asks for the reason the Sages prohibited gentiles' beer.
Rami bar Hama, citing Rabbi Yitzchak: the concern is that Jews will befriend gentiles and intermarry.
Rav Nachman: the reason is concern about exposure of the beer.
Asks what kind of exposure is meant, since exposing vats or barrels is also practiced without prohibition.
The prohibition applies to beer brewed in a place where the brewing water is allowed to settle.
If aged beer is permitted because poison prevents aging, why is all beer forbidden?
A rabbinic decree bans aged beer due to concern about new beer.
Rav Papa and Rav Achai drank gentiles' beer away from gentiles, with Rav Achai taking an extra preventive measure.
Rav Shmuel bar Bisna refused wine and beer offered to him in Marguan.
Asks why beer is refused on the same ground as wine if the concern is being discovered.
Rav rules that gentiles' beer is permitted, but a living person should not drink it.
Dilemma: if permitted for all, why forbid it to some; if forbidden for all, Rav's split ruling is unjustified.
Rav's reasoning is exposure to poison, so a person who is afflicted should refrain from drinking it.
Shmuel: the venom of a snake is deadly, but the venom of other creeping things is not.
Shmuel tells Chiyya a teaching that Rav relayed from his father about gentile elders.
Gentile elders drank exposed water without dying; the creatures harmed them only because they ate creeping things.
Rav Yosef's teaching begins here and continues on the next amud.

32a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Vinegar made from gentile beer is forbidden because it is fermented with wine used for a libation.
Rav Ashi: vinegar from a storeroom is permitted, since any added substance would spoil it over time.
The mishnah lists Hadrianic earthenware among the items that are prohibited.
Asks what Hadrianic earthenware is.
Explains that Hadrianic earthenware is earthenware of Emperor Hadrian.
Rav Dimi relates how Hadrian planted virgin soil, and the wine was absorbed by white jugs that were later soaked and drunk.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: our finest wine resembles wine from the third use of Hadrianic earthenware.
Dilemma: may one use shards holding prohibited wine to support a bed, since the wine itself is not used?
Cites a dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan on this matter and concludes that the prohibiting view is followed.
Baraita objection: wine in gentiles' jugs is forbidden to drink but permitted for benefit, against the permissive view.
Shimon ben Guda testified that Rabban Gamliel drank such wine, but the Sages did not accept the testimony.
Baraita: it is forbidden to make blankets from gentiles' wineskins to cover a donkey.
Objects that here the item is kept intact for another use, yet the baraita still forbids it.
Asks why wineskins are prohibited while gentiles' jugs may be sold.
Rava: a rabbinic decree bars selling wineskins, lest one cut one open and patch another wineskin with it.
Explains that on the view that keeping an item intact by another means is prohibited, the wineskin is forbidden.
Asks what distinguishes jugs from wineskins.
Jugs are permitted because the prohibited substance is not visible in them; in wineskins it is visible.
The Sages did not accept the testimony.
Contradiction: wine brought in gentiles' flagons is forbidden to drink but permitted for benefit.
Repeats Shimon ben Guda's testimony about Rabban Gamliel, which the Sages did not accept.
Explains the rejection: the testimony concerned his associates, while the son concedes; or two separate people are involved.
The mishnah mentions bellows-hides as the next item on the list.
Baraita defines bellows-hides as prohibited if torn opposite the heart and pierced like a chimney, with a drop of blood on them.

32b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A bloodless hide is permitted, since no trace of blood remains upon it.
Rav Huna: the leniency applies only to unsalted hides; salting removes the blood, so salted hides are forbidden.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: a circular tear around the heart renders a hide forbidden; an elongated tear is permitted.
Shmuel's ruling, transmitted through Rav Yehuda and Rav Yosef, that the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Abaye asks whether the ruling implies the Rabbis disagree, or whether all accept Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Rav Yosef responds that the practical ruling is the same either way, so the question makes no difference.
Abaye rejects mere memorization of rulings without understanding the underlying dispute.
Mishnah: meat entering a house of idolatry before it is sacrificed is permitted.
Asks which tanna holds this view.
Rabbi Chiya bar Abba cites Rabbi Yochanan: this is not the view of Rabbi Elazar.
On Rabbi Elazar's view, a gentile's unspecified slaughter intention is directed toward idolatry, so the mishnah would conflict with it.
Mishnah: meat leaving a house of idolatry is forbidden as an offering to the dead.
Asks the reason such meat is classified as an idolatrous offering.
Because it is impossible that such meat is not an idolatrous offering.
Asks whose opinion this is, and identifies it as Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's.
Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira derives from Psalms 106:28 that idolatrous offerings impart impurity by tent and are forbidden for benefit.
Mishnah: those going to a festival of idolatry may not engage with them in business.
Shmuel: a gentile traveling to a festival is barred from business on the way there, but permitted on his return.
Explains that once the worship is complete, restricting business on the return serves no purpose; what was, was.
Shmuel's counterpart: a Jew traveling to a festival may do business with a gentile on the way, since he may turn back.
Explains that a Jew on the return trip is presumed to have completed the visit, so business with him is forbidden.

33a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the earlier case: a Jew who goes to a festival might cleave to idolatry and worship again.
A baraita forbids business with a Jew going to a festival in either direction, contradicting the lenient view.
Rav Ashi: that baraita refers to an apostate Jew, who will surely go to the festival and not change his mind.
Baraita: business with a gentile going to a fair is permitted both ways; with a Jew, permitted going but forbidden returning.
Asks what distinguishes a returning Jew, such that business with him is forbidden.
A Jew who sold idolatrous objects holds money from idolatry, so business with him is forbidden.
Challenges this: the same reasoning applies to a gentile, yet business with a gentile is permitted.
Proposes that a gentile sells clothing or wine rather than idols, while a Jew may be selling idols.
Objects that the same proposal applies equally to a Jew.
If he had only wine or clothing, he would have sold it locally; traveling to a gentile fair suggests he carries idols.
Mishnah: items brought in are permitted.
Resh Lakish: this applies only to unfastened items; fastened ones are forbidden, since he may intend to return.
Mishnah: gentiles' wineskins and their jugs fall under the same rule.
Baraita: new scraped wineskins are permitted; old pitched ones are forbidden.
Example: a gentile prepares a wineskin and pours wine into it while a Jew stands by without concern.
Asks what the status is when a gentile pours wine while a Jew stands by.
Rav Papa reads the baraita as a case where a second Jew stands by the pouring Jew.
Asks why the standing Jew matters if the pouring Jew is the one doing the pouring.
Perhaps the pourer, distracted, pours a libation unintentionally, so the standing Jew's presence matters.
Rav Zavid: the case stands as stated, but a gentile's pouring is like throwing water onto clay.
Rav Pappi concludes from Rav Zavid that a gentile pouring wine into a Jew's vessel is permitted.
Rav Ashi challenges the comparison: the gentile in the earlier case goes to lose, but not here.
Story: Bar Adi the Tayyaya seized Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef's vessels, poured wine into them, and returned them.
Rabbi Ami's practical ruling: fill the vessels with water for three days, then empty them.
Rava: they must be emptied every twenty-four hours; this applies to our practice but not to theirs.
Ravin relays Resh Lakish: one ruling for ours and one for theirs.
Rav Acha bar Rava holds that the ruling covers skins but not jugs.
Rav Ashi tells him there is no difference between skins and jugs.
Baraita: new scraped jugs are permitted; old pitched ones are forbidden.
Baraita lists mixed-pouring cases, such as wine with water or with brine, and when the Jew's presence removes concern.
Introduces a dilemma the Sages raised.

33b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether brine may be placed in the jugs ab initio or only after the fact.
Rav Zevid bar Oshaya's baraita: new jugs may hold wine, and old ones may ab initio hold brine and fish stew.
Rabbi Yehuda Nesia asks whether prohibited jugs returned to a furnace and whitened are cleansed by the fire.
Rabbi Ami: if brine burns away the wine, fire surely does as well, so the question is settled.
Rabbi Yochanan: gentiles' jugs returned to the furnace are permitted once their tar disintegrates.
Rav Ashi: softening suffices; the tar need not fully fall away before the jug is permitted.
Rav Acha and Ravina dispute jugs de-tarred by burning splinters; the halakha follows the stringent view.
Asks whether it is permitted to place beer inside a prohibited vessel.
Rav Nachman and Rav Yehuda forbid it, Rava permits it, and Ravina permitted Rav Chiya bar Yitzchak to pour beer.
Rav Chiya bar Yitzchak poured wine into the jug instead of beer, against the permission given.
Ravina was unconcerned, calling it a merely incidental occurrence.
Rav Yitzchak bar Bisna had vessels of gentile origin; water left in the sun caused them to crack.
Rabbi Abba objects that by doing this he has bound them under a prohibition.
Asks whether the Sages' soak-and-expose method may be relied upon.
Rabbi Yosna, citing Rabbi Ami: a scraped vessel never attains permanent purity.
Asks what a scraped vessel is.
Rabbi Yosi bar Avin illustrates a scraped vessel with a dug-out vessel and an incident involving gentiles' wine.
People came and asked Rav Yehuda about the halakha of such vessels.
Rav Yehuda: a vessel that absorbs little is rinsed in water and is then permitted.
Rav Oira rules that gentiles' pitchers that absorb little are rinsed and permitted.
Rav Pappi rules that similar covered jugs that absorb little are rinsed and permitted.
Rav Asi forbids and Rav Ashi permits a gentile's use of such a jug.
All agree that first use is prohibited; they dispute only the second use.
Another version: all agree first and second use are prohibited; they dispute only the third use.
Halakha: first and second use are forbidden, while third use is permitted.
Rav Zevid: white and black vessels are permitted, green ones forbidden since the glaze fuses into them.
If vessels have cracks, all are forbidden; Mar bar Rimar taught that glazed vessels of any color are permitted.
Asks why the Passover chametz rules differ, and whether glazed vessels may be used on Passover.
Green vessels need no question: they fuse and absorb, so they are forbidden.
Asks about white and black glazed vessels.
Vessels with cracks need no question: they certainly absorb and are forbidden.
Asks about another type of vessel, with the answer left for the next line.

34a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Reasoning: such vessels sweat, so they certainly absorb and are therefore prohibited.
Asks why such vessels cannot be purged by hot water.
The Torah attests that substances absorbed in an earthenware vessel never leave its walls.
Asks why leavened bread differs from libation wine, given Mar's ruling that all glazed vessels are permitted.
Objects that leavened bread is Torah-prohibited while libation wine is only rabbinic, yet rabbinic enactments mirror Torah law.
The difference is use: one vessel is used with hot foods, the other with cold drinks, so absorption differs.
Rabbi Akiva is asked three questions in Ginzak and cannot answer: on fasting, on gentiles' jars, and on Moses's garments.
The study hall answers: one fasts for hours, and if he completes the fast he recites the fast prayer.
Gentiles' jars are permitted after twelve months, and Moses wore a specific garment during the seven days of inauguration.
Rav Kahana: Moses wore a white cloak without a hem.
Mishnah: residual grape seeds and skins of gentiles are prohibited.
Baraita: moist grape seeds and skins of gentiles are forbidden, while dry ones are permitted.
Asks which residues count as moist and which count as dry.
Shmuel: residues are moist for the first twelve months after pressing and dry thereafter.
Rabba bar bar Chana, citing Rabbi Yochanan: prohibited residues are forbidden even for benefit, and permitted ones even for eating.
Rav Zevid: the lees of Aramean wine become permitted after twelve months.
Rav Chaviva bar Rava: gentiles' jugs become permitted after twelve months, and his statement continues.

34b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Chaviva: the canteens of Arabs become permitted after twelve months.
Rav Acha bar Ika: Aramean grape pits become permitted after twelve months.
Rav Acha bar Rava: brown and black jugs become permitted after twelve months.
Mishnah and baraita: fish stew prepared by an expert is permitted, since professionals do not add wine.
Avimi teaches that the first and second preparations of fish stew are permitted and the third is prohibited.
Asks the reason for the distinction between first and second preparations.
Fish oil is plentiful in early uses so wine need not be added; later, wine might be added to compensate.
A boat of fish stew came to Akko, and Rabbi Abba posted guards so that no wine would be added to it.
Rava asks who guarded it until now; Rabbi Abba asks what concern there is at all.
At the place of origin fish stew costs far less than wine, so wine is unlikely to have been added.
Rabbi Yirmeya suggests the stew came via Tyre, where wine is cheap, so wine could have been added.
Rabbi Zeira replies that the route through Tyre has twists and openings, so there is no such concern.
Mishnah lists Unicorn-house cheese among the prohibited items.
Resh Lakish: Unicorn cheese is forbidden because most calves in that town are slaughtered for idolatry.
Asks why the majority alone matters, since a minority would seem to suffice too.
Rabbi Meir follows the minority; if a majority exists, the remaining cases are a minority of a minority, which he disregards.
Asks the status of meat when calves are slaughtered for idolatry, as Resh Lakish's view is put to him.
Objects that Resh Lakish himself permits such meat in another context.
Rabbi Yochanan: an animal slaughtered for idolatrous blood or fat is forbidden.
Rabbi Yochanan holds that intentions move from one form of worship to another, so the case is forbidden.
Resh Lakish says the animal is permitted.
Responds that the case applies only to one who declares the idolatrous intention at the completion of slaughter.
Rabbi Yehuda reports Rabbi Yishmael's question on the matter.
Rav Achadboi, citing Rav: one who betroths with the dung of a stoned ox is betrothed, but not with calves of idolatry.
Explains that a gentile's calves are beneficial to their mother, unlike a stoned ox, which is distinct.
Scriptural basis: Deuteronomy 13:18 and Exodus 21:28 are compared, showing the stoned ox's flesh is forbidden but its dung is not.
Rava objects that the stomach of a sacrifice is more stringent than that of a carcass, so the analogy fails.

35a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Inference: where benefit is forbidden, the excrement of such animals is nonetheless permitted.
Recounts the exchange: Yehoshua says gentile cheese is forbidden; Yishmael asks why its benefit is not forbidden too.
Asks why Yehoshua did not answer that the cheese has no visible prohibited substance.
Challenges by analogy to fish stew, whose benefit is permitted even though it may contain gentile wine.
Rennet is essential to forming the cheese, so it counts as a substantive prohibited entity even if invisible.
Yehoshua turned Yishmael's attention to another matter.
Asks the meaning of the verse 'your love is better than wine'.
Rav Dimi: Israel says the words of Your beloved Sages are more pleasant than the wine of the Torah itself.
Asks why that particular verse was chosen for the question.
Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi: Yehoshua chose it to convey a lesson derived from the verse's opening about kisses.
Cites Song of Songs 1:2, 'Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.'
Yishmael teaches from the verse about lips that one should not hasten to reply.
Asks the reason for a particular ruling.
Ulla, or Rav Shmuel bar Abba: it is a new decree, and one may not cast doubt on it.
Asks what the decree is.
Ben Pazi reports Resh Lakish that the reason is cleansing, as in Ulla's case.
Ulla: decrees issued in the West do not reveal their reason for twelve months, lest someone disregard them.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects: then dry items would also be permitted, and old ones too, on Rabbi Chanina's reasoning.
Rabbi Chanina: it cannot be done without drips of milk; Shmuel says it is curdled in the skin of a carcass's stomach.
Shmuel: since the rennet is curdled in a carcass's stomach lining, the stomach itself is permitted.
Asks whether Shmuel really holds this.
The mishnah forbids a gentile's stomach and a carcass's stomach, contradicting Shmuel's leniency.
Shmuel: the mishnah teaches one case; a gentile's slaughter stomach is forbidden as carrion, so there is no contradiction.

35b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel's comment reflects Yehoshua's earlier view, before his retraction, on the Hullin mishnah.
Rav Malkiya, citing Rav Ada bar Ahava: the reason is that the surface is smeared with pig fat.
Rav Chisda: the reason is that the rennet is curdled with vinegar.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: the reason is that the rennet is curdled with the resin of an orlah tree.
Asks whose view this is, linking it to a particular tanna.
Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer says one who curdles with orlah resin is forbidden.
Because the resin is a fruit product, the prohibition applies.
Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees with Rabbi Eliezer only regarding bark resin; regarding fruit resin he concedes.
Rabbi Yehoshua: he heard explicitly that leaf and root resin is permitted, while unripe-fruit resin is forbidden as fruit.
Both Rav Chisda and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak agree the cheese is prohibited for benefit, which is difficult.
Rav Nachman bar Chisda offers a homiletic reading of a verse.
Cites Song of Songs 1:3, 'Your oils have a goodly fragrance.'
Scholars are like a perfume flask: what is concealed becomes revealed to them.
Cites Song of Songs 1:3, 'Maidens love you,' read as a reference to hidden matters.
Continues the homily: the angel of death loves the scholar, and the verse teaches inheritance of two worlds.
Mishnah lists gentile items that are forbidden to eat but not for benefit, with Rabbi and his court permitting some oil and vegetable items.
Asks what concern underlies the milk prohibition: confusion of colors or mixing.
Distinguishes two concerns: confusion of milk's colors, and mixing with a substance that stands in the vessel.
Explains the concern is a substance added to milk for cheese, and a clean milk also has droplets, so the concern applies either way.
Rav Kahana, citing Rav Yochanan: bread was not permitted by a court, implying some do permit it.
Story: Rabbi went to the field, saw gentile-baked bread, and praised it; people thought he permitted it, but he did not.
Rav Yosef, or Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda, corrects the story: Rabbi saw bread pressed for students in a place without a Jewish baker.
Rabbi says there is no baker here; people assume a gentile baker, but he meant a Jewish baker.
Explains that the permission applies in fields where no Jewish baker is available, not where one is.
Rabbi Yochanan: even on the view that a gentile baker is prohibited, this applies to fields, not towns, due to intermarriage.
Story of Ayvo eating bread; a sage tells others not to speak with him about eating a gentile's bread.
Mishnah: the oil of gentiles is addressed next.
Rav says Daniel decreed against gentile oil; Shmuel gives a different view.

36a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether everyone eats only pure foods, so why would impure vessels render oil forbidden?
The Gemara emends Shmuel: prohibited vessels render oil forbidden because they absorb prohibited substances.
Shmuel to Rav: on his own view that prohibited vessels forbid oil, the report about Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's permission is understandable.
Rabbi Simlai reports that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his court voted to permit gentile oil.
Shmuel's explanation: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi held that a prohibited substance that spoils flavor is permitted.
Asks how Rav can reconcile Daniel's decree with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's annulment of it.
Cites the mishnah: a court may not annul another court's rulings unless it is greater in wisdom and number.
Rav rejects the proof as coming from Lod residents, who disparage decrees; Shmuel offers to summon Rabbi Simlai, and Rav is embarrassed.
Rav: if they did not expound the verse, we certainly must.
Daniel 1:8's word 'mishtav' is plural, indicating two kinds of drinking: wine and oil.
Rav holds Daniel's stance applied to all Israel, while Shmuel holds it did not; Rav says Daniel decreed against oil.
Cites Rav's own statement, via Avimi bar Nat'a, that gentile bread, oil, wine, and daughters are among the eighteen decrees, which seems to clash.
Rav's reply: Daniel decreed without acceptance, and later students of Hillel and Shammai decreed and it was accepted.
Asks what then the testimony of Rav would be.
Daniel decreed in the city; the students of Hillel and Shammai later extended it even to the field.
Asks how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi could permit what the students of Shammai and Hillel enacted.
Mishnah: a court may not annul another court's rulings unless it is greater in wisdom and number.
Rabbah bar bar Chana, citing Rabbi Yochanan: a court may annul another's rulings except the eighteen matters.
Even if Elijah came with his court, one would not listen to them regarding the eighteen matters.
Rav Mesharshiya: the reason is that the oil's prohibition did not spread among most of Israel.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Abba, citing Rabbi Yochanan: the Sages examined the oil whose prohibition did not spread, relying on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok: a decree may not be imposed on the public unless most of the public can bear it.
Quotes Rav Adda bar Ahava's statement and asks which verse it is based on.

36b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites Malachi 3:9 about the nation robbing God.
Continues the verse: the whole nation is charged, read as the whole nation's acceptance.
Derives that a decree may be instituted only if the whole nation accepts it.
Avimi of Nota citing Rav: the gentile bread, oil, wine, and daughters prohibitions all derive from eighteen matters decreed in one day.
Asks what the prohibition on the daughters actually is.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: the decree treats gentile girls as menstruants from the cradle.
Gnaiba, citing Rav: all of these were decreed because of idolatry.
Rav Acha bar Adda, citing Rabbi Yitzchak: they decreed concerning their bread because of their oil.
Asks why oil would be forbidden because of bread.
A chain: bread is forbidden because of oil, oil because of wine, wine because of daughters, and daughters because of another matter.
Cites Deuteronomy 7:3, 'do not intermarry with them,' which is Torah-based for the seven nations.
The Sages decreed against other gentiles as well, though only the seven nations are Torah-prohibited.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai reads Deuteronomy 7:4 as including every act of turning a child away.
The Torah-level prohibition is marriage; the Sages extended it to the path of intermarriage.
The Sages decreed even against the path of harlotry, and the court of Shem enacted this.
Genesis 38:24, 'Bring her out and let her be burned,' shows that adultery is a capital matter.
Torah-level: a gentile who lies with a Jewish woman, drawing her after him.
A Jew who lies with a gentile woman is not Torah-prohibited, but the Sages decreed against even that.
This is a halakha given to Moses at Sinai.
Cites Rav: one who lies with an Aramean woman is attacked by zealots.
Reply: the Torah prohibition applies publicly, as in the incident described, and the Sages decreed even in private.
The court of the Hasmoneans issued the decree.
Ravin: a Jew who lies with a gentile woman is liable, and the Hasmonean court decreed against intercourse.
The Hasmonean court decreed against intercourse, but not against seclusion.
The court of David later decreed even against seclusion, as Rav Yehuda said that at that time they decreed on seclusion.
That seclusion decree concerns a Jewish woman, not seclusion with a gentile woman.
The students of Shammai and Hillel decreed even against seclusion with a gentile woman; seclusion with a Jewish woman is Torah law.
Rabbi Yochanan, citing Shimon ben Yehotzadak: the Torah hints at seclusion.
Deuteronomy 13:7: a son who seduces his mother's side shows that seclusion with forbidden relatives is Torah-prohibited.
Seclusion with a married woman is Torah law; David decreed even seclusion with an unmarried woman, and the students of Shammai and Hillel decreed even seclusion with a gentile woman.
Asks what 'on another matter' means.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: they decreed that a gentile infant does not defile by zava, so a Jewish child not become accustomed to him.
Ravin recounts his grief while studying with several sages in a chain of teachers.
Ravin continues the chain of teachers, including Rabbi Natan bar Amram and Rav Nachman bar Amram with Rabbi.
Asks from when a gentile child defiles by zava.
Rabbi says: from the day of his birth.
Rabbi Chiya tells Ravin: nine years and one day.
When Ravin pressed his view before Rabbi, he was told to drop it and hold to Rabbi Chiya's ruling.
Rabbi Chiya's statement: a gentile child defiles by zava from nine years and one day.

37a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ravina: a three-year-and-one-day-old gentile girl who is fit for intercourse also imparts impurity through zava.
Asks why this needs stating, since a girl might seem exempt because she cannot yet lure others to sin.
Rabbi Yehuda Nesia leans on his attendant Simlai while traveling and reproaches him for missing the night's study session.
Simlai remarks that in their time the bread too will be permitted.
Yehuda Nesia replies that people would then call them a permissive court.
Mishnah in Eduyot: Yosei ben Yo'ezer's rulings on the animal, the wine-shop, and impurity were permitted by a sage named Yosef.
The two sages dispute how many matters the court has permitted, counting the disputed items.
Mishnah: a get conditioned on not returning within twelve months, if he dies within that time, is not a valid get.
Our Sages permitted her to remarry.
Asks who 'our Sages' are.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: the court that permitted the oil follows Rabbi Yosei, that the date of a document proves its validity.
Abba, son of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled, but not all accepted it; some say his whole group did.
Rabbi asks an old man whether he permitted her immediately because she would not return, or only after twelve months, citing the mishnah.
Mishnah: a get effective from now, if I do not come within twelve months and I die in that time, is a valid get.
Asks whether, if she was permitted immediately, the get is valid, or only after twelve months once the condition is met.
Abaye replies that it is so, but only because in that period the condition was met.
Abaye: all agree that a get conditioned on the sun leaving its sheath is effective from now, so a get given during life is valid.
Rav Huna: whoever says 'on condition' is like one who says 'from now'; they dispute only the case of her departure.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds like Rabbi Yosei, that the date proves the document; the Rabbis do not hold this.
Mishnah repeats Yosei ben Yo'ezer's rulings and the name Yosef used to permit them.
Asks what the animal names mean.
Shoshiba, and Rav Chiya bar Ami citing Ulla, offer identifications of the animal, with Sosvil.
Rav Pappa says Shoshiba; the authorities dispute whether a long-headed animal is forbidden.
One view holds that a long-headed animal is forbidden.
The other view holds that a long-headed animal is permitted.
Rav Chiya bar Ami, citing Ulla, states a further view.

37b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A long-headed locust is forbidden by all; they dispute a locust whose wings barely cover most of its body, one requiring a minimal majority, the other a noticeable one.
Mishnah: Yosei ben Yo'ezer testified that the liquids of the Temple slaughterhouse are pure.
Asks what Yosei ben Yo'ezer meant by calling them pure.
Rav holds they are truly pure; Shmuel holds they do not transmit impurity to others, though they may themselves become impure.
Rav: liquid impurity is rabbinic, and the decree did not extend to the Temple slaughterhouse liquids.
Shmuel: liquid impurity is Torah law, but transmitting it is rabbinic, and the decree did not cover the slaughterhouse liquids.
Mishnah: whatever touches a corpse is impure, but Yosef declares it permitted.
Objects that Yosef should have forbidden it, since the rule is Torah law.
Numbers 19:16 shows Torah-level impurity from contact with a sword-slain person in the field.
The Sages decreed even impurity from contact with contact, and the Torah itself teaches that level.
Numbers 19:22: whoever touches an impure person becomes impure.
Transmitted in Rava's presence from Mar Zutra citing Rav Nachman: impurity by contact joined to the impure is Torah-level.
Impurity of seven days versus evening impurity: the Sages decreed even seven-day impurity not joined.
Someone came and established this as Torah law.
Numbers 19:11, 19:22 and Leviticus 15 are combined to show how seven-day and evening impurities apply, joined or not joined.
Asks how these verses reconcile: here joined, there not joined.
Rava rebukes them, citing Rav Nachman: in a case of doubtful impurity in the public domain, Rav Nachman permitted it.
Objects that the halakha is derived from the sotah, which applies in the private domain, so doubtful impurity should too.
Rav Yochanan: this is the halakha, but one does not rule so; someone came and ruled it.
Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda says one sets up beams to mark the public domain from the private domain.
Rabbi Yannai tells them: here is water in a deep pool of the river; go and immerse yourselves.
Asks where the halakha on cooked foods derives from.
Rabbi Chiya bar Abba cites Rabbi Yochanan.
Deuteronomy 2:28: 'You shall sell me food for money... and water for money give me,' compares food to water.
Just as water is unchanged, food unchanged from its creation is permitted.
If so, roasted wheat should be forbidden, yet a baraita says roasted wheat is permitted.
The analogy: water unchanged from its creation, and food unchanged from its creation, is permitted.
If so, ground wheat would also be forbidden.
Baraita: roasted wheat, along with its meal and fine flour, is permitted.
Water is unchanged by fire, and food is unchanged by fire; the verse is written with fire, so only fire-altered food is in view.

38a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara: the prohibition is rabbinic, and the verse is cited merely as support.
Rav: foods eaten raw are not subject to the gentile-cooking prohibition; Sura and Pumbedita transmit different versions.
Rav's Pumbedita version: foods not eaten with bread at kings' tables are exempt from the prohibition.
Asks the practical difference: small fish, mushrooms, and porridge are treated differently by the two versions.
Rav Asi and Rav Yosef: salted small fish are exempt; a gentile's roasted fish may be relied upon, but his fried dish is forbidden.
Asks whether it is obvious that a fried dish is forbidden, and whether the flour is the main element.
Rav Bruna citing Rav: all grasshoppers in a marsh set alight by a gentile are forbidden.
Asks why the gentile's involvement matters, since a Jew would face the same mixing of pure and impure.
Rav Chanan bar Ami citing Rabbi Yochanan: a gentile's fish whose head is burned may be eaten, cited as authority.
The gentile intends only to burn the surface, not to cook; here too he intends to clear the marsh without knowing which are pure.
The incident itself concerned a gentile.
Rabbah bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan repeats: a gentile who burns the fish's head may be eaten.
Ravina: where a gentile puts material into an oven, the result is obviously permissible.
Asks whether the gentile intends to cook food or only to heat the vessel.
Clarifies that he intends to loosen the vessel's contents, so it is permissible.
Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: a Jew left meat on coals, a gentile turned it over, and the meat is permitted.
Asks what the case is: if it would not have cooked without turning, it is obvious; if it would, why is it permitted?
Clarifies: it would have cooked in two hours but now cooks in one, so the gentile's act is decisive.
Rabbi Assi citing Rabbi Yochanan: food fit to be eaten by a wolf is exempt; otherwise the gentile's cooking applies.
There the gentile placed it on a shovel and in an oven, so the cooking is his.
Baraita: a Jew leaves meat on coals; a gentile turns it over until the Jew returns from synagogue, and the Jew need not worry.
A woman cooks a pot on a stove and a gentile woman comes along.

38b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A pot left on the stove is undisturbed until the person returns from the bathhouse or synagogue, and she need not worry.
Asks whether food left by a gentile and turned by a Jew is permitted.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak reasons a fortiori from food completed by a gentile's hand to food completed by a Jew's hand.
Rabbah bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan: permitted whether the gentile begins and a Jew turns it, or the reverse; forbidden only if the gentile begins and completes it.
Ravina's ruling: bread begun by a gentile and finished by a Jew, or the reverse, is permitted in these cases.
Chizkiya and Bar Kapara permit salted fish and roasted eggs respectively, against Rabbi Yochanan; Rav Dimi reports the dispute.
Rabbi Chiya in Parvah: at the Exilarch's house they served a roasted egg; one sage's view does not outweigh two.
Rav Zevid advises against following Rabbi Yochanan; Abaye rules that the halakha follows him, with an anecdote of a man given vinegar who died.
Baraita: the Cyprian and Kapaltot cakes, and the gentiles' cooked foods, are permitted, but roasted eggs are forbidden; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his court permitted oil.
Asks what the matelia and shi'ata items are.
Rabbi Yochanan dates the incident to forty years after the Exodus from Egypt.
Rabba bar bar Chana dates it to sixty years; the two do not disagree.
The narrative describes preparing several materials together and leaving them until ready.
They bring new jugs, fill them with water, and steep the mixture in them.
They attach the mixture, enter the house, and eat the sprouted results, described from head to toe.
Rav Ashi: Rabbi Chanina told me the story in one way, but others tell it differently.
Baraita: a gentile's hot-water cooking in a large pot is forbidden, and in a small pot permitted.
Yanai: a small pot is one into which a sparrow's head cannot enter.
Objects that a baraita permits both large and small pots, contradicting the first ruling.
Resolves that the two rulings follow two views: one holds that flavor-imparting spoils make the food forbidden, the other that it is permitted.
Rav Sheshet: a gentile's cooked oil is forbidden.
Rav Safra asks what the concern is: mixing, cooking, or absorption; the item is permitted if it only spoils flavor.
They ask Rabbi Assi about gentiles' cooked vetches and bitter items, and about doubtful cases.
Rabbi Assi replies that Rabbi has already forbidden it, so there is no question.
Rav permits, while Shmuel's father and Levi forbid wheat and barley; all agree vinegar-soaked items are permitted.
Dispute over items cooked in water: one master decrees lest they be confused with the other; the other does not decree.
Rav: Barzillai the Gileadite brought David two kinds of food, citing 2 Samuel 17:28, including wheat, barley, flour, parched grain, beans, and lentils.
Now they bring out cooked dishes to the Nehardea market, and no one heeds the view of Shmuel's father and Levi.
Mishnah: pickles, which customarily have wine placed inside them.
Chizkiya: this applies only where it is customary; if it is known to be used, it is forbidden even for benefit.
Asks the difference from murei fish sauce, which the Sages permitted for benefit: there to clear away filth, here to sweeten flavor.
Rabbi Yochanan: even when known, it is permitted.
Asks the difference from murei for Rabbi Meir, who forbids it for benefit.

39a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah lists categories of known and unknown substances, including crushed items and brine without fish.
Asks what distinguishes the case of semolina from the other items.
Rav Nachman bar Abba citing Rav: semolina is forbidden because the substance mixed into it rises along with it.
Tannaim: items that neither now nor later develop a particular substance, such as semolina and vinegar, are permitted.
Items that now or later acquire a particular feature when they come from the sea are permitted, as with certain fish types.
Rabbi Abbahu announces at Caesarea that fish and their roe may be bought from anyone; Abaye agrees, citing the stench of a river.
Asks why an impure fish is permitted by the rules, since its spine does not stay in the place where water flows.
Because the impure fish does not increase the sediment.
Ravina: today, with the Gozu and Gamda rivers poured into the sea, such fish are forbidden.
Abaye gives mnemonic rules for which sea creatures are permitted or forbidden according to their purity.
Rav Ashi: Shafar Nuna is permitted and Kadesh Nuna forbidden, with Exodus 16:23, 'holy to the Lord,' as the mnemonic.
Some say a grave Nuna is forbidden, and the mnemonic is the graves of gentiles.
Rabbi Akiva is given a fish resembling a chifushah; he covers it, sees scales, and permits it.
Rav Ashi is given a fish resembling a tzelupachta; he sees sprouts in it and permits it.
Rav Ashi elsewhere is given a fish resembling a shefarnuna; he covers it in white cloths, sees scales, and permits it.
Rabba bar bar Chana smells a foul odor at a marsh bank and, hearing a man call the fish bati, concludes it has an impure part and does not eat it.
In the morning he examines it and finds an impure part inside.
Proverbs 12:21, 'no harm befalls the righteous,' is cited about the caution taken.
Reason: the knife transfers flavor, and the sharp fat of the chilitis makes it like flavor-improving, so it is forbidden.
Rav Levi's servant sold chilitis; after Rav Levi died, people asked Rabbi Yochanan whether buying from it is permitted.
Asks whether it is permitted to buy from the servant.
Rabbi Yochanan: the servant of an associate is like an associate.
Stories of Rav Huna bar Maniumi and others buying purple dye from households; Rav Yehuda reports Shmuel's rule that an associate's wife is like an associate.
Mishnah: the wife, servant, or household of a deceased associate remain in their status until suspected.
Similarly, a courtyard in which purple dye is sold keeps its status until it is disqualified.
A gentile's wife, daughter, or slave who marries or is sold to an associate must accept associates' rulings.
But an associate's wife, daughter, or slave who marries or is sold to a gentile need not accept associates' rulings.
Rabbi Meir's view; Rabbi Yehuda says even these must initially accept associates' rulings.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: a woman who married an associate tied phylacteries on his arm; when she married a tax collector she tied tax-collector knots on his arm.
Rav's mnemonic lists items forbidden in one vessel and permitted in another, including milk, meat, wine, and purple.

39b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav's list: some foods are forbidden under one seal, others permitted under one seal.
Asks why bread needs a concern at all, since one seal could suffice.
Bread's freshness or grain value would be noticed by the Jew, and forging a seal is not worth it.
Asks why cheese needs only one seal while milk, by the same logic, would too.
Rav Kahana revises the list, replacing milk with fish that lacks a kashrut sign.
Objects that fish is just meat, which already needs two seals, so it would be redundant.
Shmuel gives a different list of items needing one seal or two, and omits fish.
Sages' baraita: buy these foods only from a reputable expert, though a host's food is permitted.
Supports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: a host does not send forbidden food, so guest food is fine.
The Mishnah's item salkondarit salt is introduced as one of the forbidden foods.
Asks what salkondarit salt actually is.
Shmuel identifies it as the salt that Roman bakers use.
Baraita: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda disagree over whether black or white salt is forbidden.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Gamliel holds that both black and white salkondarit salt are forbidden.
Explains each opinion's concern about intestines of non-kosher fish mixed into the salt.
Rabbi Abbahu reports an elder who smeared the salt's surface with pig fat, so it is forbidden.
Asks what the Mishnah's closing statement is meant to exclude.
Excludes wine-tainted foods or Beit Unyaki fish stew and cheese, per the cited opinions.
Mishnah: lists foods permitted to eat, including gentile-milked milk, honey and grape clusters.
Cites a baraita about a Jew sitting by a gentile's flock while milk is taken, as support.
Asks the circumstances of that case, since the permitted milk seems obvious or unsupported.
The flock has a non-kosher animal, and the gentile fears being seen when the Jew stands.
Mishnah quote: the honey of gentiles is permitted.
Asks what concerns would apply to honey.
Wine mixing, cooking and absorbed taste do not apply, so the honey is permitted.
Mishnah quote: grape clusters dripping juice are not susceptible to impurity.
Raises a contradiction: a baraita where Shammai and Hillel say grapes do become susceptible.
Grapes in the baraita were meant for juice as a drink, unlike the Mishnah's case.
Mishnah quote and baraita defining tarit fish and brine containing fish.

40a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether teaching that brine with two kilbiyot is permitted is needed, given one suffices.
Explains the difference: open barrels need two kilbiyot, while sealed barrels need only one.
Rav Huna and Rav Nachman dispute whether tarit needs both head and spine or either one.
Rav Ukva objects from a Mishnah stating that fins and scales alone make fish kosher.
Abaye replies that the Mishnah refers to fish whose heads resemble non-kosher fish.
Rav Yehuda, in Ulla's name, limits the dispute to brine; eating the fish needs head and spine.
Rav Pappa rules that the head and spine of each and every fish must be recognizable.
Raises a baraita permitting a whole jug of fish when one piece shows a kashrut sign, against Rav Pappa.
Rav Pappa reads the baraita as referring to pieces that visibly fit together from one fish.
Asks what the baraita teaches, since matching pieces would obviously be permitted.
It guards against worry that the pieces only happened to fit together, so they are permitted.
Rav Huna bar Ḥinnana inspects a ship's fish, sees scales, and permits them.
Rava objects that such fish may come from a scaled-fish land, and prohibits the boat's fish.
Rav Yirmeya reports Rav Pappi's view: Rav Huna permitted only the brine, not the fish bodies.
Rav Ashi reports Rav Pappa's view: Rav Huna permitted even the fish bodies.
Rav Ashi states his own stance: he neither forbids nor permits the fish, given conflicting reports.
Cites Rav Yehuda in Ulla's name to support that only brine is permitted under the dispute.
Rav Ḥinnana bar Idi rules: open barrels all permitted; sealed, only the barrel with the kilbit.
Rav Adda asks where Rav Ḥinnana got this ruling.
Rav Ḥinnana cites three authorities, Rav, Shmuel and Rabbi Yoḥanan, as his source.
Rav's teaching: fish intestines and their roe may be bought only from an expert.
Ulla objects that this implies non-kosher fish have roe, contrary to a baraita on fish birth.
Rabbi Dostai concedes and proposes deleting the phrase about roe.
Rabbi Zeira says do not delete: both kinds of fish lay eggs, so non-kosher roe is a concern.
Asks why an expert is needed, when one could check roe signs as the baraita teaches.
Explains the egg-sign comparison refers to roe, since fish kashrut depends on fins and scales.
Baraita on bird egg signs: narrow-round eggs are kosher; yolk and albumen placement decides.
Rava limits Rav's ruling to eggs that have melted together, so their signs cannot be read.
Asks why the roe phrase is difficult, given Rabbi Dostai's view that non-kosher fish lay no eggs.

40b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects from a baraita that fish roe has signs like bird eggs, implying non-kosher roe exists.
Replies that the baraita really means fish intestines, so it never mentions roe at all.
Asks where one finds the roundness-and-pointedness signs in fish intestines.
Points to the swim bladder of a fish, which is kosher if shaped like a kosher egg.
Asks the halakha when no expert is present to judge whether the roe is kosher.
Rav Yehuda: if the seller says he salted kosher fish, the roe is permitted.
Rav Nachman requires showing the fish; Rav Yehuda tells his attendant to accept the seller's word.
Mishnah: the leaf of a ḥiltit plant is permitted.
Asks whether the leaf ruling is obvious, since an unsliced leaf is clearly permitted.
Slivers on the leaf stuck to it when pulled from the ground, so they are not mixed in.
Mishnah: rolled olive cakes are permitted.
Asks whether this ruling is obvious, since rolled olive cakes are plainly permitted.
Their softness comes from their oil, not from wine a gentile might have placed in them.
Mishnah: Rabbi Yosei says overripe olives are prohibited.
Asks what overripe olives are like.
Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina: any olive whose pit slips out when grasped in the hand.
Mishnah: locusts from a salesman's basket are prohibited, while those from the storeroom are permitted.
Baraita: items from storehouses and ships are permitted; market-sold wine and apples are prohibited.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asks whether anyone knows if a gentile's apple wine is permitted.
Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei recounts his father's cure with seventy-year-old apple wine.
A gentile's stock of seventy-year-old apple wine cures Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who gives thanks.
Asks the meaning of the mishna's phrase 'and likewise with regard to teruma'.
Rav Sheshet: a suspect priest selling teruma is like the market case; only items before him are prohibited.
Closing of the chapter and the start of the next mishna, on statues.
Mishnah: all statues are forbidden; the Rabbis allow those lacking a staff, bird or orb, and Shimon ben Gamliel forbids any item.
Asks the Rabbis' reason, if statues are worshipped only once a year.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: in Rabbi Meir's locale people worshipped once a year, so he decreed broadly.
Rav Yehuda, in Shmuel's name: the dispute concerns the statues of kings.
Rabba bar bar Ḥana, in Rabbi Yoḥanan's name: the dispute concerns statues at a city entrance.

41a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabba: the Meir-Rabbis dispute covers village statues; city statues are permitted as ornamental.
Asks how the Rabbis could permit village statues, which are surely made for worship.
Clarifies that Rabba's dispute concerns city statues, while village statues are forbidden by all.
Mishnah: the Rabbis say statues are forbidden only if they hold a staff, bird or orb.
Explains that a staff, bird or orb each signals the idol's dominion over the whole world.
Tosefta adds a sword, crown and ring to the items that mark a statue as an idol.
The sword, first seen as a bandit's mark, later signals the idol's power to kill the world.
The crown and ring were first seen as ordinary, later as royal and as sealing the world's fate.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel forbids a statue holding any item whatsoever.
A baraita extends the prohibition to a statue merely holding a stone or a twig.
Rav Ashi asks the halakha if a statue grasps excrement; the question is left unresolved.
Mishnah: unidentifiable statue fragments are permitted, while hand- or foot-shaped objects are forbidden.
Shmuel: one may derive benefit even from fragments of objects known to be used in idol worship.
Objects that the Mishnah permits fragments of statues, which would imply idol fragments are forbidden.
The Mishnah's wording does not exclude idol fragments; it sets up the separate hand-or-foot clause.
Mishnah: a hand-shaped or foot-shaped object is forbidden, since similar objects are worshipped.
Asks why such a hand- or foot-shaped object is forbidden.

41b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the case is really about fragments, which Shmuel permits.
Shmuel explains the Mishnah's case as figures standing on their pedestals, not mere fragments.
Rabbi Yoḥanan forbids and Resh Lakish permits benefit from idols that broke by themselves.
Explains the sides: Rabbi Yoḥanan says the owner never revoked it; Resh Lakish says he did.
Rabbi Yoḥanan objects from Dagon's fallen idol, whose worshippers still honored its threshold.
Resh Lakish replies that people revered the threshold, not Dagon, so there is no proof.
Another objection: the Mishnah permits fragments of statues, implying idol fragments are forbidden.
Resh Lakish: the unattributed Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, who forbids whole statues.
Asks why one cannot infer from Rabbi Meir the Rabbis' view on fragments of idols.
Rejects the comparison: statues may never have been worshipped, but idols certainly were, and doubt cannot override that.
Asks whether doubt cannot override certainty, given apparent counterexamples.
Cites a baraita on a ḥaver's storehouse of produce, presumed properly tithed, as support.
Infers that here a doubt about tithing does override a certainty, contrary to the principle.
Replies that the ḥaver certainly tithed, so this is certainty against certainty, following Rabbi Ḥanina Ḥoza'a.
Alternatively, the produce may never have owed tithes, so both sides are uncertain, following Rabbi Oshaya.
Raises another objection from a baraita of Rabbi Yehuda about an incident with a maidservant.

42a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita case: a non-viable newborn fell into a pit, a priest looked in, and the Sages ruled him pure.
Objects: here the woman certainly cast the newborn, so doubt about dragging should not override certainty.
Rejects that reading: the object may only have been congealed blood, so the doubt is doubled.
Asks why the baraita says to check the sex, if a non-viable newborn was certain.
The priest checked whether a mass or a newborn was cast, and the sex only if a newborn; or certainty against certainty.
Rabbi Yoḥanan objects to Resh Lakish from the Mishnah's hand and foot figures: why forbid fragments?
Replies that Shmuel explains those figures as standing on their pedestals, so they were not broken.
Rabbi Yoḥanan objects from the Mishnah: a gentile can revoke idols, yet a Jew cannot revoke a gentile's idol.
Abaye explains the Mishnah refers to a Jew bending an idol, not breaking it.
Asks what bending achieves, if no part of the idol is removed.
Objects that the Mishnah says bending revokes idol status even without removing any part.
Replies that a gentile's bending revokes idol status, but a Jew's bending does not.
Rava: a Jew's bending also revokes, but a decree stops it, lest a Jew lift and acquire the idol.
Objects from a baraita on Mercury-shrine stones used by Jews: why keep the status if the idol broke?
Answers with Rava's decree: the Sages decreed that a Jew's attempted revocation does not succeed.
Objects from a baraita on a Jew shaving an idol: why would the shavings stay forbidden if it broke?
Answers again with Rava's decree against a Jew's attempted revocation.
Objects from Rabbi Yosei's Mishnah: grinding an idol to dust still benefits the Jew, which is forbidden.
Answers with Rava's decree on this matter.
Objects from Rabbi Yosei ben Yasian's baraita on a dragon figure whose head a Jew severed.
Answers with Rava's decree on this matter.
Objects from Rabbi Yosei's baraita: fallen leaves from an idol tree keep the idol's status.
