Answers that the idol tree itself is still intact, so the case differs.

42b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why shavings are permitted if the idol still exists, so fallen leaves should also be permitted.
Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua: the leaves stay forbidden, since natural shedding does not revoke idol status.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish objects from a Mishnah on a bird's nest in an idolatrous tree, and its branches.
Explains the bird brought branches from elsewhere, so they were never part of an idol.
Cites the Mishnah's precise wording on consecrated trees to support the from-elsewhere reading.
Objects: if the branches came from the tree itself, why is there no misuse liability for them?
Replies that the branches may be growths after consecration, which carry no misuse liability.
Rabbi Abbahu reports Rabbi Yoḥanan: one may knock off the chicks, but not benefit from the nest itself.
Rabbi Ya'akov: chicks may be used but eggs are forbidden; Rav Ashi adds dependent chicks count as eggs.
Mishnah: vessels with sun, moon or dragon figures go into the Dead Sea; Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes vessels.
Asks whether these figures alone are worshipped, so that the list is restricted to them.
Contradicts a Mishnah listing slaughter for seas, rivers, stars and Michael, all forbidden offerings.
Abaye: people worship any found item, but only three celestial figures are fashioned for worship.
Rav Sheshet consolidates: constellations and faces are permitted, except the sun, moon, human face and dragon.
Quotes Rav Sheshet's ruling that all constellations are permitted except the sun and moon.
Asks whether this concerns forming figures, since that would seem to permit forming all constellations.
Objects that the verse forbids making figures of the celestial attendants, so forming them is forbidden.
Concludes the halakha concerns finding vessels with these figures; other found vessels are permitted.
Asks whether a found vessel with a human face is forbidden, given the Mishnah's list.
Objects from the Mishnah: a found dragon vessel is forbidden, but a human-face vessel is not.
Concludes the human-face prohibition concerns forming figures, following Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua.
Asks whether forming a dragon figure is forbidden, given the human-face reasoning.
Objects that the verse forbids making gods of silver or gold, which would forbid forming a dragon figure.

43a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Sages read the verse as about constellations only, so forming a dragon figure is not forbidden.
Concludes the halakha concerns found vessels, citing the Mishnah's sun, moon and dragon list.
Asks why the clauses of Rav Sheshet's ruling would differ between finding and forming figures.
Abaye: the first and last clauses concern found vessels. Rava: the middle follows Rabbi Yehuda's list of figures.
Baraita and anecdote: a dragon is defined by scales; Rabbi Elazar HaKappar has a gentile revoke a ring's idol status.
Rabbi Ḥanina objects: a lost idol-ring's status should revoke automatically, since owners despair of recovering it.
Abaye: the owner despairs of the object but not of its idol status, so revocation was still needed.
Mishnah: Rabban Gamliel showed moon figures on a tablet to test witnesses' testimony about the new moon.
Asks whether forming such figures is permitted, given the verse forbidding figures of celestial attendants.
Abaye: the verse forbids only figures that can be accurately reproduced, so the sun and moon are exempt.
Cites a baraita on not building replicas of Temple structures or a seven-lamp candelabrum.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda adds that a wooden candelabrum may not be made in the Hasmonean manner.
The Rabbis reply that the Hasmonean candelabra were improvised materials, so they prove nothing.
Asks whether attendant figures that cannot be reproduced are actually permitted.
Objects that a baraita forbids forming figures of the celestial attendants, including the sun and moon.
Abaye begins his reply; the passage continues on the next daf.

43b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Answers that only the four-faced Chariot figure is prohibited, so the sun and moon are not included.
Asks why the human face alone would be forbidden, if the Torah prohibits only the four-faced figure.
Rav Yehuda bar Rav Yehoshua: the verse can read 'make Me', so human figures are barred but other attendants are permitted.
Asks whether other attendants may be fashioned, given a baraita listing ofanim, seraphim and angels.
Abaye: the Torah bars only the upper attendants, not celestial bodies such as the sun and moon.
Asks whether celestial bodies in the lower heaven may be fashioned, given a baraita naming the sun and moon.
Answers that the baraita prohibits worshipping them, not forming their likeness.
Asks why the baraita mentions only celestial bodies, since even a tiny worm may not be worshipped.
Yes; the worm prohibition comes from the verse's later clause, and the baraita concerns worship only.
Asks whether mere fashioning of sun and moon figures is permitted, since a baraita seems to forbid it.
Alternative: Rabban Gamliel's figures were fashioned by gentiles, so a Jew merely possessing them is fine.
Asks about Rav Yehuda's human-figure seal, which Shmuel had disfigured, contrary to that resolution.
A protruding seal raises idolatry suspicion; a sunken seal may be worn but not used to seal.
Asks whether suspicion applies to human figures, citing Shmuel's father and Levi praying under a king's statue.
Asks why Rabban Gamliel's moon figures were not forbidden as suspect, since he was an individual.
Replies that as Nasi many people were present, and the figures were pieces; learning is also an exception.
Mishnah: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says figures on respectable vessels are forbidden, on disgraceful ones permitted.
Asks which vessels count as respectable and which as disgraceful.
Rav: location matters, above the water is respectable; Shmuel: utensil placements are disgraceful, jewelry respectable.
Cites a baraita in accordance with Shmuel, listing respectable jewelry and disgraceful kitchen items.
Mishnah: Rabbi Yosei says to grind an idol and scatter it; the Rabbis object that this still benefits a Jew.
Rabbi Yosei replies with another verse to uphold his view; the baraita continues on the next daf.

44a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yosei cites the verse about Moses burning and scattering the golden calf's dust as support.
The Rabbis object that the verse shows Moses ground the calf only to test the people, so it proves nothing.
Rabbi Yosei replies with a second verse about Asa burning his mother's idol at the Kidron brook.
The Rabbis object that the Kidron brook grows nothing, and a baraita says its water fertilizes gardens.
The Gemara reconciles this by explaining that some parts of the Kidron grow plants and some do not.
The Gemara asks what the word miflatztah means.
Rav Yehuda explains it as an idol that stimulated lewdness, since Maacah made a male form for sexual use.
Rabbi Yosei cites Hezekiah destroying Moses' bronze serpent as proof that breaking an idol suffices.
The Rabbis object that Moses made the serpent from his own property, so it was never a forbidden idol.
The Gemara replies that Hezekiah broke the serpent only to stop the people worshipping it, which was sufficient.
Rabbi Yosei cites David's men taking away the idols, read as scattering them, as proof.
The Gemara asks what basis there is for reading vayisa'em as scattering.
Rav Yosef's translation of Isaiah shows the root means to scatter, as the Targum renders it.
The Rabbis object that the verse says they burned the idols, so the two verses contradict each other.
The contradiction is resolved by timing: burning came before Ittai the Gittite revoked the idols' status.
The Gemara cites David's crown, which weighed a talent of gold, as the next case.
The Gemara asks how David could wear a crown that is an idol, forbidden for benefit.
Rav Naḥman says Ittai came and nullified the crown's idolatrous status.
The Gemara asks how David could possibly place a crown weighing a talent on his head.
Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav, says the crown was only fit to rest on David's head, not literally placed.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina says a lodestone held the crown suspended above David's head.
Rabbi Elazar says the crown bore a precious stone worth a talent, not the full weight.
The Gemara cites a verse from Psalms about keeping the precepts as the next source.
The Gemara asks what the verse means.
The verse means that the crown was David's testimony of fitness, as a reward for keeping God's commandments.
The Gemara asks what the testimony refers to.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says the testimony was a spot on the head where tefillin were placed.
The Gemara objects that David needed to place tefillin on his head, so the crown cannot be meant.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzḥak answers that there is a spot on the head fit for two tefillin.
The Gemara cites Chronicles about crowning the king's son and placing the crown and testimony on him.
The Gemara explains that the word nezer means a coronet and that testimony is the same thing.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, teaches the crown is a testimony for David's house: only a fit king's head suits it.
The Gemara cites Adonijah, who lifted himself up to reign, as an example from Kings.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, explains that Adonijah lifted himself to fit the crown but never fit it.
The verse continues with Adonijah preparing a chariot, horsemen, and fifty runners before him.
The Gemara asks what is novel about the statement regarding these runners.
A baraita answers that they were all without spleens and had their soles carved in grooves.

44b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Mishnah sets the scene: Proclus questions Rabban Gamliel while he bathes in Aphrodite's bathhouse in Akko.
Proclus cites the Torah ban on keeping anything from a proscribed item to challenge Rabban Gamliel's bathing.
Proclus asks why Rabban Gamliel bathes in a bathhouse dedicated to an idol.
Rabban Gamliel rules that Torah questions should not be answered inside a bathhouse.
On leaving, Rabban Gamliel answers that the bathhouse predates the idol, and the statue was built to adorn the bathhouse.
He gives a second answer: the statue stands over a sewage pipe where people urinate, so it lacks idolatrous status.
The verse speaks only of their gods, so an idol treated with disrespect is not forbidden; the rule is stated.
The Gemara asks how Rabban Gamliel could have answered a Torah question inside a bathhouse at all.
Rabba bar bar Ḥana's teaching from Rabbi Yoḥanan and Abaye's rule on languages seem to forbid his answer in the bathhouse.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's words were actually spoken when Rabban Gamliel left the bathhouse.
Rav Ḥama bar Yosef cites Rabbi Oshaya that Rabban Gamliel's reply to the officer was deceptive.
Rav Ḥama disagrees: the reply was not deceptive but truthful.
The Gemara asks what the deception in the reply actually consisted of.
Oshaya explains the deception as the claim that urinating before the statue shows it lacks idolatrous status.
Rava objects that the idol of Peor still has status, though people defecate before it daily.
Rav Ḥama replies that Peor is worshipped that way while Aphrodite is not, so disrespect shows no status.
Abaye says the deception lay in claiming the bathhouse came into Rabban Gamliel's domain, which is irrelevant.
A mishnah teaches that benefiting from an idol's bathhouse is allowed only without showing it favor, contradicting the reply.
Rav Ḥama defends the reply: Rabban Gamliel's visit counts as showing favor like others, so it is not deceptive.
Rav Shimi bar Ḥiyya says the deception was the claim that urination before the statue shows no idolatrous status.
A mishnah says that urinating, dragging, or throwing feces at an idol does not nullify its status, challenging the reply.
Rav Ḥama distinguishes: that case is a momentary rage followed by appeasement, while this statue is permanently disparaged.
Rabba bar Ulla says the deception lay in claiming people build the statue to adorn the bathhouse, not the reverse.
The Gemara objects that even saying the bathhouse adorns Aphrodite raises no real problem, so what is the deception?
A baraita teaches that dedicating a house or cup to idolatry has no effect, since idolatrous status cannot be assigned verbally.
Rav Ḥama replies that the bathhouse is not forbidden by the designation, yet remains an adornment, so the reply is not deceptive.

45a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The halakha: mountains and hills worshipped by gentiles are permitted, but what sits on them is forbidden.
The verse forbidding coveting the silver and gold on idols shows that their gold coating is forbidden to use.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili reads the verse as forbidding the idols on the hills, not the hills themselves.
The mishna asks why an ashera is forbidden, since the verse mentions leafy trees.
An ashera is forbidden because it is human-made and did not grow by itself.
Rabbi Akiva says the verse merely marks where idolatry is practiced: a high mountain, hill, or leafy tree.
The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's view is simply the same as the first tanna's.
Rami bar Ḥama cites Reish Lakish: the dispute is whether a mountain's coating has the same status as the mountain.
Rav Sheshet rejects that explanation and says everyone agrees a mountain's coating is not like the mountain itself.

45b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara frames the dispute: the first tanna permits a tree planted and later worshipped, while R. Yosei HaGelili forbids it.
The Gemara asks from where we know that R. Yosei HaGelili forbids such a tree.
The mishna's last clause, that an ashera is forbidden for human involvement, is cited as the source.
The Gemara asks what the general phrase adds, if not to include a tree planted and later worshipped.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda also forbids a tree planted and later worshipped.
A baraita derives this from the verses on mountains, hills, and trees, and from Deuteronomy 12:3 on burning asherim.
The Gemara asks why the phrase under every leafy tree is needed if worshipped trees are already forbidden.
That phrase teaches Rabbi Akiva's rule that a high mountain, hill, or leafy tree signals idolatry.
The Gemara asks what the Rabbis do with the verse about burning the asherim.
That verse covers a tree planted for idolatry from the start, which must be destroyed.
The Gemara asks whether R. Yosei son of R. Yehuda needs that same phrase for the same purpose.
The Gemara asks from where R. Yosei son of R. Yehuda derives that a tree planted then worshipped is forbidden.
He derives it from Deuteronomy 7:5, which requires hewing down the asherim, including their root.
A tree whose trunk is forbidden but root permitted must be one planted and later worshipped.
The Gemara asks how that verse can be the source, since the baraita uses the burning verse.
The burning verse makes the hewing verse superfluous, so hewing refers to a tree planted then worshipped.
The Gemara asks what the Rabbis do with the verse about hewing down the asherim.
Following R. Yehoshua ben Levi, felling idols' trees precedes conquering the land, which precedes eradicating idols.
Rav Yosef's baraita reads the repeated and leave phrases as permitting idol objects to be left unburned at first.
The Gemara asks whether it enters the mind that the Torah wants them left alone, since burning is required.
Rav Huna says to pursue the enemy first, smash the idols, conquer the land, then return to burn them.
The Gemara asks from where R. Yosei son of R. Yehuda derives the order of conquest and destruction.
He derives it from the doubled verb abbed te'abedun in Deuteronomy 12:2, meaning smash first, then destroy.
The Gemara asks what the Rabbis derive from the doubled verb.
The double verb teaches that uprooting an idol requires rooting out all traces of it.
The Gemara asks from where R. Yosei son of R. Yehuda derives the duty to root out all traces.
He derives it from Deuteronomy 12:3: you shall destroy their name out of that place.
For the Rabbis, that verse teaches that it is a mitzva to give an idol a derogatory name.
A baraita of Rabbi Eliezer derives the root-out duty from the verse that you shall destroy their name.

46a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R. Akiva objects that the destroy verse already covers rooting out, and the Gemara rejects a positive nickname.
Alternatively, one might think a neutral nickname is allowed, which a further verse must exclude.
A verse calls idols abominable and proscribed, so the nickname must be a negative one.
The Gemara asks what a negative nickname looks like in practice.
Examples: a house of elevation is called a house of digging, and an all-seeing eye becomes an eye of a thorn.
A baraita taught before Rav Sheshet: mountains are permitted but their worshippers are killed, while plants are forbidden.
Rav Sheshet says the baraita must follow R. Yosei son of R. Yehuda, who forbids a tree planted and then worshipped.
The Gemara asks why not read the baraita as about a tree planted for idolatry, matching the Rabbis.
No: the baraita compares plants to mountains, which were not planted for this purpose, so neither are these.
The sons of R. Ḥiyya and R. Yoḥanan dispute whether boulders dislodged from a mountain are forbidden once worshipped.
The Gemara asks the reason of the one who says the boulders are permitted.
Like a mountain, which has no human involvement and is permitted, these boulders are permitted too.
The Gemara objects that a mountain is lenient because it is attached to the ground, which a worshipped animal refutes.
The Gemara counters that a worshipped mountain is permitted though not alive, so being alive is not the key.
Combining the two cases, the shared feature is no human involvement, so such worshipped items, boulders included, are permitted.
The Gemara objects that the shared feature is unaltered natural form, and a dislodged boulder has been moved.
Permissibility is derived from a blemished animal and a mountain, or from an unblemished animal and a withered tree.
The Gemara asks the reason of the one who forbids worshipped boulders.
That view rests on Deuteronomy 7:26, which calls the proscribed item abominable and demands detestation.
Though reasoning permits boulders, the verse forbids deriving that leniency by inference.
The Gemara suggests concluding that the sons of R. Ḥiyya are the ones who permit boulders.
Ḥizkiyya raises a dilemma: if one erected an egg to bow to it, is deriving benefit from it forbidden?
The dilemma only arises if he erected the egg and bowed to it, so the sons of R. Ḥiyya permit boulders.
The Gemara rejects that inference: the sons may forbid boulders, and the egg is forbidden once it is worshipped.
The Gemara asks what case the dilemma really concerns.
The case is one where he erected the egg to bow to it but did not bow to it.
The Gemara asks who holds the dilemma, since under either view of when idols become forbidden it would vanish.
The case is where he erected the egg to bow, did not bow, and then a gentile bowed to it.
Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel: a Jew who erects a brick to bow to it, and a gentile bows, makes it forbidden.
Ḥizkiyya asks whether only the brick, whose erection is visible, is forbidden, or the egg too; it is left unresolved.
Rami bar Ḥama asks whether the stones of a mountain are fit for the altar when someone bowed down to the mountain.

46b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Is a worshipped attached item disqualified for the Temple like an animal, and does that extend to altar items?
Rava argues a fortiori from Deuteronomy 23:19 that an idol, forbidden even when detached, should be barred from the Temple when attached.
Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, offers the reverse a fortiori: perhaps attached idols are permitted for the Temple.
The reverse argument uses Deuteronomy 12:2, which spares the mountains themselves, and concludes the payment is permitted for the Temple.
Rav Huna answers that the verse about the House of God is needed for another halakha, excluding the red heifer.
Rava states the rule: when an a fortiori inference can yield either leniency or stringency, we infer the stringency.
Rav Pappa objects with the Paschal sprinkling dispute, where R. Akiva rightly infers a leniency rather than a stringency.
A mishna records the Eliezer and Akiva debate over sprinkling on Shabbat, cited as a source for the leniency.
R. Akiva's argument was not truly a fortiori: Eliezer had taught it to him, and he was reminding Eliezer of it.
Rami bar Ḥama asks: if one bowed to a wheat stalk, does grinding it into flour lift its idol status for meal offerings?
Mar Zutra brings a mishna saying offspring of items forbidden for the altar are permitted, while R. Eliezer forbids them.
The Gemara asks: but wasn't that very point already stated about this?
Rav Naḥman, citing Rabba bar Avuh, says the dispute concerns animals made pregnant after bestiality had made them forbidden.

47a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: All agree offspring of animals made pregnant before bestiality are forbidden, and the wheat case resembles that.
Some say the dispute is only when bestiality came first; pregnancy first is forbidden, and wheat is similar.
The Gemara asks how the cases compare: an animal stays an animal, but wheat becomes flour in a totally new form.
Reish Lakish asks whether a lulav cut from a palm tree that was bowed to may be used for the mitzva.
The dilemma excludes trees planted for idolatry, which are forbidden even for ordinary use, and R. Yosei b. R. Yehuda's view.
Per the Rabbis, is such a lulav still forbidden for a mitzva as repulsive to use for the Most High, or not?
Rav Dimi reframes it: the tree's idolatry was revoked, and the question is whether mitzva disqualification is permanent.
The Gemara suggests resolving it from a mishna on covering slaughtered blood that the wind had covered.
Rabbah bar bar Ḥana cites R. Yoḥanan: the obligation to recover applies only if the blood was then exposed again.
The Gemara asks: if exposed again, why is he obligated? Once disqualified, should he remain exempt?
Rav Pappa says this shows there is no disqualification with regard to mitzvot once the cause of exemption is removed.
The Gemara rejects this: Reish Lakish's dilemma was about Rav Pappa's own principle, and it fails in both directions.
Or perhaps the principle applies only to stringency, not leniency; the Gemara leaves the question unresolved.
Rav Pappa asks: if one bowed to an animal, is its wool permitted for the sky-blue wool of the mitzva of tekhelet?
The Gemara asks which mitzva the sky-blue wool is for: priestly garments, which ties to Rami bar Ḥama's dilemma, or fringes.
Rav Pappa had other matters: worshipped animal parts used for wool, horns, thigh bones, and innards in Levite song.
If song's primary element is instruments, the matter is clear: they facilitate an offering and are forbidden.
If song is primarily vocal, are instruments from a worshipped animal forbidden as repulsive? The question is unresolved.
Rava raises a dilemma about a spring bowed to; the Gemara asks why it concerns only libations and not ordinary use.
Clearly he bows to the water; the dilemma is whether the current flow is permitted or the spring's whole flow is forbidden.
The Gemara asks whether the water is actually forbidden by his worship.
R. Yoḥanan, citing R. Shimon ben Yehotzadak, says water belonging to the public cannot become forbidden.
The dilemma concerns a privately owned spring that flows from one specific place in the ground, not a public one.
Mishnah: if one's house was next to an idol house and the dividing wall fell, he may not rebuild it.
The mishna asks what the owner should do.
He withdraws four cubits onto his own land and rebuilds, forming his wall and the wall of the idol house.

47b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The rubble of a forbidden wall is judged half on half, and its stones, wood, and dust transmit impurity like a creeping animal.
The Deuteronomy verse using shakketz, the word for creeping things, supports this impurity.
R. Akiva says such objects transmit impurity like a menstruating woman.
He proves it from Isaiah 30:22 about putting idols away as a menstruant, who makes one impure by being carried.
The Gemara objects: how can one rebuild, since this enlarges the space available for idolatry?
R. Ḥanina of Sura: the empty space is converted into a bathroom, so there is no problem.
The Gemara objects that a bathroom needs modesty, and a baraita requires modest conduct at night as well as by day.
The space is a bathroom for children, or it is fenced in with thorns and shrubs to prevent its use.
Mishnah lists three kinds of houses: one built for idolatry is forbidden; plastered layers are removed; a temporary idol leaves it permitted.
Rav holds that bowing to a house forbids it, since a later-attached item counts as if it were still detached.
The Gemara objects that the mishna forbids a house only when built for idolatry, which seems to contradict Rav's bowing rule.
The Gemara asks why the mishna lists three houses when there are really four cases.
Regarding revoking idolatrous status, building and bowing count the same, so the mishna treats them as one.
Mishnah: three kinds of stones; one hewn for an idol platform is forbidden, plastered ones are stripped, and one with a removed idol is permitted.
R. Ami says plastering counts only when done within the stone itself, by carving or engraving it.
The Gemara objects: the mishna treats stones like houses, and a house plastered outside is still forbidden.
The Gemara answers: in a house the plaster can be inside, filling gaps between bricks, so the analogy is not exact.
R. Ami's ruling concerns revoking status: removing the added plaster makes the stone permitted, not the entire stone forbidden.

48a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: an ashera is a tree planted for idolatry, and such a tree is forbidden entirely.
Mishnah: if a tree was lopped or trimmed for idolatry, its new growth is removed and burned and the rest is permitted; removing a placed idol permits it.
The school of R. Yannai holds that only sinking a shoot or grafting it into the trunk counts for this.
The Gemara objects: the mishna says lopping or trimming for idolatry already forbids the regrowth.
R. Yannai's school's view concerns revoking status: even a sunk or grafted tree is permitted once the regrowth is removed.
Shmuel says that bowing to a tree forbids its additional growth.
R. Elazar objects with the mishna: additional growth is forbidden only when the tree was lopped or trimmed.
Shmuel follows R. Yosei b. R. Yehuda, who forbids a subsequently worshipped tree, so bowing forbids the regrowth.
Rav Ashi objects: the parties may dispute only the trunk, while all agree the regrowth is forbidden.
R. Yosei b. R. Yehuda holds the trunk is forbidden too, citing Deuteronomy 12:3 on burning the asherim.
The Rabbis hold the trunk is permitted, citing Deuteronomy 7:5 on hewing down the asherim.
A tree that is hewn is forbidden while its trunk is permitted, so it must be one planted and then worshipped.
Suppose the verse assignments were reversed, so the Rabbis and R. Yosei swap their sources.
The Gemara rejects this: then who teaches the lopping mishna? Neither side fits, so the suggestion fails.
If you wish, the Rabbis teach the mishna; if you wish, R. Yosei b. R. Yehuda does, since lopping shows intent only for the regrowth.
Mishnah: an ashera is any tree with an idol beneath it, but R. Shimon says any tree people worship; a Tzaidan tree was then permitted.
The Gemara asks: we learned three types of ashera, so why does this mishna ask which tree is an ashera?
Two of the three trees are forbidden by all, and the dispute between R. Shimon and the Rabbis concerns a tree with an idol beneath it.
The Gemara asks which tree counts as an ashera by default, without specific knowledge of worship.
Rav: any tree that priests sit beneath and whose fruit they do not taste is an ashera.
Shmuel: even if they say these dates are for the Natzrefei house, the tree is forbidden, since they throw dates into beer.
Ameimar reports that the elders of Pumbedita taught him that the halakha follows Shmuel.

48b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: sitting in an ashera's shade is forbidden but leaves one pure; passing beneath makes one impure, unless its branches overhang public space.
The Gemara asks: isn't it obvious that sitting in the shade of an idol is forbidden?
R. Yoḥanan: the mishna teaches that even the secondary shade, beyond the tree's height, is forbidden to sit in.
Some teach the discussion about sitting and remaining pure as applying to the latter clause of the mishna.
R. Yoḥanan explains the rule: even the shade of its height leaves one pure, and the mishna's point is the shade of its shade.
Mishnah: one may not pass beneath an ashera, and one who passes becomes impure.
The reason: it is impossible that no remnant of an idolatrous offering lies under the tree.
The Gemara asks whose opinion the ruling on passing beneath an ashera follows.
R. Yehuda b. Beteira's baraita derives that idolatrous offerings convey impurity in a tent from Psalms 106:28 on eating dead offerings.
Mishnah: if the tree robs the public, one who passes beneath it remains pure.
A dilemma is raised: does the mishna permit passing beneath the tree ab initio, or only after the fact?
R. Yitzḥak b. Elazar, citing Ḥizkiyya, permits passing ab initio; R. Yoḥanan permits it only after the fact.
They do not disagree: one view applies where another route exists, the other where none does.
Rav Sheshet, who was blind, asks his attendant to have him run quickly past an ashera on the path.
The Gemara asks the circumstances: if no other route existed, why run; if one existed, why pass at all?
Actually there was no other route, but an important person should pass quickly, lest others copy him when a route exists.
Mishnah: vegetables may be planted under an ashera in the rainy season, not in summer; R. Yosei forbids even in rain, since its foliage fertilizes them.
The Gemara asks whether R. Yosei holds that a result caused by both permitted and forbidden causes is forbidden.
The Gemara objects: but we learned the opposite rulings in another mishna.
That mishna: R. Yosei lets one grind an idol and scatter it, and the Rabbis reply it still benefits, citing Deuteronomy 13:18.
The Gemara notes that the Rabbis' rulings contradict each other, and so do R. Yosei's.
R. Yosei's two rulings do not conflict: where the idol is scattered and lost, use is allowed; here the leaves remain, so it is forbidden.
The Rabbis' conflict may be resolved by reversing the attribution, or by keeping it and applying a further rule.
Rav Mari b. Rav Kahana's rule: a gain to the hide is offset by damage to the flesh, so there is no net benefit here.
R. Yosei holds that when this and that cause a result together, the result is forbidden.
The Gemara objects: a baraita says R. Yosei allows planting an orla branch but not an orla nut, which is a fruit.
Rav Yehuda cites Rav: R. Yosei concedes that planting and grafting an orla tree permits its growth; a baraita agrees.

49a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav's teaching: if one planted, sank a shoot, or grafted, the resulting growth is permitted.
A possible reconciliation: R. Yosei distinguishes idol-forbidden items from other prohibitions.
The Gemara objects: baraitot conflict over a field fertilized with idolatrous dung and a cow fed idolatrous vetches, one permitting, one forbidding.
The Gemara asks whether the lenient baraita reflects R. Yosei and the stringent one reflects the Rabbis.
No: the baraitot reflect R. Eliezer and the Rabbis, who disagree with him.
The Gemara asks which dispute between R. Eliezer and the Rabbis is meant, such as the one about leaven.
A mishna on leaven: teruma leaven and non-sacred leaven combined to leaven dough, though each alone was insufficient.
R. Eliezer follows the last item to fall in; the Rabbis count only forbidden leaven that alone suffices to leaven.
Abaye explains R. Eliezer: the permitted leaven that fell in last counts only if the forbidden leaven was first removed.
The Gemara objects: R. Eliezer may simply follow the last-fallen item, so he need not hold that mixed causes forbid.
The two baraitot instead reflect R. Eliezer and the Rabbis on wood taken from an ashera.
Mishnah on wood from an ashera: benefit is forbidden, including from the oven and the bread, and mixed bread is entirely forbidden.
R. Eliezer says the benefit should be cast into the Dead Sea, but the Rabbis say idolatrous items cannot be redeemed with money.
The Gemara asks who the Rabbis disagreeing with R. Eliezer are, since neither the stringent nor the lenient Rabbis fit.
The Gemara retracts: R. Yosei holds that mixed causes are permitted, so the baraitot can be attributed to R. Yosei and the Rabbis.
R. Yosei tells the Rabbis: in my view mixed causes are permitted, so planting under an ashera in any season is allowed.
R. Yosei argues: by your rule, planting in the rainy season is forbidden since fallen foliage fertilizes, so concede that point.
The Rabbis reply by Rav Mari b. Rav Kahana's rule: a benefit outweighed by an equal loss is not a benefit.
Rav Yehuda says Shmuel ruled that the halakha follows R. Yosei.
An incident: a garden fertilized with idolatrous dung; Rav Yosef confirms Shmuel's ruling for R. Yosei, so its produce is permitted.

49b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: wood from an ashera is forbidden for benefit, a new oven heated with it is shattered, and bread baked with it is forbidden.
Mishnah: R. Eliezer says cast the benefit into the Dead Sea; the Rabbis reply that idolatrous items cannot be redeemed with money.
Mishnah repeats the case of a weaving shuttle and garment, with the same disagreement over casting the benefit into the Dead Sea.
Both cases are needed: the bread case alone might suggest R. Eliezer's leniency applies only where the wood burned up.
R. Ḥiyya cites Rav Ḥisda citing Ze'eiri: the halakha follows R. Eliezer, with a variant transmission.
Rav Adda b. Ahava limits R. Eliezer's view to bread, not wine barrels; Rav Ḥisda permits even the barrel.
A case: Rav Ḥisda rules that a man with libation wine mixed in should cast four dinars into the river and keep the rest.
Mishnah: a gentile who removes even a leaf for his own use revokes the tree's status; shaving it for its sake leaves it forbidden.
Rav Huna and R. Ḥiyya b. Rav dispute whether shavings from an idol shaved for its sake are forbidden or permitted.
A baraita supports the permissive view: a gentile's shavings are permitted, while a Jew's are forbidden.
Rav holds that every sliver of a broken idol must be actively revoked.
Shmuel holds an idol is nullified only when it breaks in its natural manner of growth.
The Gemara asks: on the contrary, can natural growth nullify an idol at all?
Shmuel means that an idol needs no active revocation only if it breaks in its natural manner of growth.
The Gemara suggests that Rav and Shmuel dispute whether fragments of idols are worshipped.
The Gemara rejects that: all agree fragments are worshipped; the dispute is over fragments of fragments.
Rav holds fragments of fragments are forbidden; Shmuel holds they are permitted.
Alternatively, the dispute concerns idols made of parts that a layman can reassemble.
Rav: a reassemblable idol keeps its status; Shmuel: only breakage in natural growth matters, since disassembly is not growth.
The chapter closes with its closing formula, ending the chapter that opens with All the images.
Mishnah: R. Yishmael says three stones adjacent to Mercury are forbidden and two are permitted; the Rabbis forbid those that appear fallen from it.
The Rabbis hold idolaters worship fragments, so stones adjacent to Mercury may have fallen from it and are forbidden.
The Gemara asks what R. Yishmael holds: if fragments are worshipped, two stones should be forbidden; if not, three should be permitted.
R. Yoḥanan: where it is known the stones fell from the pile, all forbid, even those who deny fragment worship; the dispute is when unknown.

50a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Everyone agrees stones near Mercury's pile are prohibited if they may have fallen from it; the dispute concerns distant stones.
The Gemara objects: the phrase at the side of Mercury suggests the stones are nearby, not distant.
At the side means within the four cubits belonging to the pile.
R. Yishmael holds idolaters build a small pile beside a large one, so three stones are forbidden and two permitted; the Rabbis disagree.
R. Yoḥanan's rule: where it is known the stones fell from the pile, all agree they are forbidden.
The Gemara raises a baraita in which R. Yishmael permits two fallen stones, apparently contradicting R. Yoḥanan.
Rava: the baraita should read found adjacent, not fell, since there is no certainty they fell from the pile.
The Gemara objects with another baraita: R. Yishmael forbids two stones found by the pile and three even if distant.
Rava: no contradiction, since the permissive baraita has an elevated space between the stones, while the stringent one has them in one area.
The Gemara asks whether stones merely adjacent in this way count as a pile dedicated to Mercury.
The Gemara cites a baraita describing a pile's stones: one on each side and one atop them, not merely adjacent.
Rava: that baraita describes the main pile; added stones need not be arranged that way.
After King Yannai's house was destroyed, its Mercury stones were used to pave paths; some Rabbis avoided these paths, others did not.
R. Yoḥanan says a son of holy ones walks on them, so why should we withdraw from them?
The Gemara asks who is meant by the son of holy ones.
R. Menaḥem b. R. Simai, who would not even gaze at a coin's image, since such images might be idolatrous.
The Gemara asks the reason of the one who withdraws from those paths.
Rav's teaching: from Psalms 106:28 on eating dead offerings, an idolatrous offering can never be nullified, like a corpse.
The one who does not withdraw requires an offering to resemble Temple offerings, and stones are not such offerings.
Rabba bar Yirmeya brought a baraita about a gentile who used stones from Mercury's pile to pave paths and theaters.

50b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: a gentile who paves with Mercury stones nullifies them, while a Jew's use leaves them forbidden; the difficulty is unresolved.
Rav Sheshet resolves the difficulty: offerings are comparable only if they resemble Temple offerings, and stones do not.
Rabba bar Yirmeya's baraita permits worm removal and manure on cuts in the Sabbatical Year but forbids both on festival intermediate days.
No carpenter or son of a carpenter can resolve this difficulty.
Ravina resolves it: the Sabbatical Year forbids only agricultural labor, while festival intermediate days forbid all exertion, so they are not comparable.
Ravina asks what distinguishes manure, permitted in the Sabbatical Year, from pruning, forbidden.
Not comparable: manure preserves the tree, so it is permitted, while pruning enhances it, so it is forbidden.
Ravina suggests the real difficulty is a contradiction with a mishna on placing manure in the Sabbatical Year.
The Shevi'it mishna permits manure, binding, lopping, and shelter for saplings until Rosh HaShana of the Sabbatical Year.
Rav Ukva b. Ḥama's explanation: there are two kinds of hoeing, one to enhance growth and one to preserve, so manure has two kinds too.
Ravina suggests the same kind of contradiction over smearing oil, from the pruning baraita and a mishna on figs.
The Shevi'it mishna allows oiling unripe figs until Rosh HaShana, which seems to conflict with the baraita.
