ranges.en: Suggests Shmuel delayed because he hoped to find a tanna who prohibits deriving benefit, like Rabbi Natan
Cites a baraita of Rabbi Natan: wine measured by a gentile's hand is forbidden, by his foot permitted
Objects that Rabbi Natan's view cannot be what Shmuel awaited, since he would have said foot-measured wine is forbidden
Offers instead that Shmuel awaited a tanna like Rabbi Shimon, who permits even drinking such wine
Narrates the Biram case: a gentile's palm branch touched wine unintentionally, and Rav permitted selling it
Rav Kahana and Rav Asi object that Rav himself said a one-day-old gentile baby renders wine libation wine
Rav replies that he meant the wine is forbidden for drinking, not that deriving benefit from it is prohibited
Restates Rav's ruling that a one-day-old gentile baby renders wine libation wine, even without intent
Rav Shimi bar Hiyya objects with a baraita on slaves and gentile maidservants' sons who lack immersion
Baraita: adult gentile slaves render wine libation wine, while minors do not, depending on knowledge of idolatry
Notes that this baraita contradicts Rav's ruling on minors, and tests whether it can be read otherwise
Asks whether the baraita equates slaves with maidservants' sons, given it names spittle and treading
Asks what the baraita teaches if spittle is pure, since then the equation would be unnecessary
Explains the baraita equates slaves with maidservants' sons: only the uncircumcised-immersed render wine libation
Says this excludes Rav Nachman's report of Shmuel, that slaves still render wine prohibited after immersion
Rav Nachman reports Shmuel: such slaves render wine prohibited until idolatry leaves their mouths, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi sets twelve months
Rabba objects to Rav Nachman with the same baraita, which says slaves who lack immersion render wine prohibited

57b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continues the baraita: slaves in the marketplace are impure, though some say they are pure
Baraita: adult slaves who know idolatry render wine libation wine, while minors who do not know it do not
The baraita teaches that slaves circumcised without immersion render wine prohibited, but immersed ones do not
Explains that the baraita is about the sons of maidservants raised in a Jewish home, not purchased slaves
Asks whether the baraita equates purchased slaves with sons of maidservants throughout
Asks what the baraita adds if spittle and treading are pure, since then the comparison would be unnecessary
Explains the comparison is only that adults render wine libation wine and minors do not, as with maidservants' sons
Says the baraita excludes Rav's ruling that a one-day-old gentile baby renders wine libation wine
Narrates the Mehoza incident: a gentile stirred the wine in a bucket, which the storekeeper emptied into a barrel
Rava permits selling the barrel's wine, while Rav Huna bar Hinnana and Rav Huna bar Rav Nachman forbid it

58a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Narrates that Rav Huna son of Rav Nachman came to Meḥoza and Rava had the gates closed to focus
Rav Huna son of Rav Nachman enters Rava's presence
Asks the halakha in a case where a gentile stirred wine without intending a libation
Rava replies that such wine is prohibited even for deriving benefit
Objects that Rava himself said that stirring by a gentile does not make wine libation wine
Rava replies he meant only the sale of the barrel, but not benefit from the prohibited wine's value
Rava reports that Abaye surrounded him with amoraic traditions and a baraita forbidding benefit
Recounts that Shmuel and Rabbi Yohanan forbade wine stirred by a gentile in Neharde'a and Tiberias
Rava explains they ruled so because those towns' people were not Torah scholars, requiring distance from sin
Abaye objects that Meḥoza's people are no more Torah scholars, so Rava's permission was wrong
Abaye cites a baraita on a gentile market inspector who tasted wine, which the Sages prohibited
Abaye asks whether the baraita forbids benefit, and Rava answers that it forbids only drinking
Abaye argues the baraita should simply teach that the wine may be sold, as its latter clause says
Baraita's latter clause: a gentile confiscator who touched wine thinking it oil, and the wine may be sold
Concludes that the baraita is a conclusive refutation of Rava's view
Narrates Rabbi Yohanan ben Arza and Rabbi Yosei ben Nehorai drinking wine poured by a man who was a gentile
One sage forbade the wine even for benefit, while the other permitted it even for drinking
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says both are properly deemed, since both opinions are viable

58b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the case: the rabbis drank liquor, not wine, so the gentile did not pour it as a libation
Asks why the gentile did not recognize the drink as wine by its sight or smell
Asks whether the gentile touched the wine in drawing it, which would be an unintentional touch that prohibits
Replies that the gentile poured without touching, and the Sages did not decree on wine poured by his force
Rabbi Asi asks Rabbi Yohanan the halakha for wine mixed with water by a gentile
Rabbi Asi cites Proverbs 9:2, she has mixed her wine, to justify the term mixed
Rabbi Yohanan replies that biblical and rabbinic terminology are each their own language
Rabbi Asi repeats the question: what is the halakha
Rabbi Yohanan rules it prohibited by decree, citing the maxim about keeping a nazirite away from a vineyard
Rabbi Yirmeya applies the maxim at Savta, and it is reported as Rabbi Yohanan's ruling on diluted wine
Reish Lakish at Bozrah forbids untithed produce and water bowed to by gentiles, which Jews consumed
Rabbi Yohanan tells Reish Lakish to retract, since Bozrah is outside Eretz Yisrael and public water is permitted
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yohanan follows his usual line of reasoning

59a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yohanan cites Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak: public water is not prohibited, so private water is
Objects that private water attached to the ground would be permitted anyway, so the ruling needs a detached case
Objects that the water is like boulders fallen by themselves, and asks whether Rabbi Yohanan deems those prohibited
Replies that the water case concerns water struck and detached by a human hand, so private water is prohibited
Narrates Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba at Gavla seeing converts' wives, diluted wine, and lupines, and saying nothing
Rabbi Yohanan instructs him to declare the children mamzerim, forbid the wine, and forbid the lupines
Explains Rabbi Yohanan's two standing rulings: an unimmersed convert is a gentile, and offspring of a gentile and a Jewess is a mamzer
Explains the wine instruction: diluted wine is forbidden as libation wine by the nazirite maxim
States the lupine ruling: forbidden due to gentile cooking, since the people there are not Torah scholars
Objects that Torah scholars would be permitted, and cites Rav that anything eaten raw escapes gentile cooking
Rabbi Yohanan follows another version of Rav: lupines lack importance for kings' tables, so only the ignorance is the reason
Asks Rav Kahana whether a gentile may bring grapes to the winepress without doing anything else
Rav Kahana rules it prohibited by rabbinic decree, citing the nazirite maxim about the vineyard
Rav Yeimar objects to Rav Kahana with a baraita on a gentile bringing grapes to the winepress in baskets

59b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continues the baraita: grapes in small barrels are permitted even though the juice sprays onto them
Rav Kahana replies that the baraita addresses grapes already brought, whereas he forbids bringing them ab initio
Narrates the etrog that fell into wine and the gentile who touched it, and Rav Ashi's instructions to drain the barrel
Rav Ashi rules that a gentile who intentionally poured a Jew's wine as a libation must pay its value to the owner
Asks the reason, and Rav Ashi answers that it is as if the gentile burned the wine
Rav Ashi cites a baraita: wine poured outside an idol's presence is permitted, as the Jew did not authorize it
Rav Pappa rules that all wine next to the opened stopper is prohibited, since a gentile's hand touched it

60a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Reports Rav Pappa's ruling: wine above the stopper of the barrel is prohibited, but the wine below is permitted
Rav Yeimar ties the ruling to a dispute in a mishnah on a pierced barrel, aligning it with Rabbi Yehuda
Rav Pappa rules that a gentile pouring into a Jew's beaker, or a Jew pouring with a gentile holding it, is prohibited
Explains the reason: the wine flows by the gentile's force, so it is prohibited, unless the gentile tilts the beaker
Rav Pappa rules on a gentile carrying a wineskin or beaker, depending on whether it is full or not
Rav Ashi permits both wineskin and beaker, since shaking a wineskin is not the typical manner of a libation
Rav Pappi permits wine pressed by beams without foot contact, while Rav Ashi, or Rav Shimi bar Ashi, prohibits it
Explains the dispute: all agree on direct force, and disagree when the force is generated by the gentile's force
Reports an incident where wine was pressed by generated force, and Rav Yaakov of Nehar Pekod prohibited a barrel

60b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rafram bar Pappa rules that wine in a barrel split lengthwise, held by a gentile, is prohibited only for drinking
Asks the reason, and the answer is that the gentile acts like a brick weighing the barrel down
Narrates a gentile standing in a winepress, and Rav Ashi rules how much rinsing it needs
Mishnah: a gentile standing by a vat makes the wine prohibited only if the owner owes him a loan
Mishnah continues: a gentile who fell into the vat, measured with a pole, or removed a hornet, and Rabbi Shimon's view
Shmuel holds the loan must include a lien on that wine for the prohibition to apply
Rav Ashi cites a mishnah on Beit She'an, where the wine is permitted only if the gentile released it, to support Shmuel
Rav Ashi explains that the gentile's refusal to release it gives him ownership, so the lien principle follows from the mishnah
Mishnah on a gentile who fell into the vat and emerged, with Rav Pappa limiting it to a gentile who emerged dead
Gives Rav Pappa's reason: a gentile rescued from death treats that day as a festival and offers the wine as thanksgiving
Mishnah on pole measuring and foam removal, permitted for benefit but not drinking, while Rabbi Shimon permits drinking
Rav Adda bar Ahava explains Rabbi Shimon's view is consistent: permitted for drinking means permitted for benefit too
Reports conflicting traditions that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon, and the Gemara concludes it does not
Mishnah: a gentile who threw a barrel into the vat in anger, and the wine was deemed fit for drinking
Rav Ashi's rule: a gentile renders wine libation wine by any contact that makes a zav impure, but not otherwise
Rav Huna objects to Rav Ashi from the mishnah, which implies anger matters and the zav analogy would not

61a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Ashi explains the mishna's case: the barrel is propelled by the gentile, not thrown.
Mishna: wine is permitted in a mixed city, and in an all-gentile city only if a Jew guards it.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds that all gentile domains are one.
Mishna: a gentile's written receipt for payment makes the wine permitted, as it belongs to the Jew.
Mishna: if the gentile withholds the wine until paid, it is prohibited; an incident in Beit She'an.
Objection: an all-gentile city should also permit wine, since Jewish peddlers pass through.
Shmuel: the mishna means a city with double doors and a crossbar, so residents see outsiders enter.
Rav Yosef: an open window, a trash heap, or a palm tree counts as a public thoroughfare.
Rav Aha and Ravina disagree about wine by a palm tree with its top cut off; one prohibits, one permits.
Explains each view: with no fruit no one climbs, while lost animals bring climbers, so the gentile is cautious.
Baraita: a Jew renting a house in a gentile courtyard, with another Jew there, makes the wine permitted even without a key or seal.

61b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: wine is permitted when another Jew shares the courtyard and holds the key or seal.
Rabbi Yohanan tells the reciter to teach that wine is permitted even without the key or seal.
Baraita: in a separate courtyard the wine stays prohibited even with key or seal, per Rabbi Meir.
The Sages prohibit the wine unless a watchman constantly guards it or an appointed person comes.
Gemara asks which case the Sages mean, since the first tanna also prohibits the last clause.
Resolution: the Sages refer to the first clause's last part, where a watchman or appointee is needed.
Objection: a periodic appointee helps the gentile know when to act, so the baraita must be emended.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds that all gentile domains are one.
Dilemma: was Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar lenient or stringent?
Rav Yehuda, citing Ze'eiri, says lenient; Rav Nahman, citing Ze'eiri, says stringent.
Explains the lenient reading: the first tanna prohibits wine in another gentile's domain due to collusion.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: other gentiles' domains are different, so no collusion concern applies.
Rav Nahman, citing Ze'eiri, holds that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar is stringent.
Explains the stringent reading: the first tanna's distinction still leaves another domain prohibited.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: all gentile domains are one, so the wine is prohibited in either.
A baraita supports Rav Nahman's reading, with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar stringent due to swindlers.
Context: swindlers from Parzak's house placed Jewish wine with gentile sharecroppers.
The Rabbis argue collusion is not feared here, since the sharecropper does not normally store items there.
Rava objects: the sharecropper fears the vizier and will cover for him, so collusion is feared.
Rava's ruling on a gentile seen among wine barrels: permitted if he would be caught as a thief.
Closing formula marking the end of the chapter, named after Rabbi Yishmael.

62a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: wages for making libation wine are forbidden, but wages for other work with it are permitted.
Mishna: rent for a donkey carrying libation wine is forbidden, but rent for riding it is permitted.
Why is the wage for making libation wine forbidden?
Objection: if benefit from the wine is forbidden, so is the wage; orla and diverse-kinds money refutes this.
Alternative proposal: the wage is forbidden because it takes on the idolatrous status of the wine.
Objection from a mishna: Sabbatical produce would make the wage forbidden the same way, yet the wage is permitted.
Rabbi Yohanan, via Rabbi Abbahu: the prohibition is a penalty the Sages imposed on wine and donkey drivers.
What is the penalty imposed on donkey drivers?
A baraita: donkey drivers hauling Sabbatical produce are paid in Sabbatical produce.
Objection: paying wages from Sabbatical produce violates the verse limiting it to food, not commerce.
Objection from a baraita: a wage fixed as a dinar's value is forbidden, which is similar to the donkey case.
Abaye: they are paid from Sabbatical produce, but as a permitted gift rather than as a wage.

62b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A mishna supports the distinction: an unsold gift may be given in Jerusalem, so the drivers may be paid in gifts.
Rava: the drivers' pay is sacred with Sabbatical sanctity, since their wages are large, unlike a laborer's.
Dilemma: is the wage forbidden for working on nondescript gentile wine, or lenient like its impurity status?
A case of a ship owner paid in wheat for nondescript wine; Rav Hisda orders the wheat burned and buried.
Objection: why bury the wheat, when it could be scattered or burned and scattered instead?
Objection: the wheat should be buried whole, as a baraita on execution instruments shows burial alone suffices.
Execution instruments are buried in the court graveyard, so their prohibition is clear, unlike stolen wheat here.
Rabbi Yannai's scholars borrowed Sabbatical produce and repaid it later; Rabbi Yohanan says this is not commerce.
A baraita on a prostitute's payment: permitted when the payment and intercourse are not simultaneous.
Why would the baraita need to state the case where payment is given without intercourse, which is obviously permitted?
The baraita means payment given or intercourse done after an interval, which is not proximate, so it is permitted.
If payment came before intercourse, what is the status when intercourse occurs?

63a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Eliezer: the baraita refers to a case where she sacrificed the payment in the Temple before intercourse.
What are the circumstances, given that a present gift from now would be obviously permitted?
A verse on consecrating one's house shows that only property in one's possession can be consecrated.
The baraita concerns a case where the payment stays with her until intercourse, and she may then use it.
Rav Hoshaya's dilemma: is a spoken consecration before intercourse like sacrifice, or is the animal still extant?
Suggested resolution from Rabbi Eliezer, who specifies that the case is one of sacrifice and not mere consecration.
Rejected: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling may be silent on consecration, so the dilemma stays unresolved.
A baraita: payment given after intercourse, following an interval, is permitted.
Contradicting baraita: payment given after intercourse, even three years later, is forbidden.
Rav Hisda: the forbidden case is where the specific lamb is named in advance; otherwise it is not payment.
But naming a lamb involves no pulling, so how could a gentile prostitute acquire it?
Gentiles acquire by paying money; or it is a Jewish prostitute with the lamb already in her courtyard.
If the lamb was in her courtyard, the payment was acquired before intercourse, so the case does not fit.
The case is a lamb given as a pledge, returned if dinars come, otherwise kept as payment.
Objection from a baraita: a master may tell workers to eat or drink with a dinar without concern for transgression.

63b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: an employer is not responsible for workers' purchases if they pay themselves, but must watch when he promises to reimburse.
Rav Sheshet infers that paying after a delay counts as paying for forbidden items, even if they no longer exist.
Rav Hisda reads the baraita as a storekeeper who gives credit, so the debt is incurred at once and is forbidden.
What if the storekeeper gives no credit: why not teach the distinction within the reimbursement case itself?
The tanna could have taught the distinction: the ban applies only where the storekeeper gives credit.
Objection: even without credit the employer incurs a debt, as a guarantor does under Rava's own ruling.
Rava: any commitment to pay creates a liability, but without designated coins the conduct is not prohibited.
Why must the baraita's employer worry about Sabbatical produce if no specific money is designated?
Rav Pappa: the employer paid the storekeeper a dinar in advance, so the items count as acquired.
Rav Kahana reports stating this halakha before Rav Zevid of Neharde'a.
Zevid objects: the baraita should then have said to calculate the deduction from the advance dinar.
Rav Kahana: teach the baraita as saying to go and calculate the deduction from the dinar given.
Rav Ashi: the employer took the food from the storekeeper and handed it to the laborers himself.
Rav Yeimar objects that the baraita should then say take and eat, not go and eat.
Rav Ashi: teach the baraita as saying take and eat, take and drink.
Setting: Rav Nahman, Ulla, Avimi bar Pappi and Rabbi Hiyya bar Ami sit together.
Dilemma: is hiring someone to break libation wine barrels forbidden, since the breaker is paid for the act?
Rav Nahman: he may break them, and a blessing will come upon him.
Suggested support from a baraita: one may not hoe with a gentile in a field of diverse kinds, which Rav Nahman's view would contradict.

64a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: One may uproot diverse kinds with a gentile in order to reduce impropriety.
In accordance with whose opinion is this baraita, and is it Rabbi Akiva's?
Baraita: Rabbi Akiva holds that even one who maintains diverse kinds, not only one who sows them, is flogged.
What is the reasoning of Rabbi Akiva?
A verse forbids sowing diverse kinds, and the phrase not diverse kinds is read to cover maintaining them too.
Concluding support for Rav Nahman: maintaining diverse kinds is forbidden, but permitted to be paid for uprooting them.
Rejected: the baraita follows the Rabbis, who permit maintaining diverse kinds, so it proves nothing for Rav Nahman.
Why does the baraita permit uprooting with a gentile at all, if maintaining diverse kinds is permitted?
The case is unpaid uprooting, which fits Rabbi Yehuda's view that an unpaid gift to a gentile is prohibited.
Rav Nahman's ruling can be proven from Rabbi Yehuda's view and, by parallel, Rabbi Akiva's view.
Dilemma: do proceeds from selling idolatrous objects held by a gentile take on their forbidden status?
Rav Nahman: it stands to reason that such proceeds are permitted.
Rabba bar Avuh tells converts to sell their idols before converting, implying the proceeds are permitted.
Rejected: the converts had revoked the idols' status, so they sold permitted items.
A baraita on a creditor paid from proceeds of idols or libation wine shows such proceeds are permitted.
What distinguishes the permitted first clause from the forbidden latter clause?
Rav Sheshet: the latter is forbidden because the Jew wants the idol or wine preserved to get repaid.
Objection from a mishna on a convert's inheritance from a gentile father, which forbids a later exchange.
Rava bar Ulla: the mishna concerns idols whose value survives breaking, so the convert does not care about preservation.
Does wine-soaked earthenware also lack preservation interest, given the convert wants it not stolen or lost?
Rav Pappa: a convert's inheritance is lenient by rabbinic decree, lest he return to his corrupted ways.

64b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: a convert and a gentile may divide inherited property with idols, but not partnership property.
Dilemma: can a ger toshav, who does not worship idols, revoke an idol's status as a gentile can?
Rav Nahman: only one who worships idols can revoke an idol's status; a non-worshipper cannot.
Objection from a baraita: a gentile may revoke the status of any idol, whether he worships it or not.
What do worships and does not worship mean, if both refer to the same gentile?
Both phrases refer to gentiles; the first covers a shared idol, the latter a gentile worshipping a different one.
Objection from a baraita: Rabbi Meir defines a ger toshav as one who accepts no idolatry before three companions.
The Rabbis say a ger toshav accepts the seven Noahide laws; others say he is a convert who eats carcasses.
Baraita: a ger toshav may be left alone briefly with wine, but not given wine long term, even in a Jewish town.
Objection: the oil of a gentile cannot take the status of libation wine, so the baraita is wrong.
Emendation: the baraita should say his wine is like his oil, permitted for benefit but not consumption.
Baraita: otherwise a ger toshav is like a gentile; Rabban Shimon treats his wine as libation wine.
With what halakha is the ger toshav equated to a gentile, if not revoking idol status?
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak: it concerns giving or renouncing rights in a domain for Shabbat courtyard joining.
A baraita on an apostate Jew who observes Shabbat publicly can renounce rights in a shared domain.
For a gentile to acquire such rights, a Jew must lease his courtyard domain by a verbal transfer.
Rav Yehuda sent a gift to Rav Nahman.

65a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Yehuda: he knows the gentile does not worship idols, so he is not treated as a gentile for festival gifts.
Rav Yosef objects with a baraita defining a ger toshav as one who accepts before three companions.
Rav Yosef objects further: a ger toshav uncircumcised after twelve months is like a gentile.
Rav Yehuda: that ruling concerns a gentile who took on circumcision and then recanted, not an ordinary ger toshav.
Narrative: Rava brings a festival gift to bar Sheshakh, finds him with prostitutes, and debates the afterlife with him.
A royal officer summons bar Sheshakh, and bar Sheshakh's eye bursts after Rava's blessing.
Rav Pappi and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak suggest verses Rava should have used to reply to bar Sheshakh.
Mishna: a wage is permitted for other work done with a barrel of libation wine.
Contradiction from a baraita: the wage for moving the barrel is permitted only if said toward evening.
Abaye and Rava: the cases differ by whether the work is one task for all barrels or a task per barrel.
A baraita matches Rava's distinction: a single price for all barrels forbids the wage, separate prices permit it.
Mishna: rent for a donkey carrying libation wine is forbidden.
Why is the additional clause needed, since the principle is the same as the first clause?
It teaches that if the renter only sits on the donkey, a jug of libation wine placed on it leaves the rent permitted.
Is the jug placement not part of the rental, since the renter has no right to place it?
Contradiction from a baraita on what the renter and the driver may each load onto the donkey.
Abaye: granted the renter may load the jug, the driver would not deduct its fee, so the rent is not forbidden.
What circumstances does the baraita address, given the availability of provisions along the way?
Rav Pappa: the case is where buying provisions is possible but troublesome, which suits the driver but not the renter.
The father of Rav Aha, son of Rav Ika, is mentioned, and the text breaks off there.

65b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Narrative: Rav Ika poured wine for gentiles and took the jugs as payment, and reports reached Abaye.
Abaye: Rav Ika labored with permitted wine, since the wine became forbidden only after reaching gentiles.
Does Rav Ika not care about the wineskins staying intact, since he needs the jugs as payment?
Either the buyers bore the cost of torn skins, or they brought barrels to pour the wine into.
Did Rav Ika not labor with forbidden wine when ferrying the buyers over the crossing?
He had an arrangement with the ferryman, so he did not ferry them himself.
Mishna: rinsed grapes stay permitted if uncracked; figs or dates with enough wine flavor are forbidden. Boethus ben Zunen's case.
Principle: forbidden wine is prohibited only if it adds positive flavor; forbidden vinegar on beans is permitted.
Was the Boethus incident cited to contradict the halakha stated just before it?
The mishna is incomplete: wine that harms the flavor is permitted, as in the Boethus incident.
Rava permitted selling a wheat heap onto which libation wine fell, since deriving benefit is not prohibited.
Objection from a baraita: a garment with forbidden mixed fibers may not be sold to a gentile or used as a saddle cloth.
Why can't the garment be sold to a gentile? Perhaps the gentile will sell it to a Jew.
Rava retracted: wheat may be ground and sold to gentiles, but not in Jews' presence.
Mishna restated: wine spilled on grapes permits them if rinsed; if cracked, they are forbidden.
If cracked grapes are forbidden, why is wheat with wine treated more strictly than rinsing would allow?
Rav Pappa: wheat is different, since its slits make it like cracked grapes.

66a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Old wine used for a libation renders grapes forbidden only with flavor; for new wine, Abaye says any amount suffices, Rava says flavor.
Abaye: we follow flavor here, so same-flavored wine and grapes are one kind, and any amount forbids the mixture.
Rava: we follow the name, so wine and grapes are different kinds, and only flavor forbids the mixture.
Does the mishna on new wine and cracked grapes mean any amount forbids, or only flavor?
Objection: the mishna's principle about flavor implies only flavor-imparting cases are meant.
Abaye: the mishna concerns old wine on grapes, which differ in flavor, so an amount that imparts flavor forbids them.
Abaye's view on vinegar and leaven mixtures: flavor governs, so forbidden items must impart flavor.
Rava's view on the same mixtures: the name governs, so any amount of forbidden item forbids the mixture.
From where does Abaye derive that flavor governs?
A baraita: spices known by different names or species combine to forbid a dish.
Hizkiyya: the spices are all sweeteners, so they share one flavor and combine.
Abaye: if the name governs, the spices would not combine since each name is discrete.
Rava: the baraita follows Rabbi Meir, who says all forbidden foods combine, as shown by a verse.
Forbidden vinegar in wine forbids only if it imparts flavor; wine spilled into vinegar is disputed.
Abaye: any amount of wine forbids the vinegar mixture, while Rava requires flavor.

66b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abaye's view: wine smelling of vinegar counts as vinegar, so any amount of forbidden wine forbids the mixture.
Rava's view: wine that smells of vinegar counts as wine, so only flavor forbids the mixture.
Bunghole dispute: Abaye forbids a Jew smelling gentile wine through it, since smell is substantial; Rava permits it.
Rava's proof from a mishna: bread baked with teruma cumin is permitted, since only the smell, not flavor, passed to it.
Abaye: that case differs because the forbidden cumin was burned, so its smell came from no extant substance.
Rav Mari: this parallels Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda, who disagree on whether a smell is substantial.
Rava must accept the tanna dispute, but can Abaye's view also be parallel to a tanna dispute?
Abaye: Rabbi Yehuda also holds smell is substantial, as Reish Lakish's reading of the mishna shows.

67a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Argument: a hot loaf with a stoppered barrel is disputed, so the bunghole case resembles a hot loaf with an open barrel, which is forbidden.
Mishna's principle: anything benefiting from a forbidden item's flavor is forbidden; forbidden vinegar on split beans is permitted.
Rav Yehuda reports that Shmuel holds this to be the halakha.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: vinegar in hot beans is permitted, but vinegar in cold beans later heated is forbidden.
Ravin and Rav Dimi report Rabbi Yohanan's ruling on hot and cold beans, and the cress dish customs of Tzippori.
Reish Lakish: the detriment principle applies to a dish that lacks nothing and is uneaten only because of the forbidden item.
A lenient reading of Reish Lakish: if the forbidden item already detracted from the flavor, the dish is permitted.
Rabbi Yohanan: where forbidden flavor and substance are perceptible, one is flogged for eating an olive-bulk within a half-loaf's eating time.

67b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If only the forbidden flavor shows, the mixture is forbidden without lashes; if the flavor amplified the dish's flavor, permitted.
Why does the ruling say amplified, rather than simply saying detrimental flavor is permitted?
Rabbi Yohanan's wording covers other detracting ingredients too; the halakha follows Reish Lakish's last version.
Rav Kahana: Shmuel, Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish together show detrimental flavor is permitted.
Abaye objects: Reish Lakish may only be reporting others' view, not holding it himself.
By inference, is there a view that detrimental forbidden flavor makes the mixture forbidden?
Yes: a baraita where Rabbi Meir forbids any flavor, and Rabbi Shimon forbids only enhancing flavor.
Rabbi Meir derives this from purging gentile vessels, which are forbidden though their taste is detrimental.
Rav Huna son of Rav Hiyya: the Torah forbids only a pot used that day, so Rabbi Shimon's view is coherent.
What is Rabbi Shimon's reasoning?
A baraita on Deuteronomy 14:21: anything a resident alien may eat is called carrion, so the verse supports Rabbi Shimon.

68a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A carcass unfit even for a ger toshav is not called an unslaughtered carcass for the prohibition.
Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon respond on whether verse excludes meat that was rancid from the outset.
Ulla: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon dispute only when the forbidden item first enhanced the flavor, then detracted.
Rav Hagga objects from a baraita: forbidden wine or vinegar in a dish is forbidden even when it detracted from flavor at first.
Ulla: Rav Hagga errs, as vinegar in cold beans enhances flavor first, so Rabbi Meir forbids it after heating.
Rabbi Yohanan: the dispute concerns only a forbidden item that detracts from flavor from the outset.
Dilemma: does Rabbi Yohanan's dispute also cover enhancing-then-detracting cases, or only detracting ones?
Rav Amram asks whether Rabbi Yohanan's statement has support in a mishna.
A mishna in Orla: non-sacred leaven, then forbidden leaven, leavens dough; Rabbi Shimon permits it, supporting the dispute.
Rav Amram: here the forbidden item detracted at the outset, and Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon disagree.
Rabbi Zeira: dough differs, since leaven that detracts still enhances the dough's usefulness for leavening other batches.
Another baraita on teruma and non-sacred leaven in dough, supporting Rabbi Yohanan's suggested source.
The Gemara notes that here the forbidden item detracted from the outset, and asks whether the same applies generally.

68b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita's latter clause refutes Rabbi Zeira: the lentils and beans case also has the forbidden item detracting from the outset.
Objection: the first clause of the baraita shows the dispute covers enhancing-then-detracting cases too.
Conclusion: the dispute concerns only a forbidden item that detracted from flavor from the outset.
Why are all three clauses of the baraita needed, since each teaches a different case?
Why is the first clause needed, if its ruling could be inferred from the other two clauses?
Abaye: the first clause shows Rabbi Shimon permits it, and the Sages argue the dough leavened faster due to forbidden leaven.
Rabbi Shimon responds that both leavens enhanced and detracted from the dough, so neither is singled out.
Even for Rabbi Shimon, should permitted and forbidden leaven combine, since enhancement by forbidden leaven forbids?
Rabbi Shimon's consistent view: a forbidden item does not combine with another forbidden item, nor with a permitted one.
A mishna in Me'ila: orla and diverse kinds combine per Rabbi Yehuda but not per Rabbi Shimon, supporting that view.
A mouse fell into a barrel of beer, and Rav forbade the beer.
Does Rav hold that even detrimental flavor forbids, since the mouse must have detracted from the beer?
Rav Sheshet: Rav generally permits detrimental flavor, but a mouse is an exceptional case the Torah forbids.
Objection: if the mouse is stricter, a dead mouse should be impure whether moist or dry, yet the mishna says otherwise.
Rav Sheshet: by that reasoning, semen would also be impure whether moist or dry, which the mishna rejects.
Semen and mice are both limited by verses to their state at death, so the mouse prohibition still applies even when detrimental.
Rav Shimi of Neharde'a objects that a mouse is repulsive, yet is served at kings' tables as a delicacy.
Rav Shimi: a field mouse is a delicacy, a city mouse is repulsive, so there is no contradiction.
Rava: the halakha is that detrimental flavor is permitted, as the general rule holds.
Rava does not know Rav's reason for forbidding a mouse in beer, whether detriment forbids or the mouse enhanced flavor.
A dilemma is raised before the Sages about the mouse in beer.

69a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks the halakha when a mouse falls into vinegar, and whether vinegar takes on its flavor.
Rav Hillel cites a past incident in Rav Kahana's study hall as evidence that vinegar takes on flavor.
Reports that Rav Kahana forbade the vinegar in that incident.
Rav Ashi rejects the proof: the mouse was dismembered, so the ruling concerned a substantive piece.
Ravina's view: the vinegar must be calculated at 101 times the volume of the mouse.
Another opinion, Ravina's, holds the mouse should not be treated more stringently than teruma.
Brings a mishna on teruma, nullified in a mixture by 101 times its volume, as support.
Rav Taḥlifa bar Giza objects to Ravina's reasoning.
Suggests the case resembles spice of teruma, whose flavor is not nullified even by 101 times.
Rav Aḥai's ruling: the vinegar nullifies the mouse at fifty times its volume.
Rav Shmuel bar Rav Ika's ruling: beer nullifies the mouse at sixty times its volume.
The conclusion: both vinegar and beer need sixty times, and this applies to all Torah prohibitions.
Mishna case: a gentile transporting a Jew's wine is permitted if the wine was under supervision.
Mishna case: if the Jew said he was leaving, the wine is forbidden for the time to bore and reseal.
Mishna case: wine left on a wagon or ship with a gentile is permitted, since he cannot tell when the Jew returns.
Mishna case: if the Jew announced a long absence, the wine is forbidden for the time to bore and reseal.
Mishna case: a gentile left in a shop, with the same rules for a Jew's absence and announced departure.
Mishna case: wine left on the table is forbidden, but the jug on the side table is permitted.
If the Jew told the gentile to mix and drink, the side-table jug is forbidden; open barrels are forbidden, sealed ones permitted.
Asks what the circumstances are for the presumption that the wine was under supervision.
A baraita on donkey drivers and laborers explains the case, with pure produce permitted and impure produce forbidden.
Asks what distinguishes the first clause of the baraita from the latter clause.
Rav Yitzhak answers: the first clause concerns workers purified for the assignment.
Objects that the latter clause should then apply the same way.
Replies that an am ha'aretz is not careful about contact with another person's impurity.
Objects that the first clause should then also be ruled impure.
Introduces Rava's answer to the objection, cut off at the daf's end.

69b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava explains the case as one where the Jew came back by a roundabout route the gentile could not anticipate.
Objects that if so, the latter clause should also apply the same way.
Replies that in the latter clause the Jew said he would follow, so the gentile feels at ease.
Cites the mishna's list of similar cases: a gentile in a shop, and wine in a wagon or ship.
Explains why the mishna lists the shop case separately: one might think the gentile fears the owner's return.
Explains why the wagon and ship cases are listed too, so the same ruling is seen to apply to all.
Rabbi Yohanan's view: the dispute concerns lime-plaster stoppers only; clay stoppers are forbidden after the full reopening time.
Objects with a baraita of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: resealing is noticeable from above and below.
Explains the objection: if the dispute concerns clay stoppers, the baraita's response makes sense.
Continues the objection: for lime plaster, the resealing is not noticeable from above, so the baraita is problematic.
Answers that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel misunderstood the Rabbis' position on clay stoppers.
Offers the same answer for lime plaster: it is not visible above but is visible below.
Explains the Rabbis' view: the gentile would not expect a turned stopper, or the seal may sometimes hold firmly.
Rava rules that the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, since an unattributed mishna agrees with him.
Cites the mishna's last clause on the table and side-table jugs and sealed barrels as support.
Asks whether the point is obvious, and what it adds to the mishna.
Answers that one might think the whole clause is Rabban Shimon's; Rava teaches it is not.
Asks why we do not put wine in sealed barrels with gentiles, given the rulings adopted elsewhere.
Answers that the concern is the bunghole, which a gentile might widen to drink from.
Rava rules that wine at a table shared by a gentile prostitute and Jews is permitted.
Explains that their passion for sin overwhelms their judgment, so they will not tamper with the wine.

70a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rules that a gentile's passion does not overwhelm his judgment about libations, so wine at a Jewish prostitute's table is forbidden.
Asks what the reason is for that ruling.
Explains that she is contemptible to them, so they use the wine for libation without regard for her.
Narrates a case: a gentile locked in with a Jew's wine, seen through a crack among the barrels.
Rava rules: barrels visible through the crack are permitted, while those on either side of it are forbidden.
Narrates a case: a Jew's wine in a lower story, where a gentile came back first and locked the door.
Rava rules the wine permitted, since the gentile may think the Jew is upstairs watching him.
Narrates an inn case where a gentile sits among the barrels; Rava permits the wine if he was caught as a thief.
Narrates a house case; Rava says the wine is forbidden only if the gentile has an excuse for being there.
Raises a baraita apparently requiring prohibition even without an excuse, as a contradiction to Rava.
Answers that the baraita speaks of a gentile who has an excuse for entering.
Narrates a case where a Jew and a gentile drink together, and the Jew leaves for prayer.
Rava rules the wine permitted, since the gentile will remember his wine and return.
Narrates a case where a Jew leaves a ship at the start of Shabbat, while a gentile remains aboard.
Rava rules the wine permitted, since the gentile expects the Jew to return and remember his wine.
Objects that the gentile would know the Jew will not return until Shabbat ends.
Cites Issur the Convert's testimony that gentiles assumed Jews would violate Shabbat for money.
Cites Rabbi Yitzhak's ruling on carrying a found wallet on Shabbat, as the accepted halakha.
Narrates a case where a lion roars in a winepress and a gentile hides among the barrels.
Rava rules the wine permitted in that case.
Explains that the gentile would fear a Jew hiding behind him and seeing him.
Narrates a case of thieves in Pumbedita who opened many barrels; Rava rules the wine permitted.
Asks what the reason is for permitting the wine.
Answers that most thieves in Pumbedita are Jews, and the halakha follows the majority.
Narrates a similar case in Neharde'a, where Shmuel also rules the wine permitted.
Asks whether Shmuel follows Rabbi Eliezer's view on doubt about entry into a place.
Cites a mishna on a person who doubts entering a contaminated field, where Rabbi Eliezer deems him pure.
Rejects the comparison: thieves may be gentiles or not, and may not touch the wine, so it is compound doubt.

70b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Narrates a gentile girl found among barrels holding wine froth; Rava rules the wine permitted.
Explains Rava's reason: she likely took froth from the outside of the barrel, and froth may have been there earlier.
Narrates an army unit that entered Neharde'a and opened many barrels of wine.
Rav Dimi reports a similar case, decided by Rabbi Elazar as permitted.
Asks whether Rabbi Elazar permitted the wine because of Rabbi Eliezer's doubt rule, or because most soldiers were Jews.
Asks: if so, this is doubt about contact, not entry, and Rabbi Eliezer would be stringent.
Answers that the soldiers opened many barrels seeking money, so it resembles doubt about entry.
Narrates a wine shop owner who gave a gentile woman the key to the door.
Rabbi Yitzhak reports Rabbi Elazar's case: the key was entrusted only for safekeeping, not for entering.
Abaye cites a mishna on entrusting keys to an am ha'aretz, where pure items stay pure, as support.
Asks whether the purity rules are then stricter than the rules on libation wine.
Answers yes: Rav holds a shared courtyard makes purity stricter, while Rabbi Yohanan says the items stay pure.
Objects to Rav with a baraita on an inner courtyard that a devoted person may use despite the am ha'aretz's reach.
Answers that there the am ha'aretz would be caught as a thief, so he would not tamper.
Cites Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's roof baraita in support of Rav, which challenges Rabbi Yohanan.
Answers that Rabbi Yohanan's case differs, since the am ha'aretz could claim he only stretched himself.
Cites a further baraita on adjacent roofs, which seems to contradict Rav.
Answers that Rav follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view on neighboring roofs, so there is no contradiction.
Mishna: a military unit entering in peacetime makes open barrels forbidden, sealed ones permitted; in wartime all are permitted.

71a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Raises a contradiction from a Ketubot mishna on priests' wives in a conquered city being forbidden to their husbands.
Rav Mari resolves it: soldiers have no time to pour libations, but they do have time for intercourse.
Mishna: craftsmen paid in libation wine may ask for its monetary value only before it enters their possession.
Rav Yehuda reports Rav's ruling: a person may tell a gentile to pay his wine tax for him and be reimbursed.
Objects with a baraita forbidding a Jew to tell a gentile to pay the wine tax on his behalf in libation wine.
Rav distinguishes: telling a gentile to pay in one's stead is forbidden, but asking him to save one from the tax is permitted.
Mishna: money from wine sold to a gentile is permitted if the price was fixed before the wine was measured.
Ameimar holds that acquisition by pulling an object applies to gentiles, citing Persian gift exchanges as proof.
Rav Ashi counters that pulling does not acquire from gentiles; the gifts are kept out of haughtiness, not acquisition law.
Rav Ashi cites Rav's instruction to shopkeepers to collect dinars first, as proof that pulling does not acquire.
Explains the reasoning: otherwise the wine would become libation wine in the shopkeepers' possession, so the dinars would be payment for it.

71b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Argues that a gentile acquires wine by pulling it before it becomes libation wine, so the seller may take payment.
Rejects the proof: wine reaching the gentile's vessel may become forbidden first, depending on where it lands.
Replies that Rav's ruling matters only if the gentile's vessel rests on the ground, before any acquisition.
Asks whether a buyer's vessels in the seller's domain prevent acquisition, a point the Sages dispute.
Rejects the question: the wine is forbidden by residue on the jug's mouth, so Rav told shopkeepers to take payment first.
Objects that Rav cannot follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view, which would permit the payment.
Replies that Rav's ruling follows his own position, that only barrel-to-barrel mixing is treated leniently.
Objects with a baraita on returning an idol object bought in gold scrap, which seems to contradict Ameimar.
Abaye and Rava explain: returning the object is a mistaken transaction, and the case of paying is treated differently.
Mar Kashisha objects to Rav Ashi with a mishna on payment before or after measuring, if pulling does not acquire.
Rav Ashi replies that the gentile paid a dinar in advance, so he acquired the wine with money.
A sage objects that the latter clause should then be permitted or forbidden for the same reason.
Rav Ashi turns the question back: on your view, why the distinction between the two clauses?
Rav Ashi explains the distinction: a fixed price makes the gentile rely on the sale, so acquisition completes.
Ravina objects with a baraita on a gentile executed for stealing under a peruta, which seems to contradict Rav Ashi.
Replies that the gentile is executed for causing the Jew distress, even without legal acquisition.

72a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what not subject to restitution means, and whether the second thief should then be liable to execution.
Concludes that pulling acquires from a gentile, since both thieves commit legally significant theft.
Narrates a land agreement: a man promised to sell to one buyer, then sold to another; Rav Yosef holds the first acquired it.
Abaye objects: no price was fixed, so no acquisition, citing the mishna on selling wine to a gentile.
Asks what the halakhic conclusion is, and whether libation wine's stringency makes that mishna unrepresentative.
Cites a baraita on a donkey-laden produce purchase, where acquisition depends on whether the price was fixed.
Narrates a similar land case with a higher price; Rav Kahana holds the first buyer acquired it.
Rav Yaakov of Nehar Pekod objects: the extra twenty dinars forced the seller to sell to the second buyer.
Rules that the halakha follows Rav Yaakov, and sets out how many assessors bind a seller who fixed the price.
Narrates an assessment dispute; Rav Pappa rules the buyer may prevent the price until more proficient assessors judge.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua objects: why assume the other assessors are more proficient?
Rules that the halakha follows Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua.
Mishna: a funnel used for a gentile's jug leaves a residue that makes wine in a Jew's jug forbidden.
Cites a mishna on which liquids connect for impurity; a stream and inclined water do not, but a pond does.
Rav Huna rules that a stream and inclined water do connect with regard to libation wine.
Rav Nahman asks Rav Huna where he derives this from.
Rav Nahman argues the mishna's inference cannot support the claim, since its two clauses contradict each other.
Turns to the funnel mishna as a proof for Rav Huna's view on residue connecting wine.

72b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks how the remnant in the funnel becomes forbidden, and whether the stream itself must connect the vessels.
Rabbi Hiyya explains the mishna covers wine that rose to the funnel; the stream question stays unresolved.
Cites the mishna's second case: the stream between two vessels is forbidden, so a stream connects.
Objects that if the stream connects, the wine in the vessel being poured from should be forbidden too.
Rejects the proof: the mishna's two clauses conflict on the stream, so nothing can be inferred.
Cites a baraita on pouring from a barrel into a cistern; Rav Sheshet reads it as a gentile's force moving the stream.
Objects that if a gentile moves the barrel, the wine inside it is forbidden as well.
Replies that a gentile's force is forbidden only by rabbinic decree, which covers poured-out wine but not wine still in the barrel.
Relates how Rav Hisda and Rava instructed wine pourers to avoid steady streams and keep gentiles from helping.
Narrates a case where a gentile touched a siphon tube, and Rava forbids all the wine in the barrel.
Rav Pappa asks by what mechanism the wine was forbidden, and whether that shows a stream connects.
Rava rejects the inference: the wine is drawn to both tubes, so it is as if the gentile touched all of it.
Mar Zutra permits a Jew and gentile to drink from a shared tube vessel if the Jew stops first; Rabba bar Rav Huna permits it too.

73a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Reports that some say Rabba bar Rav Huna himself drank from a kenishkanin, a shared multi-tube vessel.
Mishna: libation wine renders any mixture forbidden, while flavor-based mixing with other liquids requires imparting taste.
Rav Dimi reports Rabbi Yohanan: libation wine poured little by little into a cistern is nullified and permitted.
Objects with the mishna: if any amount forbids, the forbidden must fall into the permitted, contradicting Rav Dimi.
Objects with the mishna's second case, that wine in water forbids only when it imparts flavor, against Rav Dimi.
Answers that the mishna means permitted wine falling into forbidden water, so no contradiction arises.
Argues the mishna's latter clause also treats forbidden water, which would still conflict with Rav Dimi.
Replies that Rav Dimi can read the whole mishna as permitted falling into forbidden, one clause each way.
Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef reports Rabbi Yohanan: libation wine from a small canteen is nullified, but not from a large barrel.
Ravin reports Rabbi Yohanan: a pitcher of water falling in first nullifies libation wine, which is treated as nonexistent.
Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda reports the limit: only if water fell in first; otherwise the libation wine makes the cistern wine forbidden.
Reports the same halakha applied to the mishna itself: water that fell in nullifies the forbidden wine.
Asks what difference it makes whether the teaching is about the mishna or about Ravin's statement.
Explains that the mishna version needs no prior water fall, while Ravin's version requires water to fall in first.
States the case: libation wine fell into a wine cistern and a pitcher of water fell there as well.

73b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Hizkiyya holds forbidden wine added last forbids the mixture; Rabbi Yohanan holds even then the mixture is permitted.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether Hizkiyya and Rabbi Yohanan dispute the Eliezer versus Sages question about leaven.
Cites an Orla mishna on teruma leaven and non-sacred leaven combining in dough, with Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages disagreeing.
Asks how this can be the same dispute, citing Abaye's reading of Rabbi Eliezer, which conflicts with the attribution.
Resolves it: Hizkiyya and Rabbi Yohanan disagree about whether the same-type permitted liquid is disregarded.
Asks whether Rabbi Yohanan disregards same-type permitted liquid, citing Rabbi Asi's unresolved question about two cups.
Explains Rabbi Yohanan ultimately resolved it: same-type permitted wine is disregarded, and the water nullifies the teruma wine.
States the principle: same-type contact forbids any amount, while different-type contact forbids only if it imparts flavor.
Rav and Shmuel hold this principle applies to all Torah-forbidden foods, same-type or different-type alike.
Asks what the mishna's general principle adds, if Rav and Shmuel already state it.
Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish hold the principle for all Torah prohibitions, except untithed produce and libation wine.
Explains that the general principle is stated to include untithed produce, which the mishna does not name.
A baraita is cited in accordance with the view of Rav and Shmuel.
A second baraita is cited in accordance with the view of Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish.
Asks why untithed produce and libation wine are stricter than other forbidden foods.
Answers that untithed produce's forbidden status mirrors its permitted status, as Shmuel's teruma-grain example shows.
Cites a baraita limiting the same-type stringency for untithed produce to mixing with its own type.

74a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna lists items forbidden in themselves that forbid any mixture they join, such as libation wine and idols.
Asks by what criterion the tanna lists these items, and why he omits the carcass cuts and Passover leaven.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba says the tanna uses two criteria: items that are counted and items whose benefit is prohibited.
Objects that the tanna should then list perekh nuts and Badan pomegranates, which meet both criteria.
Replies that the Orla mishna already lists those fruits, so they need not be repeated here.
Suggests the tanna should list a homeowner's loaves for the Passover leaven prohibition.
Says Rabbi Akiva holds that a homeowner's loaves are not nullified, as the Orla mishna states.
Asks what the mishna's restated rule is meant to exclude.
Answers that it excludes counted items not prohibited in benefit, or prohibited-benefit items that are not counted.
Mishna: benefit from wine used for a libation that fell into a cistern is forbidden, but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits selling it.
Amoraic rulings on whether Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view applies to wine mixed with wine, from Rav, Shmuel and others.
Rav Naḥman's practical ruling: forbid wine mixed with libation wine, but permit barrels and nondescript wine in mixtures.

74b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a stone press lined with pitch by a gentile may be cleansed; wooden presses also cleansed, earthenware ones forbidden.
Rava rules the cleansing requirement applies only when the gentile lined the press with pitch, not when he merely trod grapes in it.
Asks whether this is obvious, since the mishna itself speaks only of lining with pitch.
Explains the mishna teaches the usual case, so Rava needed to state that trodding alone is not covered.
Reports a variant version of Rava's ruling, stating the same limit on cleansing a press lined with pitch.
Asks again whether this is obvious from the mishna.
Gives the same explanation: the mishna describes the usual case, so Rava clarifies the limit.
Restates the variant ruling: cleansing suffices only when the press was lined with pitch, not when trodden.
Narrates how Rav, sent by Rabbi Hiyya, inspected a purchased press and found wine in a crack, requiring peeling.
Cites a baraita: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi permits cleansing a gentile's press and its utensils, while the Sages forbid them.
Objects that the mishna permits a pitch-lined stone press after cleansing, which seems to conflict with the baraita.
Restates the baraita's position on the press, ladle and funnel as the Master's earlier teaching.
Objects that the mishna forbids earthenware presses even after peeling, which conflicts with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view.
Rava replies that the mishna's last clause reflects the Rabbis' opinion.
Rava scalds or seals gentile-used vessels, holding the Sages decreed prohibition even for temporary storage.
Asks how one cleanses a press or gentile utensils used for wine.
Rav says cleanse with water; Rabba bar bar Hana says with ashes; the Gemara considers whether each excludes the other.

75a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav says cleanse with water first then ashes; Rabba bar bar Hana says ashes first then water.
Reconciles the two: the first applies to a damp press, the second to a dry press.
Reports the Sura version of the dispute on the number of cleansing stages for damp and dry presses, per Rav and Shmuel.
Reports the Pumbedita version of the same dispute, with different stage counts for Rav and Shmuel.
Reconciles the Pumbedita version: Shmuel counts the final water rinse, while Rav does not.
Students ask Rabbi Abbahu how to cleanse gentile wicker nets used for treading grapes.
Rabbi Abbahu answers from a baraita on cleansing presses, planks, and baskets, with timing for each material.
Asks whether Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view is the same as the first tanna's.
Answers the difference concerns early-ripening and late-ripening grapes.
Cites the continuing baraita: Rabbi Yosei's quick cleansing methods and the rule that purity follows libation-wine practice.
Asks whether the baraita should be emended, and how long the interval between cleansings must be.
Reports Rabbi Yohanan's view on the interval, either a day or a night, or half a day and half a night.
Reconciles the two views by season: a full day or night at equinox, half and half at solstice.
Rav Yehuda sets cleansing rules for gentile straining bags and baskets by their material, such as hair, wool, flax, and palm.

75b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rules that plaited pitch-covered straining bags are cleansed with ashes and water, flax ones left dormant, and knots undone.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Hiyya dispute whether an am ha'aretz touching a cluster in a wine press makes the whole press impure.
Asks why the wine press differs from the creeping-animal mishna, where liquid flow makes the whole mill impure.
Explains the difference: grape clusters interrupt the flow of wine, so there is no continuous connection.
The Sages told Rabbi Yirmeya, or his son, to follow the view that only the cluster and its surroundings are impure.
Mishna: how to prepare gentile cooking utensils by immersion, purging in boiling water, or heating white-hot, with knives merely polished.
Derives from a verse on Midianite spoils that utensils need immersion in forty se'a, with bar Kappara adding a second source.
Asks what the verse's mention of nidda water adds, if sprinkling is not required.
Explains both verse phrases are needed: one shows the forty se'a requirement, the other shows no waiting until sunset.
Rav Naḥman, citing Rabba bar Avuh, extends immersion to new utensils bought from gentiles, since old ones are similar.
Rav Sheshet objects: then even scissors for cutting cloth would need immersion.
Rav Naḥman replies that only meal utensils are mentioned in the verse, so only those need immersion.
Rabba bar Avuh adds that the requirement applies only to purchased utensils, not to borrowed ones.
A purchased marda utensil is immersed by Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef, but Rabbi Yohanan's ruling limits immersion to metal utensils.
Rav Ashi extends immersion to glass that can be remelted; the halakha follows the utensil's final state for lead-glazed ware.
Raises a dilemma: must a Jew immerse a gentile utensil received as collateral?
Mar bar Rav Ashi reports his father immersed a silver goblet held as collateral and drank from it.
Asks whether the father's action reflected collateral as a purchase, or the gentile's intent to leave it.
The Sages list how to prepare purchased utensils by use: cold, hot, or fire, with immersion after cleaning.
Two baraitas conflict on whether food cooked in utensils used before preparation is forbidden or permitted.
Resolves the conflict by two views on whether flavor that is detrimental to a mixture makes it forbidden.
Asks how gentile utensils that need purging could exist if a detrimental flavor is not forbidden.
Rav Hiyya bar Rav Huna answers that the Torah forbids only a pot, meaning the cooking vessel itself.

76a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A pot used by a gentile the same day does not impart flavor to the detriment of food cooked in it.
Asks whether the pot should then be permitted from the next day onward.
Answers that a rabbinic decree forbids pots not used by a gentile the same day, lest one use same-day pots.
Argues from the other tanna that a forbidden flavor to the detriment of permitted food still forbids it.
Rav Amram raises a contradiction: a mishna requires heating spits white-hot, but a sacrificial-meat mishna requires only purging.
Rav Sheshet replies that sacrificial utensils absorbed permitted food, while gentile utensils absorbed forbidden food.
Rava objects that sacrificial meat also emits forbidden flavor, so the distinction fails.
Rava proposes that purging for sacrificial utensils also requires rinsing and scouring, per the Leviticus verse.
Abaye objects that rinsing and scouring are cold-water acts, unlike purging, so Rava's reading fails.
Abaye proposes the mishnas complement each other: each states one requirement that applies to the other too.
Rava objects that complementing works only if one mishna states all the requirements in one place.
Rava explains sacrificial utensils need no white-hot heating, since each day's use purges the previous day's taste.
Objects that this works for peace-offerings but not sin-offerings, whose meat is eaten only a day and night.
Sages reply that cooking a peace-offering in the same utensil on the same day expels the sin-offering taste.
Objects that if daily use purges, boiling-water purging should be unnecessary, which challenges Rava.
Rav Pappa and Rav Ashi offer resolutions: crusting from disuse, and the forbidden flavor being absent in substance.
Asks how much one must heat utensils to make them white-hot.
Rabbi Mani says heat until the outer layer sheds.
Asks how one purges utensils with boiling water.
Rav Huna says one immerses a small kettle inside a large kettle of boiling water.
Asks what is done with a large kettle.
Cites an incident involving a cauldron in Rav Akavya's house that required purging, as a practical case.

ranges.en: Describes a pot with a dough rim, filled with water and boiled so the water boils along the rim.
Rava praises Rav Akavya as clever and states his view that a rim expels what it absorbs, drop by drop.
The mishna's ruling: a knife is polished and thereby becomes pure.
Rav Ukva bar Hama requires thrusting the knife ten times into the ground.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua limits the ground requirement to untilled, hard earth.
Rav Kahana explains that the rule applies to a good knife with no notches, so it scrapes the ground fully.
A baraita is cited in support: a notch-free knife may be thrust ten times into the ground.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua rules that this suffices for eating cold food with the knife.
Introduces the incident of Mar Yehuda and Bati bar Tuvi before King Shapur, and an etrog is served.
King Shapur cuts and eats, gives Bati a slice after stabbing the ground ten times, and makes Mar Yehuda wait.
Shapur then gives the slice to Mar Yehuda.
Bati bar Tuvi challenges Mar Yehuda's kashrut by claiming that the man is not a Jew.
King Shapur upholds Mar Yehuda as certain to be meticulous, while doubting Bati bar Tuvi.
Some explain the king's remark as a reminder of what Mar Yehuda did the previous night.
Closing formula: the chapter Ha-Sochair concludes, and the tractate Avodah Zarah ends.
